Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-2,3)$ to the point $(0,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2t-2,\,3-3t⟩.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-2,3)$ and $(0,0).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-2+t(0-(-2))),\,(3+t(0-3))⟩ \\  & =⟨2t-2,\,3-3t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-2)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2t-2)^{2}(3-3t) \\  & =4(t-1)^{2}\cdot 3(1-t) \\  & =-12(t-1)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-12(t-1)^{3}\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & =-24{\int }_{0}^{1}(t-1)^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d86ee8d9-aeae-5ab1-b4a0-98c765570dca"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "![](images/f5/f5f5b235b54d2acd20297ab365d9b93907111b3fec9a86776c28e93fdfe105ee.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(2,3),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2t,\,3t⟩.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(0,0)$ and $(2,3).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(0+t(2-0)),\,(0+t(3-0))⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,3t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2t)^{2}+(3t)^{2} \\  & =4{t}^{2}+9{t}^{2} \\  & =13{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}13{t}^{2}\cdot 3\,\text{d}t \\  & =39{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2c3bc565-6668-5708-9572-740391604ada"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Evaluate ${\int }_{C}({y}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(2,3),$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(0,1)$ and $(2,3).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(0+t(2-0)),\,(1+t(3-1))⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,1+2t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={y}^{2}-2x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(1+2t)^{2}-2(2t) \\  & =1+4t+4{t}^{2}-4t \\  & =4{t}^{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+1)\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{[\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}+t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2(\frac{4}{3}+1)-2(0) \\  & =\frac{14}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8b9c47c5-4e96-58fa-ac91-5791dc11f30c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8b9c47c5-4e96-58fa-ac91-5791dc11f30c" :answer-field/id #uuid "8b9c47c5-4e96-58fa-ac91-5791dc11f30c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-6029d8a7-a6ae-5959-9ee4-f8e3ebd8e072" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c94fc212-35ff-5e38-9f57-12d4f4959a4c" "answer-6029d8a7-a6ae-5959-9ee4-f8e3ebd8e072" "answer-21702398-6680-552d-923f-027dff95a35a" "answer-ea8f272e-677d-5489-96d8-1e29db88e990" "answer-78ae96ca-4942-5362-807b-c0b65d2496c2"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c94fc212-35ff-5e38-9f57-12d4f4959a4c" :answer/id #uuid "c94fc212-35ff-5e38-9f57-12d4f4959a4c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{11}{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6029d8a7-a6ae-5959-9ee4-f8e3ebd8e072" :answer/id #uuid "6029d8a7-a6ae-5959-9ee4-f8e3ebd8e072" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{14}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-21702398-6680-552d-923f-027dff95a35a" :answer/id #uuid "21702398-6680-552d-923f-027dff95a35a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ea8f272e-677d-5489-96d8-1e29db88e990" :answer/id #uuid "ea8f272e-677d-5489-96d8-1e29db88e990" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-78ae96ca-4942-5362-807b-c0b65d2496c2" :answer/id #uuid "78ae96ca-4942-5362-807b-c0b65d2496c2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7}{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135122 :tutorial/content "Until now, we've been dealing with line integrals with respect to arc length. In this lesson, we will learn about other types of line integral. 

Suppose that $C$ is a path in the $xy$-plane with initial point $A$ and terminal point $B.$ The line integral of the function $f(x,y)$ **with respect to $\boldsymbol x$** along the path $C$ is denoted

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d x.
$$

To understand what this integral represents, we imagine traversing $C$ from $A$ to $B.$ At each point $P$ that lies on $C,$ we project the point on $f$ that lies directly above $P$ onto the plane $y=0.$ Doing this for every point on $C$ traces out a curve. The line integral of $f$ with respect to $x$ gives the (signed) area bounded by this curve and the $x$-axis.

![](images/62/62c07a36cbf79459021ee7be125536a8f9c1bc3c193a99eabfcd3fc851b8eb0c.png)

To calculate a line integral with respect to $x,$ we must first parameterize $C$ using a parameter $t\in [a,b].$ Then, we apply the change of variables formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}x  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Let's take a look at a concrete example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133995 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162107 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c60b1a3b-1eee-5254-929b-6a532b619fd6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-c60b1a3b-1eee-5254-929b-6a532b619fd6" :question/id #uuid "c60b1a3b-1eee-5254-929b-6a532b619fd6" :question/math-academy-id "q-143431" :question/problem "A sample ${X}_{1},{X}_{2}$ of two pineapples is drawn from a population. The population has pineapples of two different weights, $1\,\text{kg}$ and $1.5\,\text{kg},$ distributed in the ratio $1:4.$ Calculate the standard error of $\overset{―}{X}.$ Round your answer to two decimal places." :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population variance ${\sigma }^{2},$ then

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We're told that the pineapples in the population have weights $1\,\text{kg}$ and $\text{1.5}\,\text{kg},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $1:4.$ Therefore, to compute the population's mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $1+4=5$ pineapples only with the following weights:

$$
1\,\text{kg},\,1.5\,\text{kg},\,1.5\,\text{kg},\,1.5\,\text{kg},\,1.5\,\text{kg}.
$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1+4\cdot 1.5) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1+6) \\  & =\frac{7}{5} \\  & =1.4\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

and the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}({1}^{2}+4\cdot {1.5}^{2})-{1.4}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(10)-1.96 \\  & =2-1.96 \\  & =0.04\,{\text{kg}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the sample size is $n=2,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}=\frac{0.04}{2}=0.02\,{\text{kg}}^{2}.
$$

Finally,

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{0.02}≈0.14\,\text{kg}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-784c4051-09fc-584b-bc9b-b914c96abf6f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Find the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 6 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

If $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ then what is the value of ${x}_{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "Remember, the order of the vectors in a basis is important.

Notice that 

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}={{(\,6\,)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{{(\,-3\,)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}}
$$

which means that

$$
x=6\cdot {b}_{1}+(-3)\cdot {b}_{2}
$$

and therefore

$$
[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we have that ${x}_{2}=-3.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7bb29f16-8d05-55d0-ab1d-19d482085ecc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} I. $PQ⊙R$

II. $PQ⊙{R}^{T}$

III. $(PQ)^{T}⊙R$" :question/worked-solution "The Hadamard product of two matrices (or vectors) is only defined if they have the same dimensions.

Let's consider each expression in turn:

- The dimensions of $PQ$ are $2\times 7,$ and the dimensions of $R$ are $7\times 2.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression I is *not* well-defined.

- The dimensions of $PQ$ are $2\times 7,$ and the dimensions of ${R}^{T}$ are $2\times 7.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression II is well-defined.

- The dimensions of $(PQ)^{T}$ are $7\times 2,$ and the dimensions of $R$ are $7\times 2.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression III is well-defined.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-06b8bf76-c702-59e2-a003-890dc8fb5ea1"] :db/ensure - $P(x):$ $x\in (0,2).$

- $Q(x):$ $|x|<2.$

Then, our initial sentence can be written as $P(x)⇒Q(x),$ which is logically equivalent to 

$$
¬P(x)∨Q(x).
$$

The negation of $P(x)$ can be written as

- $¬P(x):$ $x\notin (0,2).$

Therefore, the given sentence is logically equivalent to the following:

:question/problem "Calculate $\int \frac{9x-38}{(4-x)^{2}(2-x)}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{9x-38}{(4-x)^{2}(2-x)}=\frac{A}{(4-x)}+\frac{B}{(4-x)^{2}}+\frac{C}{(2-x)}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(4-x)^{2}(2-x)$ and get

$$
9x-38=A(4-x)(2-x)+B(2-x)+C(4-x)^{2}.
$$

Plugging in $x=4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $C$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9(4)-38 & =A(4-4)(2-4)+B(2-4)+C(4-4)^{2} \\ 36-38 & =B(-2) \\ B & =\frac{-2}{-2} \\ B & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=2,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9(2)-38 & =A(4-2)(2-2)+B(2-2)+C(4-2)^{2} \\ 18-38 & =C{(2)}^{2} \\ C & =\frac{-20}{4} \\ C & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known values of $B$ and $C,$ we can solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9(0)-38 & =A(4-0)(2-0)+B(2-0)+C(4-0)^{2} \\ -38 & =8A+2B+16C \\ -38 & =8A+2(1)+16(-5) \\ -38 & =8A-78 \\ 8A & =78-38 \\ A & =\frac{40}{8} \\ A & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{9x-38}{(4-x)^{2}(2-x)}=\frac{5}{(4-x)}+\frac{1}{(4-x)^{2}}-\frac{5}{(2-x)}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9x-38}{(4-x)^{2}(2-x)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{5}{(4-x)}+\frac{1}{(4-x)^{2}}-\frac{5}{(2-x)})\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \frac{1}{4-x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{(4-x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x-5\int \frac{1}{2-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-5\operatorname{ln}⁡|4-x|+\frac{1}{4-x}+5\operatorname{ln}⁡|2-x|+K,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K$ is an integral constant." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a1fdb08d-4e9a-5aa1-bf2f-9d236664e6fc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} :question/problem "Find the equation of the tangent line to the polar curve $r=1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ at $\theta =\pi ,$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "To find the equation of the tangent line to a polar curve at a point $P,$ we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi } \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )}{-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )} \\  & =\frac{-1-2\cdot 0}{-0-2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{-1}{-2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (-1) \\  & =-1 \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi  \\  & =(1-0)\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(-1,0).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the tangent:

We find the equation of the tangent as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (x-(-1)) \\ y-0 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (x+1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

*Hint: Try to factor the denominator first.*" :question/worked-solution "First, factoring the denominator and using partial fractions, we can write the series as

$$
\frac{1}{{n}^{2}+5n+6}=\frac{1}{(n+2)(n+3)}=\frac{1}{n+2}-\frac{1}{n+3}.
$$

So, our series can be written as

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{1}{n+2}-\frac{1}{n+3}).
$$

Let's now compute the first few partial sums:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{1} & =(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}) \\ {s}_{2} & =(\frac{1}{3}-\cancel{\frac{1}{4}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{4}}-\frac{1}{5}) \\ {s}_{3} & =(\frac{1}{3}-\cancel{\frac{1}{4}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{4}}-\cancel{\frac{1}{5}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{5}}-\frac{1}{6}) \\ {s}_{4} & =(\frac{1}{3}-\cancel{\frac{1}{4}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{4}}-\cancel{\frac{1}{5}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{5}}-\cancel{\frac{1}{6}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{6}}-\frac{1}{7})\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that for each partial sum, we always end up canceling all terms except for the first and last terms. Therefore, the $N$th partial sum is

$$
{s}_{N}=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{N+3}.
$$

Finally, we can determine the sum of the series by taking the limit of ${s}_{N}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(n+2)(n+3)} & ={lim}_{N\to \infty }{s}_{N} \\  & ={lim}_{N\to \infty }(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{N+3}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186099909 :answer-field/correct 17592186099914 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id $u={x}^{2}-1.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,x\text{d}x=\frac{\text{d}u}{2}.
$$

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $1$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $0$ | $3$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}x\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3})|}_{0}^{3} \\  & ={\frac{{u}^{3/2}}{3}|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{{3}^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{{0}^{3/2}}{3} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-eb85d00d-c4fb-5b35-911e-a717db9a9969"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Find its average position between $2$ and $6$ seconds." :question/worked-solution "To calculate the average value of the position on $[{t}_{1},{t}_{2}],$ we use the average value formula

$$
{x}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{{t}_{2}-{t}_{1}}\,{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{6-2}\,{\int }_{2}^{6}2{e}^{t/2}\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {2\cdot 2({e}^{t/2})|}_{2}^{6} \\  & ={e}^{6/2}-{e}^{2/2} \\  & ={e}^{3}-e.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average position is $({e}^{3}-e)\,\text{m}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8eb043c2-db7d-5e14-932d-20ffb968ecb7"] :db/ensure Which integral gives the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?" :question/worked-solution "The volume of the solid generated when the region bounded by a curve $x=g(y),$ the $y$-axis, and the horizontal lines $y=c$ and $y=d$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
V=\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}[g(y)]^{2}\text{d}y.
$$

First, we write our equation in terms of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{x+2} \\ {y}^{2} & =x+2 \\ x & ={y}^{2}-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, in our example, $g(y)={y}^{2}-2$ and the limits of integration are from $y=2$ to $y=3.$

Finally, the volume can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}{[g(y)]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{3}{({y}^{2}-2)}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{3}({y}^{4}-4{y}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-315a9bb0-48e8-569d-b07b-4a5644ec8264"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ {y}^{4} & ={y}^{2} \\ {y}^{4}-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ {y}^{2}({y}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ {y}^{2}(y-1)(y+1) & =0 \\ y & =-1,0,1\end{aligned}
$$

The area we want consists of two regions: ${A}_{1}$ and ${A}_{2}.$

![](images/8b/8b4cbf07b9c2a6d949a58f39489889d2a3fdd4690664e530386f6f61d9aac5fd.png)

- For the area ${A}_{1},$ we have $y\in [-1,0],$ and the right function is $g(y)$ while the left function is $f(y).$ So, the area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(g(y)-f(y))\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}({y}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the area ${A}_{2},$ we have $y\in [0,1],$ and the right function is $g(y)$ while the left function is $f(y).$ So, the area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(g(y)-f(y))\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}={\int }_{-1}^{0}({y}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bfc1653c-6513-5ab7-95f5-3af895b0238c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "![](images/d4/d4bcdb6515b262c070c7ed689263efbbde8a350ad6a28b4fc106de281e69ff46.png)

Find the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=2t,\,y=t\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [0,\pi ].$" :question/worked-solution "The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\ge 0$ for all $t\in [0,\pi ].$

To solve the above integral, we use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡t & ⇒ & v=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =2t(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-2(\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -0\operatorname{cos}⁡0)+2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =-2\pi (-1) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9aa35e99-bfe0-504f-b448-591e82ea534a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =2{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x){|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡0-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2a)) \\  & =0-(-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e62dccaf-73d1-5442-9e53-eebdcd332113"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id \frac{{tanh}^{2}⁡(3x-2)}{3}\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the secant-tangent identity 

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the hyperbolic secant-tangent identity:

$$
1-{tanh}^{2}⁡\theta ={sech}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

Setting $\theta =3x-2,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{tanh}^{2}⁡(3x-2) & ={sech}^{2}⁡(3x-2) \\ {tanh}^{2}⁡(3x-2) & =1-{sech}^{2}⁡(3x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{tanh}^{2}⁡(3x-2)}{3}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int (1-{sech}^{2}⁡(3x-2))\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int 1\cdot \text{d}x-\frac{1}{3}\int {sech}^{2}⁡(3x-2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{x}{3}-\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{tanh}⁡(3x-2)+C.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-faa2ee71-4e17-514a-a333-0d36f72cde02"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "![](images/31/31d4236bf58cd579c49c7259c32a2a9171e07c771b4c34040ac92896809f695f.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x=\frac{2}{y}$ and $x=3-y$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=-2.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?" :question/worked-solution "First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{y} & =3-y \\ 2 & =3y-{y}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-3y+2 & =0 \\ (y-1)(y-2) & =0 \\ y & =1,2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $y=1$ to $y=2.$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](images/b7/b73c341f4d09b1df7bea162bc7dbe10d0ee60920c847f9c24210386a3d139e61.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=\frac{2}{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=3-y.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=3-y.$

![](images/c8/c8c8e766c66e47a54f316f54893d603b245acec8f529da3a5033d2bba547a319.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(3-y)-(-2)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[5-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=\frac{2}{y}.$

![](images/1b/1b31331f1c0da353bee6fe29d10e9e58dd531cbc8152cbce214d1adea771b032.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[\,(\frac{2}{y})-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[\frac{2}{y}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[5-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[\frac{2}{y}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({[5-y]}^{2}-{[\frac{2}{y}+2]}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-24a6b34c-6b2b-59cf-97a5-55f1d3c4912c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id #uuid "8deca7b4-0aaf-504b-958b-1e6e90c74a93" :question/math-academy-id "q-79877" :question/problem "![](images/49/49b119b378ac4f45c0c395ca77c5cefead3a7c811295b51ac8eaa8aef7100e25.png)

The base of a solid is the region enclosed by the curves $y=1-{x}^{2}$ and $y=-1,$  as shown in the picture. Cross-sections perpendicular to the $x$-axis are rectangles. If the height of each rectangle is $2$ times the length of its base, which integral gives the volume of the solid?" :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)=1-{x}^{2}$ and $g(x)=-1.$

First, we determine the limits of integration. To do that, we find the intersections of the two curves by setting the functions equal to one another and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =g(x) \\ 1-{x}^{2} & =-1 \\ {x}^{2} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the limit of integration are $x=-\sqrt{2}$ and $x=\sqrt{2}.$

Now, consider a cross-section at some point $x$, where $x\in (-\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2})$,  and its projection on the $xy$-plane: 

![](images/0c/0c2a676ecc781a2a7a78870eb93ee9fbe5a89a7bd754a446231c6e3237f75831.png)

The base of the cross-section is

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =|f(x)-g(x)| \\  & =|1-{x}^{2}-(-1)| \\  & =|2-{x}^{2}|.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of a rectangle is
$A=bh.$
  So, since we have $h=2b,$ the expression for the area of the cross-section is

$$
\begin{aligned}A(x) & =bh \\  & =2{b}^{2} \\  & =2{(2-{x}^{2})}^{2} \\  & =8-8{x}^{2}+2{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now calculate the volume of the solid, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={\int }_{c}^{d}A(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}(8-8{x}^{2}+2{x}^{4})\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-aeff073f-a16e-5f3f-a31e-6729474c2b63"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Let $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ and let ${P}_{3}(x)$ be the third-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=1.$ Use the Lagrange error bound to find an upper bound for the error when ${P}_{3}(x)$ is used to approximate $\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$" :question/worked-solution "The Lagrange error bound states that an upper bound for the error ${R}_{3}$ obtained when using the third-degree Taylor polynomial ${P}_{3}$ to approximate $f(x)$ is given by

$$
|{R}_{3}|\le \frac{M}{4!}|x-1{|}^{4},
$$

where $M$ is the maximum value of $|{f}^{(4)}(x)|$ on the interval between $a=1$ and $x=2.$ 

Plugging $x=2$ into the above formula gives

$$
\begin{aligned}|{R}_{3}| & \le \frac{M}{4!}|2-1{|}^{4} \\ |{R}_{3}| & \le \frac{M}{24}|1{|}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find $M,$ we need to compute $|{f}^{(4)}(x)|$ and then maximize it on the interval $[1,2].$ Taking the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{2}{{x}^{3}} \\ {f}^{(4)}(x) & =-\frac{6}{{x}^{4}} \\ |{f}^{(4)}(x)| & =|-\frac{6}{{x}^{4}}|=\frac{6}{{x}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $|{f}^{(4)}(x)|=\frac{6}{{x}^{4}}$ is a decreasing function in the interval $[1,2],$  its value is greatest at $x=1.$ So

$$
M=|{f}^{(4)}(1)|=\frac{6}{(1)^{4}}=6,
$$

and therefore, the upper bound is

$$
|{R}_{3}|\le \frac{6}{24}|1{|}^{4}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3dee6e17-9565-5642-81b9-7791c50bb056"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨4{e}^{2t},\,9{e}^{3t}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(1,1)$ and has velocity $⟨2,4⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨4{e}^{2t},\,9{e}^{3t}⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 4{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t,\int 9{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{2t}+{C}_{1},\,3{e}^{3t}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨2,4⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨2{e}^{2(0)}+{C}_{1},\,3{e}^{3(0)}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨2,4⟩ & =⟨2+{C}_{1},3+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=1.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v(t)=⟨2{e}^{2t},\,3{e}^{3t}+1⟩.
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2{e}^{2t},\,3{e}^{3t}+1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t,\int (3{e}^{3t}+1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{2t}+{C}_{3},\,{e}^{3t}+t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨1,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{e}^{2(0)}+{C}_{3},\,{e}^{3(0)}+0+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨1,1⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{3},\,1+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}={C}_{4}=0.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
r(t)=⟨{e}^{2t},\,{e}^{3t}+t⟩.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6c828a93-5ad8-5389-8e1d-dff274396206"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-ea94a739-28fe-50a1-b5d4-4f34307441cf" :question/id #uuid "ea94a739-28fe-50a1-b5d4-4f34307441cf" :question/math-academy-id "q-83878" :question/problem "The rate of growth in the frog population $P(t)$ in a certain lake follows the logistic growth model

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=0.1P(5\,000-P),
$$

where $t$ is the time, in years. Find an expression for the frog population after $t$ years, given that there were $100$ frogs initially." :question/worked-solution "A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

The general solution to the logistic growth equation is

$$
P(t)=\frac{a}{1+C{e}^{-akt}}.
$$

In this case, the constant of proportionality is $k=0.1,$ and the carrying capacity is $a=5\,000.$ 

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
P(t)=\frac{5\,000}{1+C{e}^{-(5\,000\cdot 0.1)t}}=\frac{5\,000}{1+C{e}^{-500t}}.
$$

We now substitute the initial condition $P(0)=100$ and solve for $C.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5\,000}{1+C{e}^{-500\cdot 0}} & =100 \\ 1+C & =\frac{5\,000}{100} \\ C & =50-1 \\  & =49.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
P(t)=\frac{5\,000}{1+49{e}^{-500t}}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-93650186-de97-555d-ac5a-338706314d50"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$

$$

D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le y\le z,\,2\le z\le 3\}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-y-z}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{4}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA & ={\int }_{2}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{z}[{\int }_{-y-z}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{4}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dy\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{z}{\int }_{-y-z}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{4}}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=-2+z=z-2.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-62838ed0-438a-5299-a107-f9a335821ea7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-62838ed0-438a-5299-a107-f9a335821ea7" :answer-field/id #uuid "62838ed0-438a-5299-a107-f9a335821ea7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-56d0d569-69e7-5401-aef9-9822b9b489fc" :answer-field/choices ["answer-6c807fef-55cf-5829-b452-0803cc158708" "answer-213676f8-b331-59a5-91dc-1bbb59780c3b" "answer-56d0d569-69e7-5401-aef9-9822b9b489fc" "answer-2576b112-e737-588e-bcf0-2d79e0be3dd1" "answer-b328e717-67f5-5280-9783-f298a5c3a64b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6c807fef-55cf-5829-b452-0803cc158708" :answer/id #uuid "6c807fef-55cf-5829-b452-0803cc158708" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-213676f8-b331-59a5-91dc-1bbb59780c3b" :answer/id #uuid "213676f8-b331-59a5-91dc-1bbb59780c3b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "z+3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-56d0d569-69e7-5401-aef9-9822b9b489fc" :answer/id #uuid "56d0d569-69e7-5401-aef9-9822b9b489fc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "z-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2576b112-e737-588e-bcf0-2d79e0be3dd1" :answer/id #uuid "2576b112-e737-588e-bcf0-2d79e0be3dd1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{y}^{2}+{z}^{4}+y+z" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b328e717-67f5-5280-9783-f298a5c3a64b" :answer/id #uuid "b328e717-67f5-5280-9783-f298a5c3a64b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{y}^{2}+{z}^{4}-y-z" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134128 :question/problem "Evaluate the mixed integral

where the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane is given by

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$

where the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane is given by

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{1}{2},\,0\le z\le y\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$

$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}24y-24{y}^{2}-24yz\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}{\int }_{0}^{y}24(y-{y}^{2})-24yz\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}24(y-{y}^{2})[z]_{z=0}^{z=y}-12y[{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}24(y-{y}^{2})y-12{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}24{y}^{2}-36{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[8{y}^{3}-9{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=1/2} \\  & =8(\frac{1}{8}-0)-9(\frac{1}{16}-0) \\  & =\frac{7}{16}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5e440dfe-c51c-5a5e-a6b4-025b490904aa"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-5e440dfe-c51c-5a5e-a6b4-025b490904aa" :answer-field/id #uuid "5e440dfe-c51c-5a5e-a6b4-025b490904aa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-85994e10-7a1c-5399-818a-6d0eb148e72c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-390a0a3f-8045-51e4-9e9a-3692b030cba3" "answer-72cceeab-ae35-5169-ba9f-38c49406c64d" "answer-a03f33e4-9c17-5d89-ba8f-89c5877bca3b" "answer-45156b6e-6526-56b2-a152-2e340488d5e1" "answer-85994e10-7a1c-5399-818a-6d0eb148e72c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-390a0a3f-8045-51e4-9e9a-3692b030cba3" :answer/id #uuid "390a0a3f-8045-51e4-9e9a-3692b030cba3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{11}{24}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-72cceeab-ae35-5169-ba9f-38c49406c64d" :answer/id #uuid "72cceeab-ae35-5169-ba9f-38c49406c64d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a03f33e4-9c17-5d89-ba8f-89c5877bca3b" :answer/id #uuid "a03f33e4-9c17-5d89-ba8f-89c5877bca3b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{12}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-45156b6e-6526-56b2-a152-2e340488d5e1" :answer/id #uuid "45156b6e-6526-56b2-a152-2e340488d5e1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{8}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-85994e10-7a1c-5399-818a-6d0eb148e72c" :answer/id #uuid "85994e10-7a1c-5399-818a-6d0eb148e72c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7}{16}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-e31a3154-dd92-51e0-baa5-7e556d0b4865" :question/id #uuid "e31a3154-dd92-51e0-baa5-7e556d0b4865" :question/math-academy-id "q-161580" :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}2xyz\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le y+z\},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the line $y=1$ and the line $z=y$ in the first quadrant." :question/worked-solution "Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2xyz\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y+z}2xyz\,dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y+z}2xyz\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}yz[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=y+z}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}yz(y+z)^{2}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}yz({y}^{2}+2yz+{z}^{2})\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](images/59/5974f852ba8dcaf9e6c4d6323709987c590e2f739524e012545738bc4bb842b0.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{y}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}{z}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{2}{z}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}y{z}^{4}]}_{z=0}^{z=y}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}\cdot {y}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{2}\cdot {y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}y\cdot {y}^{4}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{17}{12}{y}^{5}\,dy \\  & =\frac{17}{12}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{5}\,dy \\  & =\frac{17}{12}{[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{6}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{17}{12}(\frac{1}{6}-0) \\  & =\frac{17}{72}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3a706466-bb58-58a9-b091-d4ba42a7541f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-3a706466-bb58-58a9-b091-d4ba42a7541f" :answer-field/id #uuid "3a706466-bb58-58a9-b091-d4ba42a7541f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-9fd9e948-6464-58a2-a0f2-d61ae7071f1e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3fcfb3a6-bd6a-5f81-b119-ffca2871d580" "answer-9fd9e948-6464-58a2-a0f2-d61ae7071f1e" "answer-806d8ac7-8b82-599c-9872-2d84cc0bb623" "answer-8768788c-5a1c-5056-8877-7d8c7cb5dc7b" "answer-0282d2f5-2a53-58db-a10f-e26b85fe6f5a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3fcfb3a6-bd6a-5f81-b119-ffca2871d580" :answer/id #uuid "3fcfb3a6-bd6a-5f81-b119-ffca2871d580" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{11}{36}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9fd9e948-6464-58a2-a0f2-d61ae7071f1e" :answer/id #uuid "9fd9e948-6464-58a2-a0f2-d61ae7071f1e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{17}{72}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-806d8ac7-8b82-599c-9872-2d84cc0bb623" :answer/id #uuid "806d8ac7-8b82-599c-9872-2d84cc0bb623" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{29}{64}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8768788c-5a1c-5056-8877-7d8c7cb5dc7b" :answer/id #uuid "8768788c-5a1c-5056-8877-7d8c7cb5dc7b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{18}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0282d2f5-2a53-58db-a10f-e26b85fe6f5a" :answer/id #uuid "0282d2f5-2a53-58db-a10f-e26b85fe6f5a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7}{36}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186278566 :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the line $y=1$ and the parabola $z=-{y}^{2}$ in the fourth quadrant." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186278565 :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral 

$$

$$

where the region $R$ is given by

R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le yz\},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the line $y=1$ and the parabola $z={y}^{2}$ in the first quadrant." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-b38931ca-6fb1-5b3c-b019-b45d2fe482a7" :question/id #uuid "b38931ca-6fb1-5b3c-b019-b45d2fe482a7" :question/math-academy-id "q-161578" :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}2\,\text{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the type II region given by 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le z\le 1,\,0\le x\le 4-y-z\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-y-z}2\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-y-z}2\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{4-y-z}2\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[2x]_{x=0}^{x=4-y-z}dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2(4-y-z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}8-2y-2z\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z,$ treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}8-2y-2z\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}8-2y-2z\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[8z-2yz-{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}8-2y-1\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}7-2y\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*" :question/worked-solution "![](images/24/240cc6d74e266579aa848be820fd0014672aa0654f079c079472a896ad44c5fe.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 4-y+2z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 4,\,\,0\le z\le 3\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/27/27862dcc3effe5801c812f5c8944c0134d13bb38f99d337b0a4e20e9ff815639.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 4,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,0\le x\le 4-y+2z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{z}{12}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4-y+2z}\frac{z}{12}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4-y+2z}\frac{z}{12}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{4-y+2z}\frac{z}{12}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{z}{12}[x]_{x=0}^{x=4-y+2z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{z}{12}(4-y+2z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{12}(4z-yz+2{z}^{2})\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{12}(4z-yz+2{z}^{2})\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{12}(4z-yz+2{z}^{2})\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{12}{[2{z}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}y{z}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{z}^{3}]}_{z=0}^{z=3}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{12}(18-\frac{9}{2}y+18)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(3-\frac{3}{8}y)\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}(3-\frac{3}{8}y)\,dy & ={[3y-\frac{3}{16}{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=4} \\  & =(12-3)-0 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-332dc5a3-6077-5a95-b9d8-7163745f52d1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-332dc5a3-6077-5a95-b9d8-7163745f52d1" :answer-field/id #uuid "332dc5a3-6077-5a95-b9d8-7163745f52d1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-6214fdd5-48a4-5599-acaa-959b2a1436e3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-91f4c10c-f73b-509c-9c7a-360f4a6c7f87" "answer-1bc60df2-8730-5e1e-bb8a-e55cbc507546" "answer-90d7a5d8-344b-556d-9123-9417e82aa3a5" "answer-5bd647e1-d76e-51a0-9ccd-a0bd017494ce" "answer-6214fdd5-48a4-5599-acaa-959b2a1436e3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-91f4c10c-f73b-509c-9c7a-360f4a6c7f87" :answer/id #uuid "91f4c10c-f73b-509c-9c7a-360f4a6c7f87" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1bc60df2-8730-5e1e-bb8a-e55cbc507546" :answer/id #uuid "1bc60df2-8730-5e1e-bb8a-e55cbc507546" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-90d7a5d8-344b-556d-9123-9417e82aa3a5" :answer/id #uuid "90d7a5d8-344b-556d-9123-9417e82aa3a5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5bd647e1-d76e-51a0-9ccd-a0bd017494ce" :answer/id #uuid "5bd647e1-d76e-51a0-9ccd-a0bd017494ce" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6214fdd5-48a4-5599-acaa-959b2a1436e3" :answer/id #uuid "6214fdd5-48a4-5599-acaa-959b2a1436e3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281323 :question/worked-solution "![](images/2a/2a20f2651c24e48871028b44fe61da4600d632481877ef32ccdfd3241262a53b.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 5-y-\frac{z}{2}\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 4\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/1b/1ba7c02f254313a73a813e4e43c44c25523ce77dd47e594a1db3b412a6bd5c3d.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 4,\,\,0\le x\le 5-y-\frac{z}{2}\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{5-y-z/2}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{5-y-z/2}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{5-y-z/2}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}[x]_{x=0}^{x=5-y-z/2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}(5-y-\frac{z}{2})\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{2}\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{2}\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{2}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{z}{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=4}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}2\,dy & =[2y]_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =6-0 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281324 :question/worked-solution "![](images/00/0008ba406cfe8a5b61d683a6854260897cb441752a5333add281ab1279e31b0b.png)

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/bb/bbe6b6b897e5d53421080ae8e8b9dc49f2ea1b7e135f8426ee3f11af01cc2401.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,0\le 2-\frac{y}{3}+z\}

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2-y/3+z}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2-y/3+z}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{2-y/3+z}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2-y/3+z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}(2-\frac{y}{3}+z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}{[z]}_{z=0}^{z=3}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}(3)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\,dy & =[y]_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-f2d33e33-cbe1-5877-8ed6-72bcb8e7fff5" :question/id #uuid "f2d33e33-cbe1-5877-8ed6-72bcb8e7fff5" :question/math-academy-id "q-161690" :question/problem "![](images/ca/ca994203c4a3889949e3452f48ea3f7295a152c5d9d4c809758f152d7115cedf.png)

${∭}_{R}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}V=$" :question/worked-solution "For a type II region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $yz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type II region enclosed between the back surface $x={u}_{1}(y,z)=1$ and the front surface $x={u}_{2}(y,z)=2.$

![](images/a3/a39d7a27f20283b6e6814db926801f16e3e2cb42c7fe16487350b536d3b63d3c.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,1\le x\le 2\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I *plane* region in the $yz$-plane with the upper curve

$$
z=1-(y-1)^{2}.
$$

![](images/50/5058493860a1c4d919e3cd6786bb1aca156ae83d47f766c087e351e9764929c4.png)

Hence, $D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,0\le z\le 1-(y-1)^{2}\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1-(y-1)^{2}}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1-(y-1)^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡z[{x}^{2}]_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1-(y-1)^{2}}3\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e767016c-6faf-58ba-ac6e-34fede0af637"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 2+2y-z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/14/145f0d494ffe24de84e3a289b3a7316d3f4933f193d734aed118609f7fb9f94f.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le x\le 2+2y-z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2+2y-z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(2+2y-z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2{y}^{2}z+2{y}^{3}z-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}\,dy & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2})-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135156 :tutorial/content "Let's evaluate the triple integral

![](images/ae/aec90ae0e9463c8e7c9164ed980828389070a8bb4a4ded54e2586f6c5a5ea376.svg)

where the region ![](images/08/085f4d77675f3cb7323d94feaa9eaa38f2fecb26c0f8483895f9ddf36b8d319d.svg) is shown below.

![](images/3e/3ee0df491365ac117eef84055f9d14aff9e7e5073b69e8e48b0a8bb93bb2f7ee.png)

 

The region ![](images/08/085f4d77675f3cb7323d94feaa9eaa38f2fecb26c0f8483895f9ddf36b8d319d.svg) is a type II region. So, our first task is to fully describe this region.

We start by drawing an arrow parallel to the ![](images/fc/fcc5df999e3b49fae1685ee0ab5bd03709804e1dd49f2ee722c4269eb0f5506d.svg)-axis that 

- enters the region through the *back* surface ![](images/89/89c97ad93c125fc2b6f61d44fe9a90845fd289329d79d506c857f970d7586540.svg) and

- leaves the region through the *front* surface ![](images/7b/7b823cb4664e2fe98090b6a778eba3030abf589930d2526ef5a50fb0aa792b5f.svg)

as shown below.

![](images/e6/e63827168c78ff5d13898bc436e02f99d834fbd2a10ce43aa98f47001e35044d.png)

 

So, our solid can be written as the type II region

![](images/c4/c4a007ae116844babbe81721267c0526be0ee44b8b8007a799031eae12485a59.svg)

where

![](images/12/12d667e2c74a83bd8f7fe58be763862fc793d22774695995b56ccda713308381.svg)

is the projection of ![](images/08/085f4d77675f3cb7323d94feaa9eaa38f2fecb26c0f8483895f9ddf36b8d319d.svg) onto the ![](images/3f/3f84f2f8778b7916a5ee013c8a92440e5cbd510ba2768435c3139b45806d2f90.svg)-plane, shown below.

![](images/ea/ea267107ec908087a99eaea952caabb0d1a08488657b2c0f70a2502bbf4b869b.png)

| $x$ | $\,-9\,$ | $\,-4\,$ | $\,2p\,$ | $\,-1\,$ | $\,0\,$ | $\,1\,$ | $\,2\,$ |

$$

$$

Now, we know that $\frac{Δf}{Δx}=3$ on the interval $[2p,2].$ Thus, 

$$
\frac{12}{2-2p}=3.
$$

Solving for $p,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{12}{2-2p} & =3 \\ 12 & =3\cdot (2-2p) \\ 12 & =6-6p \\ 12-6 & =-6p \\ 6 & =-6p \\ \frac{6}{-6} & =\frac{-6p}{-6} \\ -1 & =p.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $p=-1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a857d99b-4347-5fe1-ae63-d9fb653c5ffc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a857d99b-4347-5fe1-ae63-d9fb653c5ffc" :answer-field/id #uuid "a857d99b-4347-5fe1-ae63-d9fb653c5ffc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-254ff639-49a7-5804-99ec-040b9ef96440" :answer-field/choices ["answer-254ff639-49a7-5804-99ec-040b9ef96440" "answer-a92b0a77-fd8a-5040-b3c0-93eeef68bf39" "answer-4b4a206e-e770-563b-b20f-5959d1004976" "answer-e73b4c6a-cd5c-55d9-93bd-aeeb22c59c0e" "answer-91c81b1e-e7fe-58fd-a39e-76fc375fb786"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-254ff639-49a7-5804-99ec-040b9ef96440" :answer/id #uuid "254ff639-49a7-5804-99ec-040b9ef96440" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "p=-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a92b0a77-fd8a-5040-b3c0-93eeef68bf39" :answer/id #uuid "a92b0a77-fd8a-5040-b3c0-93eeef68bf39" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "p=-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4b4a206e-e770-563b-b20f-5959d1004976" :answer/id #uuid "4b4a206e-e770-563b-b20f-5959d1004976" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "p=-3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e73b4c6a-cd5c-55d9-93bd-aeeb22c59c0e" :answer/id #uuid "e73b4c6a-cd5c-55d9-93bd-aeeb22c59c0e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "p=1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-91c81b1e-e7fe-58fd-a39e-76fc375fb786" :answer/id #uuid "91c81b1e-e7fe-58fd-a39e-76fc375fb786" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "p=2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-7c25ff0b-f786-5f82-b2d5-6e5163b97efc" :question/id #uuid "7c25ff0b-f786-5f82-b2d5-6e5163b97efc" :question/math-academy-id "q-21129" :question/problem "The ice level in the North Pole is decreasing due to global warming. Find $\textrm{Var}\big[Y \,|\, X=3\big]$ given that the conditional probability mass function $f_{Y|X}(y \,|\, 3)$ is shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is $\mu_{Y|3} = \dfrac{8}{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=x] & =\text{E}[(Y-{\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\,|\,X=x] \\  & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{y}{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=3] & =[{\sum }_{y}{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,3)]-{\mu }_{Y|3}^{2} \\  & =[(1)^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}+(2)^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{6}+(4)^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}]-{(\frac{8}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{2}{3}+8-\frac{64}{9} \\  & =\frac{17}{9}.\end{aligned}

In order to find $f_{Y | X}(y \,|\, x),$ let's first find the marginal distribution for $X,$ corresponding to the row totals: 

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ | $f_X(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $\dfrac{1}{10}$ | $\dfrac{1}{10}$ | $\dfrac{1}{5}$ | $\dfrac{2}{5}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x$ is

$$
f_{Y | X}(y \,|\, x)  = \dfrac{f(x,y)}{f_X(x)}.

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding row total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x{:}$

| $f_{Y | X}(y \,|\, x)$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ |  |

| $X=2$ | $\dfrac{1}{2}$ | $\dfrac{1}{3}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $1$ |

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=1] & =[{\sum }_{y}{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)]-{\mu }_{Y|1}^{2} \\  & =[{1}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}+{2}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}+{3}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}]-{(\frac{9}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+1+\frac{9}{2}-\frac{81}{16} \\  & =\frac{11}{16}.\end{aligned}

$$
\textrm{E}[X\,|\,Y=y] = \mu_{X|y}.
$$

The **conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$** is defined as

$$
\textrm{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] = \textrm{E}\big[(X - \mu_{X|y} \big)^2 \,|\, Y=y].
$$

This is similar to the definition of $\textrm{Var}[X]$ in that it represents the average  (squared) distance of the random variable $X$ from the mean. The difference here is that the expected values are now dependent on the outcome of $Y.$

Similarly to the case of $\textrm{Var}[X],$ this often isn't the easiest formula to use in practice. However, it can be shown that the definition of conditional variance is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where $f_{X|Y}(x \,|\, y)$ is the conditional PMF of $X$ given $Y.$ Note that these formulas are analogous to those for $\textrm{Var}[X].$

Finally, we have an analogous definition for the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=x] & =\text{E}[(Y-{\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\,|\,X=x] \\  & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{y}{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186188511 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186172375 :question/answer-fields 17592186169113] {:db/id 17592186278412 :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}6xyz\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,u+v,\,v⟩
$$

 
over the domain $D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\}.$

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{3}.$*" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186278391 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u+v,\,u,\,v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩,\end{aligned}

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+-{1}^{2}+-{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-2yz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}+{v}^{2})\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}({\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+u{v}^{2}]}_{u=-1}^{u=1}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{3}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{[\frac{2}{3}v+\frac{2}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186278427 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2(1)^{2}+8(1)=2+8=10, \\ y & =4(1)^{7}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(10,4).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4t+8,\,{y}^{′}(t)=28{t}^{6}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{28{t}^{6}}{4t+8}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =\frac{28\cdot (1)^{6}}{4\cdot (1)+8} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,4)$ and the slope $m=\frac{7}{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-4 & =\frac{7}{3}(x-10).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-84a0580e-1530-5142-8694-ea6e03c23e1e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-84a0580e-1530-5142-8694-ea6e03c23e1e" :answer-field/id #uuid "84a0580e-1530-5142-8694-ea6e03c23e1e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-9faef563-301f-5002-ae66-16138801d477" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f25addc9-667b-53c2-8974-4909d91dac02" "answer-f4b72991-09c1-5e53-ab67-51fa799187db" "answer-c7de3c3f-b559-579e-a3ef-c39be1c56cc0" "answer-e48643fb-0c56-523a-9ebc-a1564cea5906" "answer-9faef563-301f-5002-ae66-16138801d477"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f25addc9-667b-53c2-8974-4909d91dac02" :answer/id #uuid "f25addc9-667b-53c2-8974-4909d91dac02" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y+2=\frac{7}{6}(x-10)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f4b72991-09c1-5e53-ab67-51fa799187db" :answer/id #uuid "f4b72991-09c1-5e53-ab67-51fa799187db" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y+4=\frac{3}{7}(x-10)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c7de3c3f-b559-579e-a3ef-c39be1c56cc0" :answer/id #uuid "c7de3c3f-b559-579e-a3ef-c39be1c56cc0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y-2=7(x-10)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e48643fb-0c56-523a-9ebc-a1564cea5906" :answer/id #uuid "e48643fb-0c56-523a-9ebc-a1564cea5906" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y-4=\frac{14}{3}(x-3)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9faef563-301f-5002-ae66-16138801d477" :answer/id #uuid "9faef563-301f-5002-ae66-16138801d477" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y-4=\frac{7}{3}(x-10)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-c3009bb8-76e4-5e7a-be7f-b556ddcfdaef" :question/id #uuid "c3009bb8-76e4-5e7a-be7f-b556ddcfdaef" :question/math-academy-id "q-122700" :question/problem "A curve is defined by the parametric equations

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=2$ on the curve. Determine the point at which the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=2$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(2)^{2}+3(2)=10, \\ y & =1+\sqrt{2(2)}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(10,3).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+3,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}}{2t+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}(2t+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=2,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=2} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot 2}(2\cdot 2+3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,3)$ and the slope $m=\frac{1}{14}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{14}(x-10).\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{14}(0-10) \\ y-3 & =-\frac{5}{7} \\ y & =\frac{16}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2({1}^{5})-4({1}^{3})=2-4=-2 \\ y & ={1}^{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to find the equation of the normal at the point $(-2,1).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{2t}{10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,1} & =\frac{2(1)}{10({1}^{4})-12({1}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{10-12} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-2)} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m:$

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,(-1)\,}=1
$$

Finally, to find the Cartesian equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-2,1)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =1(x-(-2)) \\ y-1 & =x+2 \\ y & =x+2+1 \\ y & =x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the equation of the normal line  in slope-intercept form is $y=x+3.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-65d17d6d-2bde-5720-8a1c-bab17264def6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-65d17d6d-2bde-5720-8a1c-bab17264def6" :answer-field/id #uuid "65d17d6d-2bde-5720-8a1c-bab17264def6" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-716c77ef-6905-55d3-a9a4-8d54e5510e60" :answer-field/choices ["answer-716c77ef-6905-55d3-a9a4-8d54e5510e60"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-716c77ef-6905-55d3-a9a4-8d54e5510e60" :answer/id #uuid "716c77ef-6905-55d3-a9a4-8d54e5510e60" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x+3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-1cf055f3-7724-5017-8bd4-b9d8370b23a5" :question/id #uuid "1cf055f3-7724-5017-8bd4-b9d8370b23a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-122943" :question/problem "A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{\pi })=4\pi (0)=0, \\ y & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =-\pi \end{aligned}

So we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point $(0,-\pi ).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi })+4,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi })+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\pi ,$ the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi } & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi }{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{\pi })+4} \\  & =\frac{-1}{4\cdot 0+4}=-\,\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,(-\frac{1}{4})\,}=4
$$

$$

$$

$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=e$ on the curve. Find the equation of the normal to the curve at $C.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=e$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡e=4, \\ y & =2e\operatorname{ln}⁡e=2e\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(4,2e).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{4}{t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2}{(\frac{4}{t})} \\  & =\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=e,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=e} & =\frac{e\operatorname{ln}⁡e+e}{2} \\  & =\frac{e+e}{2}=e\,.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,e\,}
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(4,2e)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{\,e\,}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2e & =(-\frac{1}{\,e\,})(x-4) \\ y-2e & =-\frac{1}{\,e\,}x+\frac{4}{\,e\,} \\ y & =-\frac{1}{\,e\,}x+\frac{2{e}^{2}+4}{\,e\,}\,.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ac112813-4b74-55f0-8f43-22f46db91806"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0<t<2\pi .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ on the curve. Determine the coordinates of the point at which the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis. Do not round the answers.

The normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}},
{{field-2}}$).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})=3\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point $(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{6},$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,\frac{\pi }{6}} & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m:$

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{3}
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=\sqrt{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-\frac{1}{2} & =\sqrt{3}(x-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\ y-\frac{1}{2} & =\sqrt{3}x-\frac{3(3)}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt{3}x-\frac{9}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt{3}x-4.\end{aligned}
$$

The normal crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at  $(0,\,-4).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-298c6150-0d93-5585-9a25-200dda26c396" "answer-field-23614fcf-fbe4-5be9-ae9e-34482a74c5f3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-298c6150-0d93-5585-9a25-200dda26c396" :answer-field/id #uuid "298c6150-0d93-5585-9a25-200dda26c396" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-1c25e94b-079d-51a9-bf98-4849a2d4378b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1c25e94b-079d-51a9-bf98-4849a2d4378b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1c25e94b-079d-51a9-bf98-4849a2d4378b" :answer/id #uuid "1c25e94b-079d-51a9-bf98-4849a2d4378b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-23614fcf-fbe4-5be9-ae9e-34482a74c5f3" :answer-field/id #uuid "23614fcf-fbe4-5be9-ae9e-34482a74c5f3" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-1d9012e4-4080-5eed-b0f1-ea73de461ec2" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1d9012e4-4080-5eed-b0f1-ea73de461ec2"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1d9012e4-4080-5eed-b0f1-ea73de461ec2" :answer/id #uuid "1d9012e4-4080-5eed-b0f1-ea73de461ec2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-5a6c8612-f46a-5c05-98fb-598338ec8310" :question/id #uuid "5a6c8612-f46a-5c05-98fb-598338ec8310" :question/math-academy-id "q-122948" :question/problem "A curve is defined by the parametric equations

:question/problem "Evaluate $2 \tan{45^\circ} - 4 \sin{45^\circ}.$" :question/worked-solution "The angle $45^\circ$ is special, and its trigonometric ratios have the values

$$
