![](images/a6/a6d1e8bd928fe666859f7101be65819af5f16fe81df3900941650d279eecd496.png)

By considering either of the $45^\circ$ angles in this triangle, we find that

$$
\eqalign{
	\sin 45^\circ &= \dfrac{\textrm{opp.}}{\textrm{hyp.}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \[5pt]
	\cos 45^\circ &= \dfrac{\textrm{adj.}}{\textrm{hyp.}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \[5pt]
	\tan 45^\circ &= \dfrac{\textrm{opp.}}{\textrm{adj.}} = \dfrac{1}{1} = 1. 
}
$$

Isosceles right triangles are very common, so the values above occur a lot in trigonometry. It's a good idea to remember them." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186084413 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider the $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle whose shortest leg has a length equal to $1,$ shown below.

![](images/67/679ce670484e57ba699030de4cf6d9ba52a5d6910d22b4beb2ad5d4e8ac4e0e0.png)

Now, we can calculate some trigonometric ratios without a calculator. Let's start with the $30^\circ$-angle. By the definition of sine, cosine, and tangent, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡{30}^{∘} & =\frac{\text{opp.}}{\text{hyp.}}=\frac{1}{2}, \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡{30}^{∘} & =\frac{\text{adj.}}{\text{hyp.}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡{30}^{∘} & =\frac{\text{opp.}}{\text{adj.}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, by considering the $60^\circ$-angle, we find that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡{60}^{∘} & =\frac{\text{opp.}}{\text{hyp.}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡{60}^{∘} & =\frac{\text{adj.}}{\text{hyp.}}=\frac{1}{2}, \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡{60}^{∘} & =\frac{\text{opp.}}{\text{adj.}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1}=\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186084414 :tutorial/content "The values of the trigonometric ratios for $0^\circ$ angles are the following:

| Trigonometric ratio | Value |
| --- | --- |
| $\sin \left(0^\circ\right)$ | $0$ |
| $\cos \left(0^\circ\right)$ | $1$ |
| $\tan \left(0^\circ\right)$ | $0$ |

Why is this so? If we look at the right triangle below, we can imagine making the angle $\theta$ smaller by moving the vertex $C$ towards $A.$ 

![](images/9b/9bee0468c989067e12648e538788bcd8c7fb879e112000a942a1ee6f41d95c7d.png)

As the angle $\theta$ gets closer and closer to zero, the opposite side $AC$ also approaches zero. Also, the hypotenuse $BC$ and the adjacent side $AB$ become nearly the same length.

So, as $\theta$ approaches zero (which we can write as $\theta \rightarrow 0^\circ$) we have

$$
AC \approx 0 \quad \text{and} \quad BC \approx AB.
$$

 

Therefore, when $\theta = 0^\circ$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({0}^{∘}) & =\frac{AC}{BC}=0, \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡({0}^{∘}) & =\frac{AB}{BC}=1, \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡({0}^{∘}) & =\frac{AC}{AB}=0.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186084415 :tutorial/content "The values of the trigonometric ratios for $90^\circ$ angles are the following:

| Trigonometric ratio | Value |
| --- | --- |
| $\sin \left(90^\circ\right)$ | $1$ |
| $\cos \left(90^\circ\right)$ | $0$ |
| $\tan \left(90^\circ\right)$ | Undefined |

To understand where the values come from, this time, we can imagine increasing the value of the angle $\theta$ by moving the vertex $B$ towards $A.$ 

![](images/53/53d538ce2eca6af579b556bdac72d9fba9ba5e817de38ff73236a312b401c4cf.png)

As $B$ moves towards $A,$ the adjacent side $AB$ gets very close to zero, and the angle $\theta$ gets very close to $90^\circ.$ Also, the hypotenuse $BC$ and the opposite side $AC$ become nearly the same length.

So, as $\theta$ approaches $90^\circ$ (which we can write as $\theta \rightarrow 90^\circ$) we have

$$
AB \approx 0 \quad \text{and} \quad BC \approx AC.
$$

 

Therefore, when $\theta = 90^\circ,$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({90}^{∘}) & =\frac{AC}{BC}=1, \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡({90}^{∘}) & =\frac{AB}{BC}=0, \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡({90}^{∘}) & =\frac{AC}{AB}=\frac{AC}{0}=\text{undefined.}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when calculating the tangent, we get a $0$ in the denominator. We know that we can't divide by zero. Therefore, the tangent of a right angle is said to be undefined." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083454 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186197960 :answer-field/choices 17592186197961] [:db/retract 17592186197960 :answer-field/choices 17592186197962] [:db/retract 17592186197960 :answer-field/choices 17592186197963] [:db/retract 17592186197960 :answer-field/choices 17592186197964] [:db/retract 17592186197960 :answer-field/choices 17592186197965] [:db/retract 17592186197840 :answer-field/choices 17592186197841] [:db/retract 17592186197840 :answer-field/choices 17592186197842] [:db/retract 17592186197840 :answer-field/choices 17592186197843] [:db/retract 17592186197840 :answer-field/choices 17592186197844] [:db/retract 17592186197840 :answer-field/choices 17592186197845] {:db/id 17592186198354 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-65227920-db32-5f4f-9774-747e0bc8ffd1" "question-4b5ee114-4f6d-532e-ba84-9309871f16a7" "question-b35b0faf-35a9-5d63-9b1f-dccf9512ee2b"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198433 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0c6c3541-8949-51d1-86fa-598cbd047050" "question-5a9b6c0a-2d84-570a-8860-6a6e61ceeed3"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199015 :question/problem "Find the points of the intersection of the elliptic cone ${x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}={z}^{2}$ and the line $x=\frac{y}{2}=z+4.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the equation of our line in the parametric form:

$$
x=\frac{y}{2}=z+4=t\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x=t \\ y=2t \\ z=t-4,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Substituting the above expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ {t}^{2}+2(2t)^{2} & =(t-4)^{2} \\ {t}^{2}+8{t}^{2} & ={t}^{2}-8t+16 \\ 8{t}^{2}+8t-16 & =0 \\ 8({t}^{2}+t-2) & =0 \\ 8(t+2)(t-1) & =0 \\ t & =-2,1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line.

- For $t=-2,$ we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ y=2(-2)=-4 \\ z=-2-4=-6,\end{aligned}
$$

so the first point is $(-2,-4,-6).$

- For $t=1,$ we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ y=2(1)=2 \\ z=1-4=-3,\end{aligned}
$$

so the second point is $(1,2,-3).$

Therefore, the points of intersection are $(-2,-4,-6)$ and $(1,2,-3).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186197960 :answer-field/correct "answer-67eb7249-a648-56ce-b5ed-2207421c0d4e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-aa24d1c5-c858-5867-b4c5-389cc27692f6" "answer-67eb7249-a648-56ce-b5ed-2207421c0d4e" "answer-6867a5b5-5ca3-5049-85eb-b68832f41cd2" "answer-596f5dd6-00ad-5cc4-b4f1-c803276b16e5" "answer-3b8e61fe-84f0-5e8c-b8d0-debe0a505a86"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-aa24d1c5-c858-5867-b4c5-389cc27692f6" :answer/id #uuid "aa24d1c5-c858-5867-b4c5-389cc27692f6" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$(-1,-2,-5)$ and $(1,2,-3)$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-67eb7249-a648-56ce-b5ed-2207421c0d4e" :answer/id #uuid "67eb7249-a648-56ce-b5ed-2207421c0d4e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$(-2,-4,-6)$ and $(1,2,-3)$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6867a5b5-5ca3-5049-85eb-b68832f41cd2" :answer/id #uuid "6867a5b5-5ca3-5049-85eb-b68832f41cd2" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$(0,0,-4)$  only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-596f5dd6-00ad-5cc4-b4f1-c803276b16e5" :answer/id #uuid "596f5dd6-00ad-5cc4-b4f1-c803276b16e5" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$(1,2,-3)$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3b8e61fe-84f0-5e8c-b8d0-debe0a505a86" :answer/id #uuid "3b8e61fe-84f0-5e8c-b8d0-debe0a505a86" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$(2,4,-2)$ and $(3,6,-1)$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-0c6c3541-8949-51d1-86fa-598cbd047050" :question/id #uuid "0c6c3541-8949-51d1-86fa-598cbd047050" :question/math-academy-id "q-94780" :question/problem "Find the point(s) of the intersection of the elliptic cone ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2{z}^{2}$ and the line $x=y=z+6.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the equation of our line in parametric form:

\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2} & =8{z}^{2} \\ (4t)^{2}+4(2t)^{2} & =8(t+1)^{2} \\ 16{t}^{2}+16{t}^{2} & =8(t+1)^{2} \\ 32{t}^{2} & =8(t+1)^{2} \\ 4{t}^{2} & =(t+1)^{2} \\ 4{t}^{2} & ={t}^{2}+2t+1 \\ 3{t}^{2}-2t-1 & =0 \\ (3t+1)(t-1) & =0 \\ t & =-\frac{1}{3},1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line.

- For $t=-\frac{1}{3},$ we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=4(-\frac{1}{3})=-\frac{4}{3} \\ y=2(-\frac{1}{3})=-\frac{2}{3} \\ z=-\frac{1}{3}+1=\frac{2}{3},\end{aligned}
$$

so the first point is $(-\frac{4}{3},-\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3}).$

- For $t=1,$ we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=4(1)=4 \\ y=2(1)=2 \\ z=1+1=2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the second point is $(4,2,2).$

Therefore, the points of intersection are $(-\frac{4}{3},-\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3})$ and $(4,2,2).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields $z=x^2+y^2$
and the line with the equation
$x = -y = -z+1.$
The line, paraboloid, and their points of intersection are shown below.

![](images/51/5159ac99a1bc9f73c01df3c2cc2e6fb2093a3d68e00731609d7b62a6fa55149d.png)

 

The trick is to express the equation of the line in parametric form, substitute the parametric equations into the equation of the surface, and solve for the parameter.

So, first, we write the equation of our line in the parametric form:

![](images/01/01357a5c6b72d7c976765aeed04db8afa3e3a80e13095d9be1ea2f2594ae5bf5.svg)

where $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

Our intersection points must belong to the line and the surface simultaneously. So, substituting the expressions for $x$, $y$, and $z$ from the parametric equation of the line into the equation of the paraboloid, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ (-t+1) & =(t)^{2}+(-t)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying this equation, we get

$$
2t^2+t - 1=0.
$$

The solutions to this equation are
$t=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $t=-1.$ 

Substituting these values back into the parametric equations of the line

- For $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$, we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{1}{2} \\ y=-(\frac{1}{2})=-\frac{1}{2} \\ z=-(\frac{1}{2})+1=\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

so the first point is $(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{1}{2}).$

- For $t=-1$, we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=(-1)=-1 \\ y=-(-1)=1 \\ z=-(-1)+1=2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the second point is $(-1,1,2).$

Therefore, the points of intersection are $(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{1}{2})$ and $(-1,1,2).$

$$
f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{2n+1} x^{2n+1}
$$

and converges to $f(x)$ for $|x| < R,$ where $R$ is the radius of convergence of the Taylor series. How can we calculate the first three non-zero terms of Taylor series for the derivative, $f'(x),$ about $x=0?$

All we need to do is differentiate the Taylor series of $f(x).$ Writing out the first three terms, we get

$$
f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{2n+1} x^{2n+1} = x - \dfrac{x^3}{3} + \dfrac{x^5}{5} - \cdots.
$$

Now, to find $f'(x),$ we differentiate term-by-term and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5})-⋯ \\  & =1-{x}^{2}+{x}^{4}-⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

And that's it! The radius of convergence of the Taylor series for $f'(x)$ is $R,$ the same as $f(x).$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054898 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096685 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a2dc0eae-2d75-5993-9bdd-983fb1853b64" "question-a3b63338-dbf9-5694-b2da-0ac508216008"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096477 :question/worked-solution "To obtain the graph of $y=−f(x)$ from $y=f(x)$, we need to reflect the graph over the $x$-axis. How can we plot the graph of $y=-f(x)$?

![](images/5b/5bab57ba6ac7cd9b0ea80287457ddc7ee50cadf2580a84a802fa039bbca27e1a.png)

As usual, It's helpful to first find a few points on the graph of $y=-f(x)$. You can use the points on the graph of $y=f(x)$ to identify corresponding points on the graph of $y=-f(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Points on }y=f(x) & \text{ Points on }y=-f(x) \\ (-1,2) & (-1,-2) \\ (0,-1) & (0,1) \\ (2,0) & (2,0) \\ (3,4) & (3,-4)\end{aligned}
$$

For each point on the graph of $y=f(x)$ there is a point on the graph of $y=-f(x)$ with the *same* $x$-value and the *opposite* $y$-value. 

Let's plot our new points, and draw $y=-f(x)$.

![](images/5a/5a1e6c5a95dff6b8e1f7eba5de197ba61f0ae64a94db2eeb57fc6cd23661f877.png)

The graph of $y=-f(x)$ is a **reflection across the $x$-axis** of the graph of $y=f(x)$." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096917 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133917 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d33bfb77-09ea-5195-a418-173b3296a490" "question-e1798463-dc83-5fa2-a428-d476acd2c869" "question-ea162333-68ea-5f39-92a3-425dd5b76bfd"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133916 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0597a6d4-1752-5cad-a458-a8b2a80e68a1" "question-0f4e6580-868c-593b-ba50-63aa6d6e6e42" "question-7dfdc43a-549b-5350-87ba-ec6dde24e325"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133923 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e4e7d822-5d73-50ee-b641-1c594f9a070a" "question-7a83145c-370c-5913-b3c6-439072b6c354" "question-0bcb5cdc-84fc-59d4-a070-2f4375bf7e4a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133925 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-43d7c496-4713-50a7-87bb-4a90921bae35" "question-0d6e2493-0d92-5bdf-8874-580184f51513" "question-9c0ba772-2d81-508b-bca4-4e2298a7113a" "question-3242c4d8-39d7-5463-b665-91b0cfa5917f"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-d33bfb77-09ea-5195-a418-173b3296a490" :question/id #uuid "d33bfb77-09ea-5195-a418-173b3296a490" :question/math-academy-id "q-161723" :question/problem "Consider the type III region $R,$ given by

$$" :question/worked-solution "A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {u}_{2}(x,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](images/06/0603bed12c6af74e46544d8bebc52362aed95a9a5ad7418ea4faaf228f3b5241.png)

 

If $R$ is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(x,z)={x}^{2},\,{u}_{2}(x,z)=2+{z}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2+{z}^{2}}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d16be51a-dcbd-5540-95d0-1d9d605bbc50"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id {∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{∗}^{∗}{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{∗}^{∗}f(x,y,z)\,dy\,dz\,dx
$$

The triple integral above is defined over the type III region given by

$$
S=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le z\le 2x+1,\,0\le y\le 1+x+z\}.
$$

What is the value of $a+b?$" :question/worked-solution "A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {u}_{2}(x,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](images/06/0603bed12c6af74e46544d8bebc52362aed95a9a5ad7418ea4faaf228f3b5241.png)

 

If $R$ is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(x,z)=0,\,{u}_{2}(x,z)=1+x+z.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{1+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$

 

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le z\le 2x+1\}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{1+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2x+1}[{\int }_{0}^{1+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dz\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{2x+1}{\int }_{0}^{1+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy\,dz\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=(-1)+(2x+1)=2x.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-ea162333-68ea-5f39-92a3-425dd5b76bfd" :question/id #uuid "ea162333-68ea-5f39-92a3-425dd5b76bfd" :question/math-academy-id "q-161745" :question/problem "$$

$$

What is the value of $a-b?$" :question/worked-solution "A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {u}_{2}(x,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](images/06/0603bed12c6af74e46544d8bebc52362aed95a9a5ad7418ea4faaf228f3b5241.png)

 

If $R$ is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(x,z)=-2-z,\,{u}_{2}(x,z)=2+x+z.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2-z}^{2+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$

 

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,-2\le z\le {x}^{2}+2\}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2-z}^{2+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{{x}^{2}+2}[{\int }_{-2-z}^{2+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dz\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{{x}^{2}+2}{\int }_{-2-z}^{2+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy\,dz\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a-b=(0)-(2+x+z)=-2-x-z.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d83fd660-d05c-552a-9c9c-8182ba76ceb4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d83fd660-d05c-552a-9c9c-8182ba76ceb4" :answer-field/id #uuid "d83fd660-d05c-552a-9c9c-8182ba76ceb4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-b43658c4-c0e4-563f-a52d-4334e8d4e468" :answer-field/choices ["answer-982a8761-3b79-5432-9984-542ac899a03a" "answer-b43658c4-c0e4-563f-a52d-4334e8d4e468" "answer-30d0159a-b42b-51ba-b22a-df45c14b3437" "answer-934f89a5-9a46-5676-98f1-76182ab85055" "answer-1e42e40e-c96a-58c9-9612-0406917ecf9f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-982a8761-3b79-5432-9984-542ac899a03a" :answer/id #uuid "982a8761-3b79-5432-9984-542ac899a03a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2-x" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b43658c4-c0e4-563f-a52d-4334e8d4e468" :answer/id #uuid "b43658c4-c0e4-563f-a52d-4334e8d4e468" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2-x-z" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-30d0159a-b42b-51ba-b22a-df45c14b3437" :answer/id #uuid "30d0159a-b42b-51ba-b22a-df45c14b3437" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2-z" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-934f89a5-9a46-5676-98f1-76182ab85055" :answer/id #uuid "934f89a5-9a46-5676-98f1-76182ab85055" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2-z-x" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1e42e40e-c96a-58c9-9612-0406917ecf9f" :answer/id #uuid "1e42e40e-c96a-58c9-9612-0406917ecf9f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "z+x" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-0597a6d4-1752-5cad-a458-a8b2a80e68a1" :question/id #uuid "0597a6d4-1752-5cad-a458-a8b2a80e68a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-161666" :question/problem "Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{x}2x\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A
$$

given that the region $D$ in the $xz$-plane is given by

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le z\le 2-x\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{x}2x\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}2x[y]_{y=0}^{y=x}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $D$ is a type I region in the $xz$-plane.
Therefore, to evaluate our double integral as a repeated integral over this region, we integrate with respect to $z$ and then with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2-x}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{x}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2-x}\,\text{d}z]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{x}^{2}{[z]}_{z=0}^{z=2-x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{x}^{2}(2-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{4}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =(\frac{32}{3}-8)-0 \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-07cc355d-4413-59ca-bc08-a5af18b8dff8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-07cc355d-4413-59ca-bc08-a5af18b8dff8" :answer-field/id #uuid "07cc355d-4413-59ca-bc08-a5af18b8dff8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1fd3f49a-2cb7-53fd-81b2-5b3857da1e8e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f5e2d875-4536-53de-bade-39c60d2d073b" "answer-bfadebc0-e9ba-513f-b060-6475dd84329f" "answer-930c7ce8-022d-5e4d-bd0e-9c20804f999e" "answer-0438c001-4681-59c9-8849-bfb0fea1ea87" "answer-1fd3f49a-2cb7-53fd-81b2-5b3857da1e8e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f5e2d875-4536-53de-bade-39c60d2d073b" :answer/id #uuid "f5e2d875-4536-53de-bade-39c60d2d073b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bfadebc0-e9ba-513f-b060-6475dd84329f" :answer/id #uuid "bfadebc0-e9ba-513f-b060-6475dd84329f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-930c7ce8-022d-5e4d-bd0e-9c20804f999e" :answer/id #uuid "930c7ce8-022d-5e4d-bd0e-9c20804f999e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0438c001-4681-59c9-8849-bfb0fea1ea87" :answer/id #uuid "0438c001-4681-59c9-8849-bfb0fea1ea87" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1fd3f49a-2cb7-53fd-81b2-5b3857da1e8e" :answer/id #uuid "1fd3f49a-2cb7-53fd-81b2-5b3857da1e8e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{8}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-0f4e6580-868c-593b-ba50-63aa6d6e6e42" :question/id #uuid "0f4e6580-868c-593b-ba50-63aa6d6e6e42" :question/math-academy-id "q-161725" :question/problem "$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{x}^{\sqrt{1-z}}4xy\,dy]dA,
$$

Evaluate the repeated integral above given that $D$ is a region in the $xz$-plane bounded by the lines $z=0,$ $x=0,$ and the curve $z+{x}^{2}=1.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{x}^{\sqrt{1-z}}4xy\,dy]dA & ={∬}_{D}2x[{y}^{2}]_{y=x}^{y=\sqrt{1-z}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x(1-z-{x}^{2})\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\,2x(1-z)-2{x}^{3}\,)\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to calculate this double integral, we plot $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xz$-plane.

![](images/80/8079d8f9796c1f863a515ced0091c1f420318be1c4bfe0eb2da641bddfa426ce.png)

 

Therefore, to evaluate our double integral as a repeated integral over this region, we integrate with respect to $z$ and then with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(\,2x(1-z)-2{x}^{3}\,)\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}(\,2x(1-z)-2{x}^{3}\,)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x[-(1-z)^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=1-{x}^{2}}-2{x}^{3}[z]_{z=0}^{z=1-{x}^{2}}\,)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-{x}^{5}+x-2{x}^{3}+2{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{5}+x-2{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}{x}^{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-59fa8c03-9424-5baf-a214-fbd3a612fb42"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-59fa8c03-9424-5baf-a214-fbd3a612fb42" :answer-field/id #uuid "59fa8c03-9424-5baf-a214-fbd3a612fb42" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-79072c2d-8f08-5f5d-b719-e8897f0003bf" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d4818782-d4a8-5e32-83a7-0f9ae23058c9" "answer-9acf82d9-0415-5a81-99b2-8d7595b0a6f9" "answer-ea550bee-68b7-502c-8b85-afcf994105bf" "answer-79072c2d-8f08-5f5d-b719-e8897f0003bf" "answer-86d4e147-37c0-5de6-9297-866f2a3e212e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d4818782-d4a8-5e32-83a7-0f9ae23058c9" :answer/id #uuid "d4818782-d4a8-5e32-83a7-0f9ae23058c9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9acf82d9-0415-5a81-99b2-8d7595b0a6f9" :answer/id #uuid "9acf82d9-0415-5a81-99b2-8d7595b0a6f9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ea550bee-68b7-502c-8b85-afcf994105bf" :answer/id #uuid "ea550bee-68b7-502c-8b85-afcf994105bf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-79072c2d-8f08-5f5d-b719-e8897f0003bf" :answer/id #uuid "79072c2d-8f08-5f5d-b719-e8897f0003bf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-86d4e147-37c0-5de6-9297-866f2a3e212e" :answer/id #uuid "86d4e147-37c0-5de6-9297-866f2a3e212e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134287 :question/problem "Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{x}2xyz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A
$$

given that the region $D$ in the $xz$-plane is given by

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le \sqrt{4-2z},\,0\le z\le 2\}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-7dfdc43a-549b-5350-87ba-ec6dde24e325" :question/id #uuid "7dfdc43a-549b-5350-87ba-ec6dde24e325" :question/math-academy-id "q-161689" :question/problem "Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}5yz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A
$$

given that the region $D$ in the $xz$-plane is given by

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 2,\,0\le x\le 2-z\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $z$ and $x$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}5yz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}5z{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{∬}_{D}z(4-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $D$ is a type II region in the $xz$-plane.
Therefore, to evaluate our double integral as a repeated integral over this region, we integrate with respect to $x$ and then with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2}{∬}_{D}z(4-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2-z}z(4-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}z[{\int }_{0}^{2-z}(4-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}z{[(4x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})]}_{x=0}^{x=2-z}\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}z(4(2-z)-\frac{(2-z)^{3}}{3})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{16z}{3}-2{z}^{3}+\frac{{z}^{4}}{3})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{[\frac{8{z}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{z}^{4}}{2}+\frac{{z}^{5}}{15}]}_{z=0}^{z=2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}[\frac{32}{3}-8+\frac{32}{15}] \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0e152976-df66-5055-a7f1-93a051729b6f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0e152976-df66-5055-a7f1-93a051729b6f" :answer-field/id #uuid "0e152976-df66-5055-a7f1-93a051729b6f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-88b8ff89-b6c2-573a-9042-004cee1995e9" :answer-field/choices ["answer-16859933-75c0-53cc-92d2-abc0eb0131cf" "answer-88b8ff89-b6c2-573a-9042-004cee1995e9" "answer-25582ec9-aea6-53c2-b2a3-0a0449093e1b" "answer-9886d286-2a1c-56a0-abf4-404d3ebfd465" "answer-5dbf81b7-4c30-539d-840c-554a9ef51ef3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-16859933-75c0-53cc-92d2-abc0eb0131cf" :answer/id #uuid "16859933-75c0-53cc-92d2-abc0eb0131cf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-88b8ff89-b6c2-573a-9042-004cee1995e9" :answer/id #uuid "88b8ff89-b6c2-573a-9042-004cee1995e9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-25582ec9-aea6-53c2-b2a3-0a0449093e1b" :answer/id #uuid "25582ec9-aea6-53c2-b2a3-0a0449093e1b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "14" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9886d286-2a1c-56a0-abf4-404d3ebfd465" :answer/id #uuid "9886d286-2a1c-56a0-abf4-404d3ebfd465" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "15" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5dbf81b7-4c30-539d-840c-554a9ef51ef3" :answer/id #uuid "5dbf81b7-4c30-539d-840c-554a9ef51ef3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-e4e7d822-5d73-50ee-b641-1c594f9a070a" :question/id #uuid "e4e7d822-5d73-50ee-b641-1c594f9a070a" :question/math-academy-id "q-161738" :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral

$$

$$
{∭}_{R}xyz\,\text{d}V

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 2,\,0\le x\le \sqrt{4-2z},\,0\le y\le x\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}xyz\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}{\int }_{0}^{x}xyz\,dy\,dx\,dz.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}{\int }_{0}^{x}xyz\,dy\,dx\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}[{\int }_{0}^{x}xyz\,dy]dx\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}xz{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}dx\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}xz(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})\,dx\,dz \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}{x}^{3}z\,dx\,dz\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $z$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}{x}^{3}z\,dx\,dz & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}z[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2z}}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}z{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{4-2z}}\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{4}(4-2z)^{2}z\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4z-4{z}^{2}+{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4z-4{z}^{2}+{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z & =\frac{1}{2}{[2{z}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{z}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}{z}^{4}]}_{z=0}^{z=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(8-\frac{32}{3}+4)-0 \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3888cc3d-bb90-568c-bfd5-048cece1217d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-3888cc3d-bb90-568c-bfd5-048cece1217d" :answer-field/id #uuid "3888cc3d-bb90-568c-bfd5-048cece1217d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-78e4424f-a2d2-5162-a013-91916d289fbf" :answer-field/choices ["answer-10b3f812-017d-59eb-99e5-5a00f74bf7d2" "answer-49e17673-b9ad-517c-bb9b-8d3f2668d8ba" "answer-78e4424f-a2d2-5162-a013-91916d289fbf" "answer-e438768b-4435-5fed-b94f-351a63a4645d" "answer-35e1c9bf-ea2b-560e-8f70-12de88c73f78"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-10b3f812-017d-59eb-99e5-5a00f74bf7d2" :answer/id #uuid "10b3f812-017d-59eb-99e5-5a00f74bf7d2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-49e17673-b9ad-517c-bb9b-8d3f2668d8ba" :answer/id #uuid "49e17673-b9ad-517c-bb9b-8d3f2668d8ba" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-78e4424f-a2d2-5162-a013-91916d289fbf" :answer/id #uuid "78e4424f-a2d2-5162-a013-91916d289fbf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e438768b-4435-5fed-b94f-351a63a4645d" :answer/id #uuid "e438768b-4435-5fed-b94f-351a63a4645d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-35e1c9bf-ea2b-560e-8f70-12de88c73f78" :answer/id #uuid "35e1c9bf-ea2b-560e-8f70-12de88c73f78" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-0bcb5cdc-84fc-59d4-a070-2f4375bf7e4a" :question/id #uuid "0bcb5cdc-84fc-59d4-a070-2f4375bf7e4a" :question/math-academy-id "q-161764" :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}4xy\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,x\le y\le \sqrt{1-z}\},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $xz$-plane enclosed between the $x$-axis, the $z$-axis, and the curve $z=1-{x}^{2},$ in the first quadrant." :question/worked-solution "Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}4xy\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{x}^{\sqrt{1-z}}4xy\,dy]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{x}^{\sqrt{1-z}}4xy\,dy]dA & ={∬}_{D}2x[{y}^{2}]_{y=x}^{y=\sqrt{1-z}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x(\,(1-z)-{x}^{2})\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x(1-z)-2{x}^{3}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate this double integral over the region $D$ in the $xz$-plane shown below.

![](images/95/95a2b4e28dbfae5ce447b3b975b2f74bf04883441217f42a24636970948402a0.png)

  

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2x(1-z)-2{x}^{3}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-z}}2x(1-z)-2{x}^{3}\,dx\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1-z)[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-z}}2x\,dx]dz+{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-z}}-2{x}^{3}\,dx]dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1-z)[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{1-z}}dz+{\int }_{0}^{1}{[-\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{1-z}}dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1-z)^{2}\,dz-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(1-z)^{2}\,dz \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(1-z)^{2}\,dz \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{[-(1-z)^{3}]}_{z=0}^{z=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-84189abc-599a-55c9-aabf-a7a75d8a52db"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-84189abc-599a-55c9-aabf-a7a75d8a52db" :answer-field/id #uuid "84189abc-599a-55c9-aabf-a7a75d8a52db" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-de78bae8-e4d7-569c-a55e-af9dd522c7c8" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3b7d98c9-02ac-5603-afb5-66c0e4f344f8" "answer-aa0afc20-5227-5ba6-b5db-de3861c4378d" "answer-de78bae8-e4d7-569c-a55e-af9dd522c7c8" "answer-40bf70c8-60bf-5224-82fd-7ff84ef20808" "answer-b718d3fb-6237-5710-a206-2a584cc97e02"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3b7d98c9-02ac-5603-afb5-66c0e4f344f8" :answer/id #uuid "3b7d98c9-02ac-5603-afb5-66c0e4f344f8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-aa0afc20-5227-5ba6-b5db-de3861c4378d" :answer/id #uuid "aa0afc20-5227-5ba6-b5db-de3861c4378d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-de78bae8-e4d7-569c-a55e-af9dd522c7c8" :answer/id #uuid "de78bae8-e4d7-569c-a55e-af9dd522c7c8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-40bf70c8-60bf-5224-82fd-7ff84ef20808" :answer/id #uuid "40bf70c8-60bf-5224-82fd-7ff84ef20808" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b718d3fb-6237-5710-a206-2a584cc97e02" :answer/id #uuid "b718d3fb-6237-5710-a206-2a584cc97e02" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281317 :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral

Evaluate the triple integral 
${∭}_{R}4x\,dV$
over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the right one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*" :question/worked-solution "![](images/f1/f112dd83a8cbb7563979dc170db23db7e178ba1762aca23fd4073c50e1c7a343.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le 5-x-z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 2\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/71/71974fddc8e0e0b6a12fc6a248c15eea08c9f6b8a0823d50aede8aadc31a41fa.png)

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 5-x-z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}4x\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{5-x-z}4x\,dy\,dz\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{5-x-z}4x\,dy\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{5-x-z}4x\,dy]dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4x[y]_{y=0}^{y=5-x-z}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4x(5-x-z)\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(20x-4{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(20x-4{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2}(20x-4{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[20xz-4{x}^{2}z-2x{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(32x-8{x}^{2})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}(32x-8{x}^{2})\,dx & ={[16{x}^{2}-\frac{8{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =(64-\frac{64}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{128}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-35cfb42e-572e-5b24-aa8c-8d68254f52ca"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-35cfb42e-572e-5b24-aa8c-8d68254f52ca" :answer-field/id #uuid "35cfb42e-572e-5b24-aa8c-8d68254f52ca" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-70deb780-c887-5dc9-85bd-f3b01ab2a24b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3b6f618c-bcbb-5ea7-9f0c-1e592526ff75" "answer-c0d3ac95-6cd9-512a-9fab-45c1bf14a2cb" "answer-cd88dea5-2a41-5c70-9ba3-d70de53ad32d" "answer-c4cd7a9d-8989-5c58-b2bd-dbc2dff6d515" "answer-70deb780-c887-5dc9-85bd-f3b01ab2a24b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3b6f618c-bcbb-5ea7-9f0c-1e592526ff75" :answer/id #uuid "3b6f618c-bcbb-5ea7-9f0c-1e592526ff75" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c0d3ac95-6cd9-512a-9fab-45c1bf14a2cb" :answer/id #uuid "c0d3ac95-6cd9-512a-9fab-45c1bf14a2cb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cd88dea5-2a41-5c70-9ba3-d70de53ad32d" :answer/id #uuid "cd88dea5-2a41-5c70-9ba3-d70de53ad32d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{5}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c4cd7a9d-8989-5c58-b2bd-dbc2dff6d515" :answer/id #uuid "c4cd7a9d-8989-5c58-b2bd-dbc2dff6d515" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-70deb780-c887-5dc9-85bd-f3b01ab2a24b" :answer/id #uuid "70deb780-c887-5dc9-85bd-f3b01ab2a24b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{128}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-0d6e2493-0d92-5bdf-8874-580184f51513" :question/id #uuid "0d6e2493-0d92-5bdf-8874-580184f51513" :question/math-academy-id "q-161932" :question/problem "![](images/6f/6f4bf1fe2f1a49f84b56702c4a83272c2f927ea4774eb677f43e525bf6cfb1f7.png)

Evaluate the triple integral 
${∭}_{R}8x\,dV$
over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the right one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*" :question/worked-solution "![](images/71/71f3fd0cbbde8adeca71688d6b53e2cd4cdf72076be3efa770cfebb8c10ffb76.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le 3-\frac{3x}{4}-\frac{z}{2}\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/cd/cd84968e9e5300a18d087ba566202aba2b7166818a590cca03eac90d4f3f7a89.png)

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,0\le y\le 3-\frac{3x}{4}-\frac{z}{2}\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}8x\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3-3x/4-z/2}8x\,dy\,dz\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3-3x/4-z/2}8x\,dy\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{3-3x/4-z/2}8x\,dy]dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}8x[y]_{y=0}^{y=3-3x/4-z/2}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}8x(3-\frac{3x}{4}-\frac{z}{2})\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(24x-6{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(24x-6{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{3}(24x-6{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[24xz-6{x}^{2}z-2x{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=3}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(72x-18{x}^{2}-18x)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(54x-18{x}^{2})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(54x-18{x}^{2})\,dx & ={[27{x}^{2}-6{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =(27-6)-0 \\  & =21.\end{aligned}

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le 4-z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/ca/ca74bf149c1371fe9f1622586d9eb92fe180a9c9bb6a0c53d16f538b3c55f4a4.png)

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,0\le y\le 4-z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}4{x}^{2}z\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4-z}4{x}^{2}z\,dy\,dz\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4-z}4{x}^{2}z\,dy\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{4-z}4{x}^{2}z\,dy]dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{2}z[y]_{y=0}^{y=4-z}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{2}z(4-z)\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(16{x}^{2}z-4{x}^{2}{z}^{2})\,dz\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(16{x}^{2}z-4{x}^{2}{z}^{2})\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{3}(16{x}^{2}z-4{x}^{2}{z}^{2})\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[8{x}^{2}{z}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{x}^{2}{z}^{3}]_{z=0}^{z=3}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}36{x}^{2}\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}36{x}^{2}\,dx & ={[12{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =(12-0) \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-9c0ba772-2d81-508b-bca4-4e2298a7113a" :question/id #uuid "9c0ba772-2d81-508b-bca4-4e2298a7113a" :question/math-academy-id "q-163509" :question/problem "![](images/33/335bf5e4e2a4ee9d0286eadb968e0e82c6afb18d47cd5258d6d1b6cee3d5c5a6.png)

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type III region enclosed between the back surface $y={u}_{1}(x,z)=1$ and the front surface $y={u}_{2}(x,z)=3.$

![](images/b1/b176bcf502a0801eae2bf470dfe4bf92852a34b06675fd74be78b30ccb4f6469.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,1\le y\le 3\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I *plane* region in the $xz$-plane with the upper curve

$$
z=1-{x}^{2}.
$$

![](images/eb/eb054b5f1567aa2c56842d79133fbbefc41a8b40730c688381d88e3ef06ccab7.png)

Hence, $D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le z\le 1-{x}^{2}\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}xz\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{3}xz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{1}^{3}xz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}xz[y]_{y=1}^{y=3}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}2xz\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bbe73ac4-9782-563c-b73e-8c4d198957b7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type III region enclosed between the back surface $y={u}_{1}(x,z)=1$ and the front surface $y={u}_{2}(x,z)=2.$

![](images/2f/2f1112a1fa4e540ce8ef2d1337383a2adcb378ba519cfb9c49a4521e5bc1b02f.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,1\le y\le 2\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type II *plane* region in the $xz$-plane with the left curve

$$
x={z}^{2}.
$$

![](images/2d/2dcbae12ed3351892c63117f86bab7ffe6e1818b7a16666b42c2efdcc6bd787f.png)

Hence, $D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,{z}^{2}\le x\le 1\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2y\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}[{y}^{2}]_{y=1}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}3\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-47db12a1-3244-5a01-bb35-553d717703fe"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :answer.type/math :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135158 :tutorial/content "Let's evaluate the triple integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R 2xz  \: \mathrm{d}V
$$

where the region $R$ is shown below.

![](images/9b/9b00702b941e40061ff242e63c0d1b33642cce9aefc1ffa9f88e9d94cd02897a.png)

 

The region $R$ is a type III region. So, our first task is to describe this region fully.

We start by drawing an arrow parallel to the $y$-axis that 

- enters the region through the *left* surface $y=0,$ and

- leave the region through the *right* surface $y=6-x-z,$

as shown below.

![](images/51/5102f786fa91eb862fd3f5ef8f0b2cbc85fbdff6fc616f86f498aa0da8088f14.png)

 

So, our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (x,z) \in D, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 6-x-z \big\},
$$

where

$$
D = \big\{ (x,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 3, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1 \big\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/30/30f320f2e77c95c13e59bc3fdd6b273d1ad367018af3cd12bd6d2fde7cc09132.png)

To evaluate our triple integral, we start by expressing it as a mixed integral:

$$
\iiint\limits_R 2xz \:\textrm{d}V
=
\iint\limits_D \left[ \int_{0}^{6-x-z} 2xz \:\textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}A
$$

Now, since the region $D$ is a type I *plane* region, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 3, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 6-x-z \big\},
$$

and therefore, our mixed integral can be written as the following repeating integral:

$$
\iint\limits_D \left[ \int_0^{6-x-z} 2xz \:\textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}A
=
\int_{0}^{3} \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{6-x-z} 2xz \:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}x
$$

Evaluating this using the usual methods, we get

$$
\int_{0}^{3} \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{6-x-z} 2xz \:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}x = 15.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\iiint\limits_R 2xz \:\textrm{d}V = 15.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135159 :tutorial/content "When writing down a triple integral as a repeated integral, we can often skip the intermediate step of expressing our triple integral as a mixed integral.

For example, suppose we wish to evaluate

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R f(x,y,z) \:\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the type III region given by 

$$
R= \big\{(x,y,z) \: : \: {\color{red}a} \leq x \leq {\color{red}b}, \: {\color{blue}v_1(x)} \leq z \leq {\color{blue}v_2(x)}, \: {\color{purple}u_1(x,z)} \leq y \leq {\color{purple}u_2(x,z)} \big\}.
$$

Notice that the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane is a type II plane region. Therefore, we can immediately express our triple integral as follows:

$$
\iiint\limits_R f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}V
=
\int_{\color{red}a}^{\color{red}b} \int_{\color{blue}v_1(x)}^{\color{blue}v_2(x)} \int_{\color{purple}u_1(x,z)}^{\color{purple}u_2(x,z)} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}x
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134015 :activity/expected-seconds 960.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-2,3)$ to the point $(0,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2t-2,\,3-3t⟩.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-2,3)$ and $(0,0).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-2+t(0-(-2))),\,(3+t(0-3))⟩ \\  & =⟨2t-2,\,3-3t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-2)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2t-2)^{2}(3-3t) \\  & =4(t-1)^{2}\cdot 3(1-t) \\  & =-12(t-1)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-12(t-1)^{3}\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & =-24{\int }_{0}^{1}(t-1)^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d86ee8d9-aeae-5ab1-b4a0-98c765570dca"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "![](images/f5/f5f5b235b54d2acd20297ab365d9b93907111b3fec9a86776c28e93fdfe105ee.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(2,3),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2t,\,3t⟩.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(0,0)$ and $(2,3).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(0+t(2-0)),\,(0+t(3-0))⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,3t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2t)^{2}+(3t)^{2} \\  & =4{t}^{2}+9{t}^{2} \\  & =13{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}13{t}^{2}\cdot 3\,\text{d}t \\  & =39{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2c3bc565-6668-5708-9572-740391604ada"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Evaluate ${\int }_{C}({y}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(2,3),$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(0,1)$ and $(2,3).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(0+t(2-0)),\,(1+t(3-1))⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,1+2t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={y}^{2}-2x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(1+2t)^{2}-2(2t) \\  & =1+4t+4{t}^{2}-4t \\  & =4{t}^{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+1)\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{[\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}+t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2(\frac{4}{3}+1)-2(0) \\  & =\frac{14}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8b9c47c5-4e96-58fa-ac91-5791dc11f30c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8b9c47c5-4e96-58fa-ac91-5791dc11f30c" :answer-field/id #uuid "8b9c47c5-4e96-58fa-ac91-5791dc11f30c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-6029d8a7-a6ae-5959-9ee4-f8e3ebd8e072" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c94fc212-35ff-5e38-9f57-12d4f4959a4c" "answer-6029d8a7-a6ae-5959-9ee4-f8e3ebd8e072" "answer-21702398-6680-552d-923f-027dff95a35a" "answer-ea8f272e-677d-5489-96d8-1e29db88e990" "answer-78ae96ca-4942-5362-807b-c0b65d2496c2"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c94fc212-35ff-5e38-9f57-12d4f4959a4c" :answer/id #uuid "c94fc212-35ff-5e38-9f57-12d4f4959a4c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{11}{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6029d8a7-a6ae-5959-9ee4-f8e3ebd8e072" :answer/id #uuid "6029d8a7-a6ae-5959-9ee4-f8e3ebd8e072" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{14}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-21702398-6680-552d-923f-027dff95a35a" :answer/id #uuid "21702398-6680-552d-923f-027dff95a35a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ea8f272e-677d-5489-96d8-1e29db88e990" :answer/id #uuid "ea8f272e-677d-5489-96d8-1e29db88e990" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-78ae96ca-4942-5362-807b-c0b65d2496c2" :answer/id #uuid "78ae96ca-4942-5362-807b-c0b65d2496c2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7}{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135122 :tutorial/content "Until now, we've been dealing with line integrals with respect to arc length. In this lesson, we will learn about other types of line integral. 

Suppose that $C$ is a path in the $xy$-plane with initial point $A$ and terminal point $B.$ The line integral of the function $f(x,y)$ **with respect to $\boldsymbol x$** along the path $C$ is denoted

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d x.
$$

To understand what this integral represents, we imagine traversing $C$ from $A$ to $B.$ At each point $P$ that lies on $C,$ we project the point on $f$ that lies directly above $P$ onto the plane $y=0.$ Doing this for every point on $C$ traces out a curve. The line integral of $f$ with respect to $x$ gives the (signed) area bounded by this curve and the $x$-axis.

![](images/62/62c07a36cbf79459021ee7be125536a8f9c1bc3c193a99eabfcd3fc851b8eb0c.png)

To calculate a line integral with respect to $x,$ we must first parameterize $C$ using a parameter $t\in [a,b].$ Then, we apply the change of variables formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}x  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Let's take a look at a concrete example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133995 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162107 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c60b1a3b-1eee-5254-929b-6a532b619fd6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-c60b1a3b-1eee-5254-929b-6a532b619fd6" :question/id #uuid "c60b1a3b-1eee-5254-929b-6a532b619fd6" :question/math-academy-id "q-143431" :question/problem "A sample ${X}_{1},{X}_{2}$ of two pineapples is drawn from a population. The population has pineapples of two different weights, $1\,\text{kg}$ and $1.5\,\text{kg},$ distributed in the ratio $1:4.$ Calculate the standard error of $\overset{―}{X}.$ Round your answer to two decimal places." :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population variance ${\sigma }^{2},$ then

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We're told that the pineapples in the population have weights $1\,\text{kg}$ and $\text{1.5}\,\text{kg},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $1:4.$ Therefore, to compute the population's mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $1+4=5$ pineapples only with the following weights:

$$
1\,\text{kg},\,1.5\,\text{kg},\,1.5\,\text{kg},\,1.5\,\text{kg},\,1.5\,\text{kg}.
$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1+4\cdot 1.5) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1+6) \\  & =\frac{7}{5} \\  & =1.4\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

and the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}({1}^{2}+4\cdot {1.5}^{2})-{1.4}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(10)-1.96 \\  & =2-1.96 \\  & =0.04\,{\text{kg}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the sample size is $n=2,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}=\frac{0.04}{2}=0.02\,{\text{kg}}^{2}.
$$

Finally,

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{0.02}≈0.14\,\text{kg}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-784c4051-09fc-584b-bc9b-b914c96abf6f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Find the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 6 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

If $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ then what is the value of ${x}_{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "Remember, the order of the vectors in a basis is important.

Notice that 

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}={{(\,6\,)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{{(\,-3\,)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}}
$$

which means that

$$
x=6\cdot {b}_{1}+(-3)\cdot {b}_{2}
$$

and therefore

$$
[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we have that ${x}_{2}=-3.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7bb29f16-8d05-55d0-ab1d-19d482085ecc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} matrix, $Q$ is a $5\times 7$ matrix, and $R$ is a $7\times 2$ matrix, in which of the following expressions are the Hadamard products well-defined?

I. $PQ⊙R$

II. $PQ⊙{R}^{T}$

III. $(PQ)^{T}⊙R$" :question/worked-solution "The Hadamard product of two matrices (or vectors) is only defined if they have the same dimensions.

Let's consider each expression in turn:

- The dimensions of $PQ$ are $2\times 7,$ and the dimensions of $R$ are $7\times 2.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression I is *not* well-defined.

- The dimensions of $PQ$ are $2\times 7,$ and the dimensions of ${R}^{T}$ are $2\times 7.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression II is well-defined.

- The dimensions of $(PQ)^{T}$ are $7\times 2,$ and the dimensions of $R$ are $7\times 2.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression III is well-defined.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-06b8bf76-c702-59e2-a003-890dc8fb5ea1"] :db/ensure Which of the following is logically equivalent to the conditional predicate above?" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote by $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ the following predicates:

- $P(x):$ $x\in (0,2).$

- $Q(x):$ $|x|<2.$

Then, our initial sentence can be written as $P(x)⇒Q(x),$ which is logically equivalent to 

$$
¬P(x)∨Q(x).
$$

The negation of $P(x)$ can be written as

- $¬P(x):$ $x\notin (0,2).$

Therefore, the given sentence is logically equivalent to the following:

$\,$ $x\notin (0,2),$ or $|x|<2.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8a43a5f5-8ea0-5a0e-95e4-95914ae5bdd0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/problem "Calculate $\int \frac{9x-38}{(4-x)^{2}(2-x)}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{9x-38}{(4-x)^{2}(2-x)}=\frac{A}{(4-x)}+\frac{B}{(4-x)^{2}}+\frac{C}{(2-x)}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(4-x)^{2}(2-x)$ and get

$$
9x-38=A(4-x)(2-x)+B(2-x)+C(4-x)^{2}.
$$

Plugging in $x=4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $C$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9(4)-38 & =A(4-4)(2-4)+B(2-4)+C(4-4)^{2} \\ 36-38 & =B(-2) \\ B & =\frac{-2}{-2} \\ B & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=2,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9(2)-38 & =A(4-2)(2-2)+B(2-2)+C(4-2)^{2} \\ 18-38 & =C{(2)}^{2} \\ C & =\frac{-20}{4} \\ C & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known values of $B$ and $C,$ we can solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9(0)-38 & =A(4-0)(2-0)+B(2-0)+C(4-0)^{2} \\ -38 & =8A+2B+16C \\ -38 & =8A+2(1)+16(-5) \\ -38 & =8A-78 \\ 8A & =78-38 \\ A & =\frac{40}{8} \\ A & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{9x-38}{(4-x)^{2}(2-x)}=\frac{5}{(4-x)}+\frac{1}{(4-x)^{2}}-\frac{5}{(2-x)}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9x-38}{(4-x)^{2}(2-x)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{5}{(4-x)}+\frac{1}{(4-x)^{2}}-\frac{5}{(2-x)})\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \frac{1}{4-x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{(4-x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x-5\int \frac{1}{2-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-5\operatorname{ln}⁡|4-x|+\frac{1}{4-x}+5\operatorname{ln}⁡|2-x|+K,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K$ is an integral constant." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a1fdb08d-4e9a-5aa1-bf2f-9d236664e6fc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} :question/problem "Find the equation of the tangent line to the polar curve $r=1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ at $\theta =\pi ,$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "To find the equation of the tangent line to a polar curve at a point $P,$ we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi } \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )}{-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )} \\  & =\frac{-1-2\cdot 0}{-0-2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{-1}{-2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (-1) \\  & =-1 \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi  \\  & =(1-0)\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(-1,0).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the tangent:

We find the equation of the tangent as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (x-(-1)) \\ y-0 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (x+1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

*Hint: Try to factor the denominator first.*" :question/worked-solution "First, factoring the denominator and using partial fractions, we can write the series as

$$
\frac{1}{{n}^{2}+5n+6}=\frac{1}{(n+2)(n+3)}=\frac{1}{n+2}-\frac{1}{n+3}.
$$

So, our series can be written as

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{1}{n+2}-\frac{1}{n+3}).
$$

Let's now compute the first few partial sums:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{1} & =(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}) \\ {s}_{2} & =(\frac{1}{3}-\cancel{\frac{1}{4}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{4}}-\frac{1}{5}) \\ {s}_{3} & =(\frac{1}{3}-\cancel{\frac{1}{4}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{4}}-\cancel{\frac{1}{5}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{5}}-\frac{1}{6}) \\ {s}_{4} & =(\frac{1}{3}-\cancel{\frac{1}{4}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{4}}-\cancel{\frac{1}{5}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{5}}-\cancel{\frac{1}{6}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{6}}-\frac{1}{7})\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that for each partial sum, we always end up canceling all terms except for the first and last terms. Therefore, the $N$th partial sum is

$$
{s}_{N}=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{N+3}.
$$

Finally, we can determine the sum of the series by taking the limit of ${s}_{N}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(n+2)(n+3)} & ={lim}_{N\to \infty }{s}_{N} \\  & ={lim}_{N\to \infty }(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{N+3}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186099909 :answer-field/correct 17592186099914 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id $u={x}^{2}-1.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,x\text{d}x=\frac{\text{d}u}{2}.
$$

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $1$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $0$ | $3$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}x\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3})|}_{0}^{3} \\  & ={\frac{{u}^{3/2}}{3}|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{{3}^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{{0}^{3/2}}{3} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-eb85d00d-c4fb-5b35-911e-a717db9a9969"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Find its average position between $2$ and $6$ seconds." :question/worked-solution "To calculate the average value of the position on $[{t}_{1},{t}_{2}],$ we use the average value formula

$$
{x}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{{t}_{2}-{t}_{1}}\,{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{6-2}\,{\int }_{2}^{6}2{e}^{t/2}\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {2\cdot 2({e}^{t/2})|}_{2}^{6} \\  & ={e}^{6/2}-{e}^{2/2} \\  & ={e}^{3}-e.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average position is $({e}^{3}-e)\,\text{m}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8eb043c2-db7d-5e14-932d-20ffb968ecb7"] :db/ensure Which integral gives the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?" :question/worked-solution "The volume of the solid generated when the region bounded by a curve $x=g(y),$ the $y$-axis, and the horizontal lines $y=c$ and $y=d$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
V=\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}[g(y)]^{2}\text{d}y.
$$

First, we write our equation in terms of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{x+2} \\ {y}^{2} & =x+2 \\ x & ={y}^{2}-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, in our example, $g(y)={y}^{2}-2$ and the limits of integration are from $y=2$ to $y=3.$

Finally, the volume can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}{[g(y)]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{3}{({y}^{2}-2)}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{3}({y}^{4}-4{y}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-315a9bb0-48e8-569d-b07b-4a5644ec8264"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Which expression gives the total finite area enclosed between the curves $x={y}^{4}$ and $x={y}^{2},$ as shown above?

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*" :question/worked-solution "Let $f(y)={y}^{4}$ and $g(y)={y}^{2}.$ First, we find the intersections of the two curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ {y}^{4} & ={y}^{2} \\ {y}^{4}-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ {y}^{2}({y}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ {y}^{2}(y-1)(y+1) & =0 \\ y & =-1,0,1\end{aligned}
$$

The area we want consists of two regions: ${A}_{1}$ and ${A}_{2}.$

![](images/8b/8b4cbf07b9c2a6d949a58f39489889d2a3fdd4690664e530386f6f61d9aac5fd.png)

- For the area ${A}_{1},$ we have $y\in [-1,0],$ and the right function is $g(y)$ while the left function is $f(y).$ So, the area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(g(y)-f(y))\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}({y}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the area ${A}_{2},$ we have $y\in [0,1],$ and the right function is $g(y)$ while the left function is $f(y).$ So, the area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(g(y)-f(y))\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}={\int }_{-1}^{0}({y}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bfc1653c-6513-5ab7-95f5-3af895b0238c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "![](images/d4/d4bcdb6515b262c070c7ed689263efbbde8a350ad6a28b4fc106de281e69ff46.png)

Find the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=2t,\,y=t\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [0,\pi ].$" :question/worked-solution "The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\ge 0$ for all $t\in [0,\pi ].$

To solve the above integral, we use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡t & ⇒ & v=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =2t(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-2(\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -0\operatorname{cos}⁡0)+2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =-2\pi (-1) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9aa35e99-bfe0-504f-b448-591e82ea534a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =2{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x){|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡0-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2a)) \\  & =0-(-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e62dccaf-73d1-5442-9e53-eebdcd332113"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id \frac{{tanh}^{2}⁡(3x-2)}{3}\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the secant-tangent identity 

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the hyperbolic secant-tangent identity:

$$
1-{tanh}^{2}⁡\theta ={sech}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

Setting $\theta =3x-2,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{tanh}^{2}⁡(3x-2) & ={sech}^{2}⁡(3x-2) \\ {tanh}^{2}⁡(3x-2) & =1-{sech}^{2}⁡(3x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{tanh}^{2}⁡(3x-2)}{3}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int (1-{sech}^{2}⁡(3x-2))\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int 1\cdot \text{d}x-\frac{1}{3}\int {sech}^{2}⁡(3x-2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{x}{3}-\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{tanh}⁡(3x-2)+C.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-faa2ee71-4e17-514a-a333-0d36f72cde02"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "![](images/31/31d4236bf58cd579c49c7259c32a2a9171e07c771b4c34040ac92896809f695f.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x=\frac{2}{y}$ and $x=3-y$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=-2.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?" :question/worked-solution "First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{y} & =3-y \\ 2 & =3y-{y}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-3y+2 & =0 \\ (y-1)(y-2) & =0 \\ y & =1,2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $y=1$ to $y=2.$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](images/b7/b73c341f4d09b1df7bea162bc7dbe10d0ee60920c847f9c24210386a3d139e61.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=\frac{2}{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=3-y.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=3-y.$

![](images/c8/c8c8e766c66e47a54f316f54893d603b245acec8f529da3a5033d2bba547a319.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(3-y)-(-2)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[5-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=\frac{2}{y}.$

![](images/1b/1b31331f1c0da353bee6fe29d10e9e58dd531cbc8152cbce214d1adea771b032.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[\,(\frac{2}{y})-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[\frac{2}{y}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[5-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[\frac{2}{y}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({[5-y]}^{2}-{[\frac{2}{y}+2]}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-24a6b34c-6b2b-59cf-97a5-55f1d3c4912c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id
