Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le 3-\frac{3x}{4}-\frac{z}{2}\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/cd/cd84968e9e5300a18d087ba566202aba2b7166818a590cca03eac90d4f3f7a89.png)

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,0\le y\le 3-\frac{3x}{4}-\frac{z}{2}\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}8x\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3-3x/4-z/2}8x\,dy\,dz\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3-3x/4-z/2}8x\,dy\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{3-3x/4-z/2}8x\,dy]dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}8x[y]_{y=0}^{y=3-3x/4-z/2}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}8x(3-\frac{3x}{4}-\frac{z}{2})\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(24x-6{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(24x-6{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{3}(24x-6{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[24xz-6{x}^{2}z-2x{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=3}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(72x-18{x}^{2}-18x)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(54x-18{x}^{2})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(54x-18{x}^{2})\,dx & ={[27{x}^{2}-6{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =(27-6)-0 \\  & =21.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-36d55e5e-4911-5da7-af48-d3ee67db6281"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-36d55e5e-4911-5da7-af48-d3ee67db6281" :answer-field/id #uuid "36d55e5e-4911-5da7-af48-d3ee67db6281" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-2d8a1e4b-eb13-5f55-ba55-4b5dc6ff93cb" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b4001b41-6468-5fa7-9631-47ce66435f95" "answer-d304075d-a560-5677-ac5a-03672fe435b6" "answer-af68ffb6-0b68-527c-9426-425189a60c7e" "answer-2d8a1e4b-eb13-5f55-ba55-4b5dc6ff93cb" "answer-89ab1fef-8fcd-5fa1-bf90-fadaaa814b18"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b4001b41-6468-5fa7-9631-47ce66435f95" :answer/id #uuid "b4001b41-6468-5fa7-9631-47ce66435f95" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-18" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d304075d-a560-5677-ac5a-03672fe435b6" :answer/id #uuid "d304075d-a560-5677-ac5a-03672fe435b6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "18" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-af68ffb6-0b68-527c-9426-425189a60c7e" :answer/id #uuid "af68ffb6-0b68-527c-9426-425189a60c7e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "19" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2d8a1e4b-eb13-5f55-ba55-4b5dc6ff93cb" :answer/id #uuid "2d8a1e4b-eb13-5f55-ba55-4b5dc6ff93cb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "21" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-89ab1fef-8fcd-5fa1-bf90-fadaaa814b18" :answer/id #uuid "89ab1fef-8fcd-5fa1-bf90-fadaaa814b18" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "25" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281358 :question/worked-solution "![](images/91/9165163be9ce95e7165f04d26e6ce8080699ab4d477eba3f804c849fdf1fb679.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le 4-z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/ca/ca74bf149c1371fe9f1622586d9eb92fe180a9c9bb6a0c53d16f538b3c55f4a4.png)

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,0\le y\le 4-z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}4{x}^{2}z\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4-z}4{x}^{2}z\,dy\,dz\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4-z}4{x}^{2}z\,dy\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{4-z}4{x}^{2}z\,dy]dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{2}z[y]_{y=0}^{y=4-z}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{2}z(4-z)\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(16{x}^{2}z-4{x}^{2}{z}^{2})\,dz\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(16{x}^{2}z-4{x}^{2}{z}^{2})\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{3}(16{x}^{2}z-4{x}^{2}{z}^{2})\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[8{x}^{2}{z}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{x}^{2}{z}^{3}]_{z=0}^{z=3}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}36{x}^{2}\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}36{x}^{2}\,dx & ={[12{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =(12-0) \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-9c0ba772-2d81-508b-bca4-4e2298a7113a" :question/id #uuid "9c0ba772-2d81-508b-bca4-4e2298a7113a" :question/math-academy-id "q-163509" :question/problem "![](images/33/335bf5e4e2a4ee9d0286eadb968e0e82c6afb18d47cd5258d6d1b6cee3d5c5a6.png)

Given that $R$ is the type III region shown above, 
${∭}_{R}xz\,\text{d}V=$" :question/worked-solution "For a type III region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type III region enclosed between the back surface $y={u}_{1}(x,z)=1$ and the front surface $y={u}_{2}(x,z)=3.$

![](images/b1/b176bcf502a0801eae2bf470dfe4bf92852a34b06675fd74be78b30ccb4f6469.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,1\le y\le 3\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I *plane* region in the $xz$-plane with the upper curve

$$
z=1-{x}^{2}.
$$

![](images/eb/eb054b5f1567aa2c56842d79133fbbefc41a8b40730c688381d88e3ef06ccab7.png)

Hence, $D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le z\le 1-{x}^{2}\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type III region enclosed between the back surface $y={u}_{1}(x,z)=1$ and the front surface $y={u}_{2}(x,z)=2.$

![](images/2f/2f1112a1fa4e540ce8ef2d1337383a2adcb378ba519cfb9c49a4521e5bc1b02f.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,1\le y\le 2\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type II *plane* region in the $xz$-plane with the left curve

$$
x={z}^{2}.
$$

![](images/2d/2dcbae12ed3351892c63117f86bab7ffe6e1818b7a16666b42c2efdcc6bd787f.png)

Hence, $D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,{z}^{2}\le x\le 1\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2y\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}[{y}^{2}]_{y=1}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}3\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-47db12a1-3244-5a01-bb35-553d717703fe"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :answer.type/math :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135158 :tutorial/content "Let's evaluate the triple integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R 2xz  \: \mathrm{d}V
$$

where the region $R$ is shown below.

![](images/9b/9b00702b941e40061ff242e63c0d1b33642cce9aefc1ffa9f88e9d94cd02897a.png)

 

The region $R$ is a type III region. So, our first task is to describe this region fully.

We start by drawing an arrow parallel to the $y$-axis that 

- enters the region through the *left* surface $y=0,$ and

- leave the region through the *right* surface $y=6-x-z,$

as shown below.

![](images/51/5102f786fa91eb862fd3f5ef8f0b2cbc85fbdff6fc616f86f498aa0da8088f14.png)

 

So, our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (x,z) \in D, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 6-x-z \big\},
$$

where

$$
D = \big\{ (x,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 3, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1 \big\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/30/30f320f2e77c95c13e59bc3fdd6b273d1ad367018af3cd12bd6d2fde7cc09132.png)

To evaluate our triple integral, we start by expressing it as a mixed integral:

$$
\iiint\limits_R 2xz \:\textrm{d}V
=
\iint\limits_D \left[ \int_{0}^{6-x-z} 2xz \:\textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}A
$$

Now, since the region $D$ is a type I *plane* region, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 3, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 6-x-z \big\},
$$

and therefore, our mixed integral can be written as the following repeating integral:

$$
\iint\limits_D \left[ \int_0^{6-x-z} 2xz \:\textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}A
=
\int_{0}^{3} \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{6-x-z} 2xz \:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}x
$$

Evaluating this using the usual methods, we get

$$
\int_{0}^{3} \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{6-x-z} 2xz \:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}x = 15.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\iiint\limits_R 2xz \:\textrm{d}V = 15.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135159 :tutorial/content "When writing down a triple integral as a repeated integral, we can often skip the intermediate step of expressing our triple integral as a mixed integral.

$$

where $R$ is the type III region given by 

$$
R= \big\{(x,y,z) \: : \: {\color{red}a} \leq x \leq {\color{red}b}, \: {\color{blue}v_1(x)} \leq z \leq {\color{blue}v_2(x)}, \: {\color{purple}u_1(x,z)} \leq y \leq {\color{purple}u_2(x,z)} \big\}.
$$

Notice that the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane is a type II plane region. Therefore, we can immediately express our triple integral as follows:

$$
\iiint\limits_R f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}V
=
\int_{\color{red}a}^{\color{red}b} \int_{\color{blue}v_1(x)}^{\color{blue}v_2(x)} \int_{\color{purple}u_1(x,z)}^{\color{purple}u_2(x,z)} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}x

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-2,3)$ to the point $(0,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2t-2,\,3-3t⟩.$*"] ["question-ca5fbd9d-06c2-5516-a2aa-caaa1b2a1fc6" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-2,3)$ and $(0,0).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-2+t(0-(-2))),\,(3+t(0-3))⟩ \\  & =⟨2t-2,\,3-3t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-2)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2t-2)^{2}(3-3t) \\  & =4(t-1)^{2}\cdot 3(1-t) \\  & =-12(t-1)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-12(t-1)^{3}\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & =-24{\int }_{0}^{1}(t-1)^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ca5fbd9d-06c2-5516-a2aa-caaa1b2a1fc6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d86ee8d9-aeae-5ab1-b4a0-98c765570dca" :answer-field/id #uuid Evaluate ${\int }_{C}({y}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(2,3),$ as shown above."] ["question-ada3d128-ac86-51c2-88c8-3e672e4cad88" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(0,1)$ and $(2,3).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(0+t(2-0)),\,(1+t(3-1))⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,1+2t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={y}^{2}-2x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(1+2t)^{2}-2(2t) \\  & =1+4t+4{t}^{2}-4t \\  & =4{t}^{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+1)\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{[\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}+t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2(\frac{4}{3}+1)-2(0) \\  & =\frac{14}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ada3d128-ac86-51c2-88c8-3e672e4cad88" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-8b9c47c5-4e96-58fa-ac91-5791dc11f30c" :answer-field/id #uuid been dealing with line integrals with respect to arc length. In this lesson, we will learn about other types of line integral. 

Suppose that $C$ is a path in the $xy$-plane with initial point $A$ and terminal point $B.$ The line integral of the function $f(x,y)$ **with respect to $\boldsymbol x$** along the path $C$ is denoted

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d x.
$$

To understand what this integral represents, we imagine traversing $C$ from $A$ to $B.$ At each point $P$ that lies on $C,$ we project the point on $f$ that lies directly above $P$ onto the plane $y=0.$ Doing this for every point on $C$ traces out a curve. The line integral of $f$ with respect to $x$ gives the (signed) area bounded by this curve and the $x$-axis.

![](images/62/62c07a36cbf79459021ee7be125536a8f9c1bc3c193a99eabfcd3fc851b8eb0c.png)

To calculate a line integral with respect to $x,$ we must first parameterize $C$ using a parameter $t\in [a,b].$ Then, we apply the change of variables formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}x  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Let's take a look at a concrete example."] [17592186133995 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0] ["question-c60b1a3b-1eee-5254-929b-6a532b619fd6" :question/id #uuid "c60b1a3b-1eee-5254-929b-6a532b619fd6"] ["question-c60b1a3b-1eee-5254-929b-6a532b619fd6" :question/math-academy-id "q-143431"] ["question-c60b1a3b-1eee-5254-929b-6a532b619fd6" :question/problem "A sample ${X}_{1},{X}_{2}$ of two pineapples is drawn from a population. The population has pineapples of two different weights, $1\,\text{kg}$ and $1.5\,\text{kg},$ distributed in the ratio $1:4.$ Calculate the standard error of $\overset{―}{X}.$ Round your answer to two decimal places."] ["question-c60b1a3b-1eee-5254-929b-6a532b619fd6" :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population variance ${\sigma }^{2},$ then

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We're told that the pineapples in the population have weights $1\,\text{kg}$ and $\text{1.5}\,\text{kg},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $1:4.$ Therefore, to compute the population's mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $1+4=5$ pineapples only with the following weights:

$$
1\,\text{kg},\,1.5\,\text{kg},\,1.5\,\text{kg},\,1.5\,\text{kg},\,1.5\,\text{kg}.
$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1+4\cdot 1.5) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1+6) \\  & =\frac{7}{5} \\  & =1.4\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

and the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}({1}^{2}+4\cdot {1.5}^{2})-{1.4}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(10)-1.96 \\  & =2-1.96 \\  & =0.04\,{\text{kg}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the sample size is $n=2,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}=\frac{0.04}{2}=0.02\,{\text{kg}}^{2}.
$$

Finally,

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{0.02}≈0.14\,\text{kg}.
$$"] ["question-c60b1a3b-1eee-5254-929b-6a532b619fd6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-784c4051-09fc-584b-bc9b-b914c96abf6f" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-9c36f01c-b274-57ce-a233-5c5a47d4ef94" :question/math-academy-id "q-274929"] ["question-9c36f01c-b274-57ce-a233-5c5a47d4ef94" :question/problem "Given that $P$ is a $2\times 5$ matrix, $Q$ is a $5\times 7$ matrix, and $R$ is a $7\times 2$ matrix, in which of the following expressions are the Hadamard products well-defined?

I. $PQ⊙R$

II. $PQ⊙{R}^{T}$

III. $(PQ)^{T}⊙R$"] ["question-9c36f01c-b274-57ce-a233-5c5a47d4ef94" :question/worked-solution "The Hadamard product of two matrices (or vectors) is only defined if they have the same dimensions.

Let's consider each expression in turn:

- The dimensions of $PQ$ are $2\times 7,$ and the dimensions of $R$ are $7\times 2.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression I is *not* well-defined.

- The dimensions of $PQ$ are $2\times 7,$ and the dimensions of ${R}^{T}$ are $2\times 7.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression II is well-defined.

["question-504684ef-507d-57b1-81c3-7c9672d3e28f" :question/math-academy-id "q-11372"] ["question-504684ef-507d-57b1-81c3-7c9672d3e28f" :question/problem "Calculate $\int \frac{9x-38}{(4-x)^{2}(2-x)}\,\text{d}x.$"] ["question-504684ef-507d-57b1-81c3-7c9672d3e28f" :question/worked-solution "First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{9x-38}{(4-x)^{2}(2-x)}=\frac{A}{(4-x)}+\frac{B}{(4-x)^{2}}+\frac{C}{(2-x)}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(4-x)^{2}(2-x)$ and get

$$
9x-38=A(4-x)(2-x)+B(2-x)+C(4-x)^{2}.
$$

Plugging in $x=4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $C$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9(4)-38 & =A(4-4)(2-4)+B(2-4)+C(4-4)^{2} \\ 36-38 & =B(-2) \\ B & =\frac{-2}{-2} \\ B & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=2,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9(2)-38 & =A(4-2)(2-2)+B(2-2)+C(4-2)^{2} \\ 18-38 & =C{(2)}^{2} \\ C & =\frac{-20}{4} \\ C & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known values of $B$ and $C,$ we can solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9(0)-38 & =A(4-0)(2-0)+B(2-0)+C(4-0)^{2} \\ -38 & =8A+2B+16C \\ -38 & =8A+2(1)+16(-5) \\ -38 & =8A-78 \\ 8A & =78-38 \\ A & =\frac{40}{8} \\ A & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{9x-38}{(4-x)^{2}(2-x)}=\frac{5}{(4-x)}+\frac{1}{(4-x)^{2}}-\frac{5}{(2-x)}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9x-38}{(4-x)^{2}(2-x)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{5}{(4-x)}+\frac{1}{(4-x)^{2}}-\frac{5}{(2-x)})\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \frac{1}{4-x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{(4-x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x-5\int \frac{1}{2-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-5\operatorname{ln}⁡|4-x|+\frac{1}{4-x}+5\operatorname{ln}⁡|2-x|+K,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K$ is an integral constant."] ["question-504684ef-507d-57b1-81c3-7c9672d3e28f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-a1fdb08d-4e9a-5aa1-bf2f-9d236664e6fc" \begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-0e54ebb5-b13c-5b43-a434-8a77b6f9b884" :question/worked-solution "To find the equation of the tangent line to a polar curve at a point $P,$ we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi } \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )}{-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )} \\  & =\frac{-1-2\cdot 0}{-0-2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{-1}{-2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (-1) \\  & =-1 \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi  \\  & =(1-0)\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(-1,0).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the tangent:

We find the equation of the tangent as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (x-(-1)) \\ y-0 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (x+1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

*Hint: Try to factor the denominator first.*"] [17592186101458 :question/worked-solution "First, factoring the denominator and using partial fractions, we can write the series as

$$
\frac{1}{{n}^{2}+5n+6}=\frac{1}{(n+2)(n+3)}=\frac{1}{n+2}-\frac{1}{n+3}.
$$

So, our series can be written as

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{1}{n+2}-\frac{1}{n+3}).
$$

Let's now compute the first few partial sums:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{1} & =(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}) \\ {s}_{2} & =(\frac{1}{3}-\cancel{\frac{1}{4}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{4}}-\frac{1}{5}) \\ {s}_{3} & =(\frac{1}{3}-\cancel{\frac{1}{4}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{4}}-\cancel{\frac{1}{5}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{5}}-\frac{1}{6}) \\ {s}_{4} & =(\frac{1}{3}-\cancel{\frac{1}{4}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{4}}-\cancel{\frac{1}{5}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{5}}-\cancel{\frac{1}{6}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{6}}-\frac{1}{7})\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that for each partial sum, we always end up canceling all terms except for the first and last terms. Therefore, the $N$th partial sum is

$$
{s}_{N}=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{N+3}.
$$

Finally, we can determine the sum of the series by taking the limit of ${s}_{N}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(n+2)(n+3)} & ={lim}_{N\to \infty }{s}_{N} \\  & ={lim}_{N\to \infty }(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{N+3}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186101458 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] [17592186099909 :answer-field/correct 17592186099914] ["answer-field-7e7684e4-e06c-57a4-94c9-8c4065eb02cc" :answer-field/id #uuid }_{1}^{2}x\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\,\text{d}x.$"] ["question-dc80cc6c-733b-50ec-85a0-e9f5b6f29bef" :question/worked-solution "Let $u={x}^{2}-1.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,x\text{d}x=\frac{\text{d}u}{2}.
$$

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $1$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $0$ | $3$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}x\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3})|}_{0}^{3} \\  & ={\frac{{u}^{3/2}}{3}|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{{3}^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{{0}^{3/2}}{3} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-dc80cc6c-733b-50ec-85a0-e9f5b6f29bef" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-eb85d00d-c4fb-5b35-911e-a717db9a9969" :answer-field/id #uuid Find its average position between $2$ and $6$ seconds."] ["question-881af2f1-aaf5-5e5d-a46a-df43ce3ea5ee" :question/worked-solution "To calculate the average value of the position on $[{t}_{1},{t}_{2}],$ we use the average value formula

$$
{x}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{{t}_{2}-{t}_{1}}\,{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{6-2}\,{\int }_{2}^{6}2{e}^{t/2}\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {2\cdot 2({e}^{t/2})|}_{2}^{6} \\  & ={e}^{6/2}-{e}^{2/2} \\  & ={e}^{3}-e.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average position is $({e}^{3}-e)\,\text{m}.$"] ["question-881af2f1-aaf5-5e5d-a46a-df43ce3ea5ee" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-d18dd5ed-e185-5cfc-926d-0d7b2a92c6df" :question/worked-solution "The volume of the solid generated when the region bounded by a curve $x=g(y),$ the $y$-axis, and the horizontal lines $y=c$ and $y=d$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
V=\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}[g(y)]^{2}\text{d}y.
$$

First, we write our equation in terms of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{x+2} \\ {y}^{2} & =x+2 \\ x & ={y}^{2}-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, in our example, $g(y)={y}^{2}-2$ and the limits of integration are from $y=2$ to $y=3.$

Finally, the volume can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}{[g(y)]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{3}{({y}^{2}-2)}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{3}({y}^{4}-4{y}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-d18dd5ed-e185-5cfc-926d-0d7b2a92c6df" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-315a9bb0-48e8-569d-b07b-4a5644ec8264" :answer-field/id #uuid *(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*"] ["question-33a96099-4464-57a6-87f9-11f8046b2b50" :question/worked-solution "Let $f(y)={y}^{4}$ and $g(y)={y}^{2}.$ First, we find the intersections of the two curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ {y}^{4} & ={y}^{2} \\ {y}^{4}-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ {y}^{2}({y}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ {y}^{2}(y-1)(y+1) & =0 \\ y & =-1,0,1\end{aligned}
$$

The area we want consists of two regions: ${A}_{1}$ and ${A}_{2}.$

![](images/8b/8b4cbf07b9c2a6d949a58f39489889d2a3fdd4690664e530386f6f61d9aac5fd.png)

- For the area ${A}_{1},$ we have $y\in [-1,0],$ and the right function is $g(y)$ while the left function is $f(y).$ So, the area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(g(y)-f(y))\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}({y}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the area ${A}_{2},$ we have $y\in [0,1],$ and the right function is $g(y)$ while the left function is $f(y).$ So, the area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(g(y)-f(y))\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}={\int }_{-1}^{0}({y}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-33a96099-4464-57a6-87f9-11f8046b2b50" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-bfc1653c-6513-5ab7-95f5-3af895b0238c" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
x=2t,\,y=t\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [0,\pi ].$"] ["question-8222fa21-5fa3-52f1-a894-4b100aeb534d" :question/worked-solution "The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\ge 0$ for all $t\in [0,\pi ].$

To solve the above integral, we use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡t & ⇒ & v=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =2t(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-2(\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -0\operatorname{cos}⁡0)+2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =-2\pi (-1) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8222fa21-5fa3-52f1-a894-4b100aeb534d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-9aa35e99-bfe0-504f-b448-591e82ea534a" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Evaluate ${\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.$"] ["question-46e4a876-e7eb-598f-bbec-ff44b3be1391" :question/worked-solution "We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =2{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x){|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡0-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2a)) \\  & =0-(-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-46e4a876-e7eb-598f-bbec-ff44b3be1391" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-e62dccaf-73d1-5442-9e53-eebdcd332113" :answer-field/id #uuid \frac{{tanh}^{2}⁡(3x-2)}{3}\,\text{d}x=$"] ["question-cef928b3-a5b9-5b14-83bc-17bf537996f2" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the secant-tangent identity 

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the hyperbolic secant-tangent identity:

$$
1-{tanh}^{2}⁡\theta ={sech}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

Setting $\theta =3x-2,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{tanh}^{2}⁡(3x-2) & ={sech}^{2}⁡(3x-2) \\ {tanh}^{2}⁡(3x-2) & =1-{sech}^{2}⁡(3x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{tanh}^{2}⁡(3x-2)}{3}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int (1-{sech}^{2}⁡(3x-2))\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int 1\cdot \text{d}x-\frac{1}{3}\int {sech}^{2}⁡(3x-2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{x}{3}-\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{tanh}⁡(3x-2)+C.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-cef928b3-a5b9-5b14-83bc-17bf537996f2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-faa2ee71-4e17-514a-a333-0d36f72cde02" :answer-field/id #uuid The region enclosed by the curves $x=\frac{2}{y}$ and $x=3-y$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=-2.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?"] ["question-7bcaaf90-d33e-5a2f-9583-78877f436c71" :question/worked-solution "First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{y} & =3-y \\ 2 & =3y-{y}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-3y+2 & =0 \\ (y-1)(y-2) & =0 \\ y & =1,2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $y=1$ to $y=2.$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](images/b7/b73c341f4d09b1df7bea162bc7dbe10d0ee60920c847f9c24210386a3d139e61.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=\frac{2}{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=3-y.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=3-y.$

![](images/c8/c8c8e766c66e47a54f316f54893d603b245acec8f529da3a5033d2bba547a319.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(3-y)-(-2)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[5-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=\frac{2}{y}.$

![](images/1b/1b31331f1c0da353bee6fe29d10e9e58dd531cbc8152cbce214d1adea771b032.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[\,(\frac{2}{y})-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[\frac{2}{y}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[5-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[\frac{2}{y}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({[5-y]}^{2}-{[\frac{2}{y}+2]}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-7bcaaf90-d33e-5a2f-9583-78877f436c71" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-24a6b34c-6b2b-59cf-97a5-55f1d3c4912c" :answer-field/id #uuid The base of a solid is the region enclosed by the curves $y=1-{x}^{2}$ and $y=-1,$  as shown in the picture. Cross-sections perpendicular to the $x$-axis are rectangles. If the height of each rectangle is $2$ times the length of its base, which integral gives the volume of the solid?"] ["question-8deca7b4-0aaf-504b-958b-1e6e90c74a93" :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)=1-{x}^{2}$ and $g(x)=-1.$

First, we determine the limits of integration. To do that, we find the intersections of the two curves by setting the functions equal to one another and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =g(x) \\ 1-{x}^{2} & =-1 \\ {x}^{2} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the limit of integration are $x=-\sqrt{2}$ and $x=\sqrt{2}.$

Now, consider a cross-section at some point $x$, where $x\in (-\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2})$,  and its projection on the $xy$-plane: 

![](images/0c/0c2a676ecc781a2a7a78870eb93ee9fbe5a89a7bd754a446231c6e3237f75831.png)

The base of the cross-section is

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =|f(x)-g(x)| \\  & =|1-{x}^{2}-(-1)| \\  & =|2-{x}^{2}|.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of a rectangle is
$A=bh.$
  So, since we have $h=2b,$ the expression for the area of the cross-section is

$$
\begin{aligned}A(x) & =bh \\  & =2{b}^{2} \\  & =2{(2-{x}^{2})}^{2} \\  & =8-8{x}^{2}+2{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now calculate the volume of the solid, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={\int }_{c}^{d}A(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}(8-8{x}^{2}+2{x}^{4})\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8deca7b4-0aaf-504b-958b-1e6e90c74a93" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-aeff073f-a16e-5f3f-a31e-6729474c2b63" :answer-field/id #uuid ${P}_{3}(x)$ be the third-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=1.$ Use the Lagrange error bound to find an upper bound for the error when ${P}_{3}(x)$ is used to approximate $\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$"] ["question-15fdecd3-2bb4-5c94-a4a3-305e0c26984d" :question/worked-solution "The Lagrange error bound states that an upper bound for the error ${R}_{3}$ obtained when using the third-degree Taylor polynomial ${P}_{3}$ to approximate $f(x)$ is given by

$$
|{R}_{3}|\le \frac{M}{4!}|x-1{|}^{4},
$$

where $M$ is the maximum value of $|{f}^{(4)}(x)|$ on the interval between $a=1$ and $x=2.$ 

Plugging $x=2$ into the above formula gives

$$
\begin{aligned}|{R}_{3}| & \le \frac{M}{4!}|2-1{|}^{4} \\ |{R}_{3}| & \le \frac{M}{24}|1{|}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find $M,$ we need to compute $|{f}^{(4)}(x)|$ and then maximize it on the interval $[1,2].$ Taking the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{2}{{x}^{3}} \\ {f}^{(4)}(x) & =-\frac{6}{{x}^{4}} \\ |{f}^{(4)}(x)| & =|-\frac{6}{{x}^{4}}|=\frac{6}{{x}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $|{f}^{(4)}(x)|=\frac{6}{{x}^{4}}$ is a decreasing function in the interval $[1,2],$  its value is greatest at $x=1.$ So

$$
M=|{f}^{(4)}(1)|=\frac{6}{(1)^{4}}=6,
$$

and therefore, the upper bound is

$$
|{R}_{3}|\le \frac{6}{24}|1{|}^{4}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$"] ["question-15fdecd3-2bb4-5c94-a4a3-305e0c26984d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-3dee6e17-9565-5642-81b9-7791c50bb056" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-743918b2-4124-5be2-a1fd-716500b8cb35" :question/math-academy-id "q-83470"] ["question-743918b2-4124-5be2-a1fd-716500b8cb35" :question/problem "The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨4{e}^{2t},\,9{e}^{3t}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(1,1)$ and has velocity $⟨2,4⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$"] ["question-743918b2-4124-5be2-a1fd-716500b8cb35" :question/worked-solution "To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨4{e}^{2t},\,9{e}^{3t}⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 4{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t,\int 9{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{2t}+{C}_{1},\,3{e}^{3t}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨2,4⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨2{e}^{2(0)}+{C}_{1},\,3{e}^{3(0)}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨2,4⟩ & =⟨2+{C}_{1},3+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=1.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v(t)=⟨2{e}^{2t},\,3{e}^{3t}+1⟩.
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2{e}^{2t},\,3{e}^{3t}+1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t,\int (3{e}^{3t}+1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{2t}+{C}_{3},\,{e}^{3t}+t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨1,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{e}^{2(0)}+{C}_{3},\,{e}^{3(0)}+0+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨1,1⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{3},\,1+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}={C}_{4}=0.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
r(t)=⟨{e}^{2t},\,{e}^{3t}+t⟩.
$$"] ["question-743918b2-4124-5be2-a1fd-716500b8cb35" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-6c828a93-5ad8-5389-8e1d-dff274396206" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "The rate of growth in the frog population $P(t)$ in a certain lake follows the logistic growth model

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=0.1P(5\,000-P),
$$

where $t$ is the time, in years. Find an expression for the frog population after $t$ years, given that there were $100$ frogs initially."] ["question-ea94a739-28fe-50a1-b5d4-4f34307441cf" :question/worked-solution "A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

The general solution to the logistic growth equation is

$$
P(t)=\frac{a}{1+C{e}^{-akt}}.
$$

In this case, the constant of proportionality is $k=0.1,$ and the carrying capacity is $a=5\,000.$ 

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
P(t)=\frac{5\,000}{1+C{e}^{-(5\,000\cdot 0.1)t}}=\frac{5\,000}{1+C{e}^{-500t}}.
$$

We now substitute the initial condition $P(0)=100$ and solve for $C.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5\,000}{1+C{e}^{-500\cdot 0}} & =100 \\ 1+C & =\frac{5\,000}{100} \\ C & =50-1 \\  & =49.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
P(t)=\frac{5\,000}{1+49{e}^{-500t}}.
$$"] ["question-ea94a739-28fe-50a1-b5d4-4f34307441cf" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-93650186-de97-555d-ac5a-338706314d50" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}2xyz\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le y+z\},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the line $y=1$ and the line $z=y$ in the first quadrant."] ["question-e31a3154-dd92-51e0-baa5-7e556d0b4865" :question/worked-solution "Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2xyz\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y+z}2xyz\,dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y+z}2xyz\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}yz[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=y+z}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}yz(y+z)^{2}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}yz({y}^{2}+2yz+{z}^{2})\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](images/59/5974f852ba8dcaf9e6c4d6323709987c590e2f739524e012545738bc4bb842b0.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{y}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}{z}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{2}{z}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}y{z}^{4}]}_{z=0}^{z=y}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}\cdot {y}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{2}\cdot {y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}y\cdot {y}^{4}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{17}{12}{y}^{5}\,dy \\  & =\frac{17}{12}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{5}\,dy \\  & =\frac{17}{12}{[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{6}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{17}{12}(\frac{1}{6}-0) \\  & =\frac{17}{72}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e31a3154-dd92-51e0-baa5-7e556d0b4865" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-3a706466-bb58-58a9-b091-d4ba42a7541f" :answer-field/id #uuid where $R$ is the type II region given by

$$
{∭}_{R}2\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-y-z}2\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-y-z}2\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{4-y-z}2\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[2x]_{x=0}^{x=4-y-z}dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2(4-y-z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}8-2y-2z\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z,$ treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}8-2y-2z\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}8-2y-2z\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[8z-2yz-{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}8-2y-1\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}7-2y\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}7-2y\,dy & ={[7y-{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =7-1 \\  & =6\end{aligned}

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 4-y+2z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 4,\,\,0\le z\le 3\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/27/27862dcc3effe5801c812f5c8944c0134d13bb38f99d337b0a4e20e9ff815639.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 4,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,0\le x\le 4-y+2z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{z}{12}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4-y+2z}\frac{z}{12}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4-y+2z}\frac{z}{12}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{4-y+2z}\frac{z}{12}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{z}{12}[x]_{x=0}^{x=4-y+2z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{z}{12}(4-y+2z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{12}(4z-yz+2{z}^{2})\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{12}(4z-yz+2{z}^{2})\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{12}(4z-yz+2{z}^{2})\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{12}{[2{z}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}y{z}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{z}^{3}]}_{z=0}^{z=3}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{12}(18-\frac{9}{2}y+18)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(3-\frac{3}{8}y)\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}(3-\frac{3}{8}y)\,dy & ={[3y-\frac{3}{16}{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=4} \\  & =(12-3)-0 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-00568ac8-b77a-5f52-9484-f19c655aa6d0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-332dc5a3-6077-5a95-b9d8-7163745f52d1" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 5-y-\frac{z}{2}\},

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 4\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/1b/1ba7c02f254313a73a813e4e43c44c25523ce77dd47e594a1db3b412a6bd5c3d.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 4,\,\,0\le x\le 5-y-\frac{z}{2}\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{5-y-z/2}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{5-y-z/2}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{5-y-z/2}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}[x]_{x=0}^{x=5-y-z/2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}(5-y-\frac{z}{2})\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{2}\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{2}\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{2}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{z}{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=4}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type II region enclosed between the back surface $x={u}_{1}(y,z)=1$ and the front surface $x={u}_{2}(y,z)=2.$

![](images/a3/a39d7a27f20283b6e6814db926801f16e3e2cb42c7fe16487350b536d3b63d3c.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,1\le x\le 2\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I *plane* region in the $yz$-plane with the upper curve

$$
z=1-(y-1)^{2}.
$$

![](images/50/5058493860a1c4d919e3cd6786bb1aca156ae83d47f766c087e351e9764929c4.png)

Hence, $D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,0\le z\le 1-(y-1)^{2}\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1-(y-1)^{2}}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1-(y-1)^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡z[{x}^{2}]_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1-(y-1)^{2}}3\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f2d33e33-cbe1-5877-8ed6-72bcb8e7fff5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-e767016c-6faf-58ba-ac6e-34fede0af637" :answer-field/id #uuid Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 2+2y-z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/14/145f0d494ffe24de84e3a289b3a7316d3f4933f193d734aed118609f7fb9f94f.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le x\le 2+2y-z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2+2y-z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(2+2y-z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{Δh}{Δt} & =\frac{h(b)-h(a)}{b-a} \\  & =\frac{h(4)-h(0)}{4-0} \\  & =\frac{[3({4}^{3/2})-2(4)]-[3({0}^{3/2})-2(0)]}{4} \\  & =\frac{24-8}{4} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=2]$ given that $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is ${\mu }_{Y|2}=\frac{11}{2}.$"] ["question-3104fe5f-1fab-5144-bd0b-8c85fa4d01fa" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=x] & =\text{E}[(Y-{\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\,|\,X=x] \\  & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{y}{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ let's first find the marginal distribution for $X,$ corresponding to the row totals: 

| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ | ${f}_{X}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=2$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |
| $X=4$ | $\frac{5}{16}$ | $\frac{1}{16}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x$ is

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)}.
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding row total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x:$

| ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=2$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ |
| $X=4$ | $\frac{5}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=2] & =[{\sum }_{y}{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,2)]-{\mu }_{Y|2}^{2} \\  & =[{2}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}+{4}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}+{8}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}]-{(\frac{11}{2})}^{2} \\  & =1+4+32-\frac{121}{4} \\  & =\frac{27}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-3104fe5f-1fab-5144-bd0b-8c85fa4d01fa" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-c14a0fdb-ff7e-57f0-b03c-3708c9d22c3b" :answer-field/id #uuid Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=4]$ given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is ${\mu }_{X|4}=\frac{4}{5}.$"] ["question-7e4093f7-c4fd-5107-9969-358e958506e1" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ let's first find the marginal distribution of $Y,$ corresponding to the column totals: 

| $f$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\frac{1}{16}$ | $\frac{3}{16}$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $\frac{5}{16}$ | $\frac{11}{16}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$ is

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding column total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y:$

| ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ | $\frac{3}{11}$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{4}{5}$ | $\frac{8}{11}$ |
|  | $1$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=4] & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,4)]-{\mu }_{X|4}^{2} \\  & =[{0}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{5}+{1}^{2}\cdot \frac{4}{5}]-{(\frac{4}{5})}^{2} \\  & =0+\frac{4}{5}-\frac{16}{25} \\  & =\frac{4}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-7e4093f7-c4fd-5107-9969-358e958506e1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-90de2426-d3b0-54f0-abb8-0e8cf9780d48" :answer-field/id #uuid $Y$ are discrete random variables, where the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is given by $\mu_{X|y}.$ In other words,

$$
\textrm{E}[X\,|\,Y=y] = \mu_{X|y}.
$$

The **conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$** is defined as

$$
\textrm{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] = \textrm{E}\big[(X - \mu_{X|y} \big)^2 \,|\, Y=y].
$$

This is similar to the definition of $\textrm{Var}[X]$ in that it represents the average  (squared) distance of the random variable $X$ from the mean. The difference here is that the expected values are now dependent on the outcome of $Y.$

Similarly to the case of $\textrm{Var}[X],$ this often isn't the easiest formula to use in practice. However, it can be shown that the definition of conditional variance is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where $f_{X|Y}(x \,|\, y)$ is the conditional PMF of $X$ given $Y.$ Note that these formulas are analogous to those for $\textrm{Var}[X].$

Finally, we have an analogous definition for the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=x] & =\text{E}[(Y-{\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\,|\,X=x] \\  & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{y}{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186188511 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0] [17592186278412 :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{3}.$*"] [17592186278391 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u+v,\,u,\,v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+-{1}^{2}+-{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & ={x}^{2}-2yz\,{|}_{x=u+v\,y=u\,z=v} \\  & =(u+v)^{2}-2uv \\  & ={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-2yz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}+{v}^{2})\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}({\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+u{v}^{2}]}_{u=-1}^{u=1}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{3}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{[\frac{2}{3}v+\frac{2}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186278427 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =2xz\,{|}_{x=u\,y=u+v\,z=2v} \\  & =2u(2v) \\  & =4uv\end{aligned}

Therefore, if we denote 

$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}2xz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,4uv\cdot 3\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{∬}_{D}\,4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =3\cdot [{u}^{2}]_{0}^{2}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =3\cdot 4\cdot 4 \\  & =48.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186278442 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨0,\,-8,\,-6⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+(-8)^{2}+(-6)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+64+36} \\  & =\sqrt{100} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

Therefore, if we denote

our surface integral can be written as

$$"] ["question-9473c03d-7209-5d2d-815a-9982b2c23f32" :question/id #uuid "9473c03d-7209-5d2d-815a-9982b2c23f32"] ["question-9473c03d-7209-5d2d-815a-9982b2c23f32" :question/math-academy-id "q-75267"] ["question-9473c03d-7209-5d2d-815a-9982b2c23f32" :question/problem "A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$"] ["question-9473c03d-7209-5d2d-815a-9982b2c23f32" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2(1)^{2}+8(1)=2+8=10, \\ y & =4(1)^{7}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(10,4).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4t+8,\,{y}^{′}(t)=28{t}^{6}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{28{t}^{6}}{4t+8}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =\frac{28\cdot (1)^{6}}{4\cdot (1)+8} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,4)$ and the slope $m=\frac{7}{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-4 & =\frac{7}{3}(x-10).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-9473c03d-7209-5d2d-815a-9982b2c23f32" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-84a0580e-1530-5142-8694-ea6e03c23e1e" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}x & =(2)^{2}+3(2)=10, \\ y & =1+\sqrt{2(2)}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(10,3).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+3,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}}{2t+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}(2t+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=2,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=2} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot 2}(2\cdot 2+3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,3)$ and the slope $m=\frac{1}{14}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{14}(x-10).\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{14}(0-10) \\ y-3 & =-\frac{5}{7} \\ y & =\frac{16}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}."] ["question-52b01e00-7882-5db4-abc3-b8cfaaac3472" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{2t}{10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,1} & =\frac{2(1)}{10({1}^{4})-12({1}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{10-12} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-2)} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the Cartesian equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-2,1)$ and the slope $m=-1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-1(x-(-2)) \\ y-1 & =-(x+2) \\ y & =-x-2+1 \\ y & =-x-1.\end{aligned}

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$"] ["question-5579ca0e-f803-5d9f-87c0-8c8636fd4e81" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}}{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t+1}})} \\  & =6{t}^{2}\sqrt{(t+1)}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =6\cdot {1}^{2}\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\sqrt{2},5)$ and the slope $m=6\sqrt{2}.$ We get

$$

{{field-2}}$).$"] ["question-cdc93f1c-a598-5c34-91ec-6e0adc895b1e" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=-1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(-1)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(-1)+\frac{3}{2}=1-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=2 \\ y & =(-1)^{3}+7(-1)^{2}+8(-1)=-1+7-8=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(2,-2).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+\frac{1}{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}+14t+8
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}+14t+8}{2t+\frac{1}{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=-1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,-1} & =\frac{3(-1)^{2}+14(-1)+8}{2(-1)+\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3}{(-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(2,-2)$ and the slope $m=2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =2(x-2) \\ y+2 & =2x-4 \\ y & =2x-4-2 \\ y & =2x-6.\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2(0)-6 \\ y & =0-6 \\ y & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at  $(0,\,-6).$"] ["question-cdc93f1c-a598-5c34-91ec-6e0adc895b1e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] :question/problem "A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=2{t}^{5}-4{t}^{3},\,y={t}^{2},\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=1$ on the curve. Find the Cartesian equation of the normal to the curve at $C.$

The Cartesian equation of the normal line at $C$ is $y=$
{{field-1}}."] ["question-947f538f-26d4-542e-9645-e3e57363dc38" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2({1}^{5})-4({1}^{3})=2-4=-2 \\ y & ={1}^{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to find the equation of the normal at the point $(-2,1).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{2t}{10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,1} & =\frac{2(1)}{10({1}^{4})-12({1}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{10-12} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-2)} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m:$

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,(-1)\,}=1
$$

Finally, to find the Cartesian equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-2,1)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =1(x-(-2)) \\ y-1 & =x+2 \\ y & =x+2+1 \\ y & =x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the equation of the normal line  in slope-intercept form is $y=x+3.$"] ["question-947f538f-26d4-542e-9645-e3e57363dc38" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-65d17d6d-2bde-5720-8a1c-bab17264def6" :answer-field/id #uuid "65d17d6d-2bde-5720-8a1c-bab17264def6"] ["answer-716c77ef-6905-55d3-a9a4-8d54e5510e60" :answer/id #uuid "716c77ef-6905-55d3-a9a4-8d54e5510e60"] ["answer-716c77ef-6905-55d3-a9a4-8d54e5510e60" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-716c77ef-6905-55d3-a9a4-8d54e5510e60" :answer/value "x+3"] ["answer-field-65d17d6d-2bde-5720-8a1c-bab17264def6" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-65d17d6d-2bde-5720-8a1c-bab17264def6" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-65d17d6d-2bde-5720-8a1c-bab17264def6" :answer-field/correct "answer-716c77ef-6905-55d3-a9a4-8d54e5510e60"] ["answer-field-65d17d6d-2bde-5720-8a1c-bab17264def6" :answer-field/choices "answer-716c77ef-6905-55d3-a9a4-8d54e5510e60"] ["question-947f538f-26d4-542e-9645-e3e57363dc38" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-65d17d6d-2bde-5720-8a1c-bab17264def6"] [17592186083245 :knowledge-point/questions "question-947f538f-26d4-542e-9645-e3e57363dc38"] ["question-1cf055f3-7724-5017-8bd4-b9d8370b23a5" :question/id #uuid "1cf055f3-7724-5017-8bd4-b9d8370b23a5"] ["question-1cf055f3-7724-5017-8bd4-b9d8370b23a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-122943"] ["question-1cf055f3-7724-5017-8bd4-b9d8370b23a5" :question/problem "A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=4t\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi }),\,y=t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in (0,\infty ).
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=\pi $ on the curve. Determine the point at which the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $x$-axis."] ["question-1cf055f3-7724-5017-8bd4-b9d8370b23a5" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\pi $ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{\pi })=4\pi (0)=0, \\ y & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point $(0,-\pi ).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi })+4,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi })+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\pi ,$ the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi } & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi }{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{\pi })+4} \\  & =\frac{-1}{4\cdot 0+4}=-\,\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,(-\frac{1}{4})\,}=4
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(0,-\pi )$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=4.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-\pi ) & =4(x-0) \\ y & =4x-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The normal intersects the $x$-axis when $y=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-\pi  & =0 \\ 4x & =\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ is the $x$-intercept."] ["question-1cf055f3-7724-5017-8bd4-b9d8370b23a5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] $$
x=4\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,y=2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,0<t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=e$ on the curve. Find the equation of the normal to the curve at $C.$"] ["question-f508d724-e816-5421-91b6-b8baa491ba13" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=e$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡e=4, \\ y & =2e\operatorname{ln}⁡e=2e\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(4,2e).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{4}{t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2}{(\frac{4}{t})} \\  & =\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=e,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=e} & =\frac{e\operatorname{ln}⁡e+e}{2} \\  & =\frac{e+e}{2}=e\,.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,e\,}
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(4,2e)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{\,e\,}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2e & =(-\frac{1}{\,e\,})(x-4) \\ y-2e & =-\frac{1}{\,e\,}x+\frac{4}{\,e\,} \\ y & =-\frac{1}{\,e\,}x+\frac{2{e}^{2}+4}{\,e\,}\,.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f508d724-e816-5421-91b6-b8baa491ba13" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-ac112813-4b74-55f0-8f43-22f46db91806" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0<t<2\pi .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ on the curve. Determine the coordinates of the point at which the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis. Do not round the answers.

The normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}},
{{field-2}}$).$"] ["question-8516a769-888c-5185-902e-1a5250ccaa04" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})=3\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point $(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{6},$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,\frac{\pi }{6}} & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m:$

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{3}
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=\sqrt{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-\frac{1}{2} & =\sqrt{3}(x-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\ y-\frac{1}{2} & =\sqrt{3}x-\frac{3(3)}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt{3}x-\frac{9}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt{3}x-4.\end{aligned}
$$

The normal crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at  $(0,\,-4).$"] ["question-8516a769-888c-5185-902e-1a5250ccaa04" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] :question/problem "A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$

Determine the value of the parameter $t$ at which the normal line to the curve is vertical."] ["question-5a6c8612-f46a-5c05-98fb-598338ec8310" :question/worked-solution "The normal line is vertical when the tangent to the curve is horizontal. Therefore, we require ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${x}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-3{e}^{3t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=12{t}^{2}
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
12{t}^{2}=0\,⟹\,t=0.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
{x}^{′}(0)=-3{e}^{3(0)}=-3\ne 0,\,\,
$$

:question/problem "A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={e}^{-t},\,y=5{t}^{2}+1,\,0\le t\le 2.
$$

Determine the value of the parameter $t$ at which the normal line to the curve is vertical."] ["question-ab667ef1-091e-5d1a-aa96-b7c759cdc55d" :question/worked-solution "The normal line is vertical when the tangent to the curve is horizontal. Therefore, we require ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${x}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-{e}^{-t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=10t
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
10t=0\,⟹\,t=0.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
{x}^{′}(0)=-{e}^{-0}=-1\ne 0,\,\,
$$

which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed vertical when $t=0.$"] ["question-ab667ef1-091e-5d1a-aa96-b7c759cdc55d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy]
