finite region enclosed between curves the curves

$$
f(x)=x^3-2x
$$

and $g(x)=2x$, as shown below.

![](images/e6/e651f9df1fbc9f0f9ad8ffa49822e4e3640a3555570ca3d0f82c155c5141843e.png)

First, we find the points where the curves intersect:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x) &= g(x) \\
x^{3} - 2x &= 2x \\
x^{3} - 4x &= 0 \\
x(x^{2} - 4) &= 0 \\
x(x - 2)(x + 2) &= 0 \\
x &= 0, 2,-2
\end{aligned}
$$

The area we want consists of two symmetric regions: $A_1$ and $A_2$.

![](images/4f/4fd6173127725bd771a753217002ab9656cf36a97dd37c4fe80f7d76e672ee86.png)

For the area $A_1$, we have $x \in [-2,0]$, and the upper function is $f(x)$ while the lower function is $g(x)$. So, the area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{1} &= \int_{-2}^{0}(f(x) - g(x))dx \\
&= \int_{-2}^{0}((x^{3} - 2x) - 2x)dx \\
&= \int_{-2}^{0}(x^{3} - 4x)dx \\
&= \int_{-2}^{0}x^{3}dx - 4\int_{-2}^{0}xdx \\
&= \left.\frac{x^{4}}{4}\right|_{-2}^{0} - 4 \cdot \left.\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right|_{-2}^{0} \\
&= (0 - 4) - 4(0 - 2) \\
&=-4 + 8 \\
&= 4
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the regions are symmetric, we have that $A_2=A_1=4$.

Finally, the required area is given by

$$
A = A_1 + A_2 = 4 + 4 = 8
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "988c723b-81d1-541c-9ab3-bebbece1cf06" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1003 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3d1d4c5b-f669-5ef8-ae3a-069d89747d69" :step/math-academy-id 17592186176692 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176978 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the following infinite power series.

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{(x-2)^n}{n^2} = (x-2) + \dfrac{(x-2)^2}{2^2} + \dfrac{(x-2)^3}{3^2} + \cdots
$$

How do we determine the radius and interval of convergence for this series?

First, note that the terms of the series are all powers of $(x-2).$ For this reason, we say that the series is **centered** at $x=2.$

To compute the radius of convergence, we use the ratio test for convergence. We define 

$$
a_n = \dfrac{(x-2)^n}{n^2},
$$

and we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(x-2)^{n+1}}{(n+1)^{2}}\cdot \frac{{n}^{2}}{(x-2)^{n}}| \\  & =|x-2|{lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{{n}^{2}}{(n+1)^{2}}) \\  & =|x-2|{lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}+2n+1}) \\  & =|x-2|{lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{1}{(1+\frac{2}{n}+\frac{1}{{n}^{2}})}) \\  & =|x-2|\cdot 1 \\  & =|x-2|\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if 

$$
L < {\color{blue}1}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\left| x-{\color{red}2} \right| < {\color{blue}1}.
$$

Therefore, 

- the radius of convergence is ${\color{blue}1},$ and

- the interval of convergence is centered at the point $x={\color{red}2}.$

To find the interval of convergence, we solve the inequality $\left| x-2 \right| < 1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|x-2| & <1 \\ -1<x-2 & <1 \\ 1<x & <3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the series converges for any $x$ in the open interval $(1,3).$

The ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series at the endpoints of this interval. So, we need to investigate the endpoints $x=1$ and $x=3$ separately using another test for convergence.

- We start with the left endpoint. When $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(x-2)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(1-2)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} \\  & =-1+\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{16}+⋯,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the alternating series test.

- We then look at the right endpoint. When $x=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(x-2)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(3-2)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{1}^{n}}{{n}^{2}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}} \\  & =1+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{16}+⋯,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the $p$-series test.

Finally, we conclude that the interval of convergence is $I=[1,3].$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3711e5cb-ff53-5f13-a62a-da24f59e888b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5191 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "638d27e8-a48f-5883-adc8-de19b25a5a0e" :step/math-academy-id 32549 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176674}}] :activity/title "Radius of Convergence of Power Series" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186176111} {:db/id 17592186176692 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176978 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the following infinite power series.

$$
\sum_{n = 1}^\infty \dfrac 1 {n (n + 1)}
$$

First, we can use partial fractions to write

$$
\dfrac{1}{n(n+1)} = \dfrac{1}{n} - \dfrac{1}{n+1}
$$

Then the sum is given by

$$
\sum_{n = 1}^\infty \dfrac 1 {n (n + 1)} = \sum_{n = 1}^\infty\left(\dfrac{1}{n} - \dfrac{1}{n+1}\right)
$$

Computing the first few partial sums, *without* simplifying, notice that many terms cancel:

$\require{cancel}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
s_{1} &= (1- \frac{1}{2}) \\
s_{2} &= (1 - \frac{1}{2}) + (\frac{1}{2}- \frac{1}{3}) \\
s_{3} &= (1 - \frac{1}{2}) + (\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3}) + (\frac{1}{3}- \frac{1}{4}) \\
s_{4} &= (1 - \frac{1}{2}) + (\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3}) + (\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{4}) + (\frac{1}{4}- \frac{1}{5})
\end{aligned}
$$

For each partial sum, we always end up canceling all terms except for the first and last terms. We say that this infinite series is a **telescoping series**, meaning that it consists of only a finite number of terms after canceling.

So, if $s_N$ is the $N$th partial sum of the series, we have

$$
s_N = {\color{blue}{1}} {\color{red}{\,-\, \dfrac 1 {N + 1}}}
$$

Finally, we can determine the sum of the series by computing the limit of $s_N$ as $N\to\infty$. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}
∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(1)/(n(n + 1)) &= lim_(N → ∞)(1 - \frac{1}{N + 1}) \\
&= 1 - 0 \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7785a1f9-f6fd-5dac-bbab-9da2b149e341" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6768 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f09ad925-45f1-583f-9d96-f7db4c4c6d03" :step/math-academy-id $$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x
$$

Evaluating two improper integrals can be quite time-consuming. However, we can shorten the process if we see that $f(x)$ is an even or odd function. 

- Recall that $f(x)$ is an even function if $f(-x) = f(x).$ Even functions are symmetrical about the $y$-axis. Therefore, if $f(x)$ is even, we have

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x,
$$

provided that the integrals are convergent. Moreover, if $f(x)$ is even and the above integrals are convergent, then

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = 2\int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

- Recall that $f(x)$ is an odd function if $f(-x) = -f(x).$ Therefore, if $f(x)$ is odd, we have

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = -\int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x,
$$

provided that the integrals are convergent. Moreover, if $f(x)$ is odd and the above integrals are convergent, then

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "04e63304-93d0-5edd-985c-6a732614917f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4359 :tutorial/title "Improper Integrals of Even and Odd Functions"} :step/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Let's consider the differential equation $y' = -4xy.$ The slope field for this equation is shown below.

![](images/a4/a47ec9497553fdcc9d20607f309bdaee00bb1fc0af4d39dea8a6a843a2e417e6.png)

Let's see how much information we can gather about the differential equation by referring *only* to its slope field.

- First, note that the slope field has neither vertical nor horizontal symmetry. Therefore, the associated differential equation must be of the form $y' = f(x,y).$ Indeed, the equation $y' =-4xy$ is of this form.

- Second, notice that the solution curves appear to have stationary points along the lines $x=0$ and $y=0.$ This means that the right-hand side of our differential equation must evaluate to zero on these lines. Indeed, this is true of our equation.

![](images/7b/7beccfd6840c2715bfd3c923f4fe6ac05bdf07f9ed65931b016efd937b1a0b63.png)

- Third, the lines $x=0$ and $y=0$ split the plane into four regions. The slopes of the solution curves in each of these regions are summarized in the table below.

| $y > 0$ | $\nearrow$

$({\color{blue}{+}})$ | $\searrow$

$({\color{red}{-}})$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $y <       0$ | $\searrow$

$({\color{red}{-}})$ | $\nearrow$

$({\color{blue}{+}})$ |
|  | $x<       0$ | $x> 0$ |

Notice that the sign of $f(x,y)$ in the four regions agrees with the above table:

- $f(x,y)=-4xy$ is positive in the second and fourth quadrants, and

- $f(x,y)=-4xy$ is negative in the first and third quadrants." :tutorial/id #uuid "dd16b3e1-53b3-55bf-af84-540daaefde15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5672 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9018b840-14fc-5403-a85b-0696a121416b" :step/math-academy-id 34802 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172982}} {:db/id 17592186172982 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172082 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171888 :question/id #uuid "95746e3f-5cdf-58e2-8dbb-39b3cbe5cfc1" :question/math-academy-id "e-9356"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cd82d96b-34d5-5d20-b810-7ea88b0b5797" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048489} {:db/id 17592186049722} {:db/id 17592186050480}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172566} {:db/id 17592186172568} {:db/id 17592186253664} {:db/id 17592186332800} {:db/id 17592186332801} {:db/id 17592186332803}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying an Equation That Generates a Slope Field Using Stationary Points"} :step/id #uuid "de33aa28-2c66-5a35-b972-8287ff822b59" :step/math-academy-id 35034 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172870}}] :activity/title "Analyzing Slope Fields for Nonautonomous Differential Equations" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186172172} {:db/id 17592186172979 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173195 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the differential equation $y' = -4xy.$ The slope field for this equation is shown below.

:tutorial/content "Let's consider the differential equation $y' = -4xy.$ The slope field for this equation is shown below.

![](images/a4/a47ec9497553fdcc9d20607f309bdaee00bb1fc0af4d39dea8a6a843a2e417e6.png)

Let's see how much information we can gather about the differential equation by referring *only* to its slope field.

- First, note that the slope field has neither vertical nor horizontal symmetry. Therefore, the associated differential equation must be of the form $y' = f(x,y).$ Indeed, the equation $y' =-4xy$ is of this form.

- Second, notice that the solution curves appear to have stationary points along the lines $x=0$ and $y=0.$ This means that the right-hand side of our differential equation must evaluate to zero on these lines. Indeed, this is true of our equation.

![](images/7b/7beccfd6840c2715bfd3c923f4fe6ac05bdf07f9ed65931b016efd937b1a0b63.png)

- Third, the lines $x=0$ and $y=0$ split the plane into four regions. The slopes of the solution curves in each of these regions are summarized in the table below.

| $y > 0$ | $\nearrow$

$({\color{blue}{+}})$ | $\searrow$

$({\color{red}{-}})$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $y <       0$ | $\searrow$

$({\color{red}{-}})$ | $\nearrow$

$({\color{blue}{+}})$ |
|  | $x<       0$ | $x> 0$ |

Notice that the sign of $f(x,y)$ in the four regions agrees with the above table:

- $f(x,y)=-4xy$ is positive in the second and fourth quadrants, and

- $f(x,y)=-4xy$ is negative in the first and third quadrants." :tutorial/id #uuid "dd16b3e1-53b3-55bf-af84-540daaefde15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5672 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186172982 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172082 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171888 :question/id #uuid "95746e3f-5cdf-58e2-8dbb-39b3cbe5cfc1" :question/math-academy-id "e-9356"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cd82d96b-34d5-5d20-b810-7ea88b0b5797" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048489} {:db/id 17592186049722} {:db/id 17592186050480}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172566} {:db/id 17592186172568} {:db/id 17592186253664} {:db/id 17592186332800} {:db/id 17592186332801} {:db/id 17592186332803}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying an Equation That Generates a Slope Field Using Stationary Points"} :step/id #uuid "de33aa28-2c66-5a35-b972-8287ff822b59" :step/math-academy-id 35034 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172870}} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186097588} :activity/id #uuid "85353624-7ac2-52d1-8562-1afe91b8759a" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048976 :topic/id #uuid "d0827a60-1270-5e75-a5db-1a9836dc00b1" :topic/math-academy-id 1079} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186097588 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097791 :tutorial/content "For a particle with position $x(t)$, the **average velocity** of the particle over the time interval $[a,b]$ is given by the average rate of change of position:

$$
v_{\textrm{avg}} = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{x(b) - x(a)}{b-a}
$$

Similarly, the **average acceleration** of a particle with velocity $v(t)$ over the time interval $[a,b]$ is given by the average rate of change of velocity:

$$
a_{\textrm{avg}} = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{v(b) - v(a)}{b-a}
$$

To demonstrate, suppose that a particle moves along a straight line, and its position (in meters) relative to a fixed origin $O$ is given by the function

$$
x(t) = 2t^3
$$

where

$$
t \geq 0
$$

is the time measured in seconds. The average velocity of the particle over the time interval $[0,1]$ is

$$
v_{avg} = \frac{Δx}{Δt} = (x(1) - x(0))/(1 - 0) = (2(1)^{3} - 2(0)^{3})/(1 - 0) = 2m/s
$$

Likewise, the velocity is

$$
v(t) = x'(t) = 6t^2
$$

so the average acceleration of the particle over the time interval $[0,1]$ is

$$
a_{avg} = \frac{Δv}{Δt} = (v(1) - v(0))/(1 - 0) = (6(1)^{2} - 6(0)^{2})/(1 - 0) = 6m/s^{2}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e1c49e4b-7206-5819-b127-c2f562fa1043" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1023 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "defa2861-ea0b-5be8-a72a-4101e1177359" :step/math-academy-id 2011 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097589}} {:db/id 17592186097589 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096717 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096517 :question/id #uuid "924d743e-4984-5d94-84be-381c99697940" :question/math-academy-id "e-571"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b7a24f6a-aa0d-576a-a4ff-945335f3301b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050572} {:db/id 17592186050901}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097203} {:db/id 17592186097286}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Average Velocity of a Particle Given Its Position Function"} :step/id #uuid "c2c3e774-0466-5687-8348-ec20933d1013" :step/math-academy-id 2012 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097590}} {:db/id 17592186097590 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096718 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096521 :question/id #uuid "523927ce-8e24-554d-8558-07f51a3d4120" :question/math-academy-id "e-572"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6d62ff71-fe48-5612-8f37-bab7cb7f2931" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048713}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097285} {:db/id 17592186097291}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Average Acceleration of a Particle Given Its Velocity Function"} :step/id #uuid "9c935206-0fc0-512a-9bf5-4f346bee6bcf" :step/math-academy-id 2014 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097591}} {:db/id 17592186097591 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097792 :tutorial/content "So, we now know how to find

- the average *velocity* (given the *position*), and

v_{\textrm{avg}} = \dfrac{1}{t_2-t_1}\int_{t_1}^{t_2} v(t)\,\textrm d t
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b25ff39d-cfec-5109-8c49-31a8d54ad75d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1026 :tutorial/title "Calculating Average Velocity Using Integration"} :step/id #uuid "12ea46a3-a7a9-5273-ae68-f843dba89bf3" :step/math-academy-id 2016 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097592}} {:db/id 17592186097592 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096719 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096525 :question/id #uuid "62944da5-875f-542a-9b54-9c3d3c5db947" :question/math-academy-id "e-573"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "803ac4f0-61fe-5efc-b7a5-c73a4235f4bc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049280}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097293} {:db/id 17592186097294}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Average Velocity of a Particle Using Integration"} :step/id #uuid "7fa5d198-6f76-58fe-a0de-a2eede2c04f2" :step/math-academy-id 2017 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097676}} {:db/id 17592186097593 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096720 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096526 :question/id #uuid "aa1e2c54-80dc-5e38-a149-c7db63deb418" :question/math-academy-id "e-574"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3046ebca-8a30-5228-a003-b8155cd1a62a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097287} {:db/id 17592186097292}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Average Position or Acceleration of a Particle Using Integration"} :step/id #uuid "63d935f4-c3b0-5692-aa00-a8d6bc7db985" :step/math-academy-id 2019} {:db/id 17592186097676 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097881 :tutorial/content "We can also calculate the average position $x_{\textrm{avg}}$ and average acceleration $a_{\textrm{avg}}$ of a particle over an interval $[t_1, t_2]$ using the following formulas:

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8e1cdc1f-de87-5b91-9ad0-f2bcab98be3f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5192 :tutorial/title "Calculating Average Position and Acceleration Using Integration"} {:activity/expected-seconds 1500.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186069637} :activity/id #uuid "a5eebdd0-457e-5351-b479-fdec034c955a" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049227 :topic/id #uuid "e5039159-d776-5d2a-8b00-bb798bc20935" :topic/math-academy-id 446} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186069637 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070036 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given the integral  $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{3x+2}{(x+1)^2} \textrm{d}x.$ Note that we have the repeated factor $(x+1)$ in the denominator. 

The correct form of the partial fraction expansion of the integrand is
 

$$
\dfrac{3x+2}{(x+1)^2}=\dfrac{A}{(x+1)} +\dfrac{B}{(x+1)^2} \,.
$$

To determine the coefficients $A$ and $B,$ we first multiply both sides the above equation by $(x+1)^2$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+2 & =A(x+1)+B.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=-1,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(-1)+2 & =A(-1+1)+B \\ B & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known value of $B,$ we can solve for $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(0)+2 & =A(0+1)+B \\ 2 & =A+B \\ 2 & =A-1 \\ A & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{3x+2}{(x+1)^2}= \dfrac{3}{(x+1)} -\dfrac{1}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Now this function can be integrated term by term. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x+2}{(x+1)^{2}}\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{3}{(x+1)}-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{x+1}\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}|x+1|+\frac{1}{x+1}+C\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant of integration." :tutorial/id #uuid "de271889-71f4-5fa2-8346-7ed8fa03e000" :tutorial/math-academy-id 922 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid 17592186068974} {:db/id 17592186069637 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070036 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given the integral  $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{3x+2}{(x+1)^2} \textrm{d}x.$ Note that we have the repeated factor $(x+1)$ in the denominator. 

The correct form of the partial fraction expansion of the integrand is
 

$$
\dfrac{3x+2}{(x+1)^2}=\dfrac{A}{(x+1)} +\dfrac{B}{(x+1)^2} \,.
$$

To determine the coefficients $A$ and $B,$ we first multiply both sides the above equation by $(x+1)^2$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+2 & =A(x+1)+B.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=-1,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(-1)+2 & =A(-1+1)+B \\ B & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known value of $B,$ we can solve for $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(0)+2 & =A(0+1)+B \\ 2 & =A+B \\ 2 & =A-1 \\ A & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{3x+2}{(x+1)^2}= \dfrac{3}{(x+1)} -\dfrac{1}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Now this function can be integrated term by term. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x+2}{(x+1)^{2}}\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{3}{(x+1)}-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{x+1}\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}|x+1|+\frac{1}{x+1}+C\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant of integration." :tutorial/id #uuid "de271889-71f4-5fa2-8346-7ed8fa03e000" :tutorial/math-academy-id 922 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d3ab3699-46bb-5348-b28d-d90ed53084d6" :step/math-academy-id 1800 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069644}} {:db/id 17592186070036 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given the integral  $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{3x+2}{(x+1)^2} \textrm{d}x.$ Note that we have the repeated factor $(x+1)$ in the denominator.

"![](images/a0/a0b4ad67ea80f6d6eec3a15b3df18d551d84263c7424405588bd15162ef4e7c2.png)

The polar curve shown above is defined as

$$
r(\theta) = 4 - 3\cos \theta, \qquad 0\leq \theta < 2\pi
$$

We have

$$
\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}
$$

at the point $P$. The tangent to the curve at $P$ is shown in the diagram.

To find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at $P$, we follow four steps.

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

Using techniques that we've previously discussed, we can show that

$$
y^{′}(θ) = 4\cos θ - 3\cos 2θ, x^{′}(θ) = 3\sin 2θ - 4\sin θ
$$

Therefore, we can find

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dy}{dx} &= (y^{′}(θ))/(x^{′}(θ)) \\
&= \frac{4\cos θ - 3\cos 2θ}{3\sin 2θ - 4\sin θ}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P$.

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}
m &= \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{θ = π/2} \\
&= (4\cos (\frac{π}{2}) - 3\cos (2 \cdot \frac{π}{2}))/(3\sin (2 \cdot \frac{π}{2}) - 4\sin (\frac{π}{2})) \\
&= (4\cos (\frac{π}{2}) - 3\cos (π))/(3\sin (π) - 4\sin (\frac{π}{2})) \\
&= \frac{0 + 3}{0 - 4} \\
&=-\frac{3}{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P$.

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{1} &= r\cos θ \\
&= (4 - 3\cos θ)\cos θ \\
&= (4 - 3\cos (\frac{π}{2}))\cos (\frac{π}{2}) \\
&= 0 \\
y_{1} &= r\sin θ \\
&= (4 - 3\cos θ)\sin θ \\
&= (4 - 3\cos (\frac{π}{2}))\sin (\frac{π}{2}) \\
&= 4
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are

$$
\left(0, 4 \right)
$$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the tangent.

We find the equation of the tangent as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y - y_{1} &= m(x - x_{1}) \\
y - 4 &= -\frac{3}{4} \cdot (x - 0) \\
y &= -\frac{3}{4}x + 4
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "febc7b49-9662-5e78-a7a5-cbe9b1f596ba" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6186 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a1e51e4b-71cf-5749-aae1-c001b3a5a59b" :step/math-academy-id 37501 :step/next {:db/id 17592186184944}}] :activity/title "Tangent and Normal Lines to Polar Curves" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186184419} {:db/id 17592186185006 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185342 :tutorial/content "![](images/a0/a0b4ad67ea80f6d6eec3a15b3df18d551d84263c7424405588bd15162ef4e7c2.png)

$$
S_\infty = \dfrac{a_1}{1-r}, \qquad \mid r \mid < 1
$$

To see where this formula comes from, first, we remember the formula for the sum of the first $n$ terms of a geometric series is given by

$$
S_n = a_1 \cdot \dfrac {1 - r ^ n} {1 - r}
$$

Notice that if $\mid r \mid < 1$ then $r^n\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$. Therefore, as $n\to\infty$, we have:

$$

$$

$$

For example, suppose we want to calculate the sum of the infinite geometric series

$$

$$

The first term is $a_1=3$, and the common ratio is

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}

&= (3)/((1 - \frac{1}{3})) \\
&= (3)/((\frac{2}{3})) \\
&= 3(\frac{3}{2}) \\

\end{aligned}

17592186049507 :topic/id #uuid "fa777873-dae5-503a-8b8d-d333b158b938" :topic/math-academy-id 1080} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186097751 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097803 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to *approximate*

$$
f(x) = e^x
$$

for some value of $x$. We can do this using the second-degree Taylor polynomial about a point $x=a$. For example, the second-degree Taylor polynomial for $e^x$ about the point $x=1$ is shown below:

$$
e^x \approx P_2(x) = e + e(x-1) + \dfrac 1 2 e(x-1)^2
$$

In general, the polynomial $P_2(x)$ is only an approximation to the function $f(x)$, which means that there will usually be some error whenever we use $P_2$ to approximate $f$. We want to know how bad this error can get. Can we find an upper bound for the error?

Let $R_2(x)$ be the **error** (or **remainder**) that we get when we use $P_2$ to approximate

$$
f(x)=e^x
$$

so

$$
R_2(x) = e^x - P_2(x)
$$

The **Lagrange error bound** states that an upper bound for $R_2$ is given by,

$$
\begin{vmatrix}R_2 & \leq \dfrac{M}{3!}\end{vmatrix}x-\left.a\right|^{3}
$$

where $M$ the maximum value of $\mid f^{(3)}(x) \mid$ on the interval between $a$ and $x$.

In our case, since our Taylor polynomial is taken about the point $a=1$, the Lagrange error bound becomes

$$
\begin{vmatrix}R_2 & \leq \dfrac{M}{3!}\end{vmatrix}x-\left.1\right|^{3}
$$

Notice that the Lagrange error bound looks a lot like the last term of the *next* Taylor polynomial, $P_3(x)$.

The tricky part is finding the value of $M$. We'll learn how to do that in the following example." :tutorial/id #uuid "fcb4053a-c61a-538b-8b44-5a92f73f053f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1292 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c93a74b3-e513-5fb9-9595-6bf177ec940a" :step/math-academy-id 4844 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097752}} {:db/id 17592186097752 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096820 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096562 :question/id #uuid "c946c1c9-f3d2-5d9d-9390-8ee542ca15a5" :question/math-academy-id "e-745"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "360b8076-1b27-5630-a07e-221a0e53011d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048515} {:db/id 17592186050718} {:db/id 17592186050866} {:db/id 17592186050955}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186096971} {:db/id 17592186097317}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Upper Bound for the Error Using the Second-Degree Taylor Polynomial"} :step/id #uuid "82542d7a-3ec1-5979-8dd2-13a732ad5eb1" :step/math-academy-id 4845 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097753}} {:db/id 17592186097753 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097804 :tutorial/content "The Lagrange error bound that we've discussed so far is valid only for the error associated with a second-degree Taylor polynomial. But we can generalize the result to higher-order Taylor polynomials.

Let $R_n(x)$ be the error involved in approximating a function $f(x)$ by its $n$th-degree Taylor polynomial $P_n(x)$ about $x=a$. So, we have

$$
R_n(x) = f(x) - P_n(x)
$$

Then the Lagrange error bound for $R_n$ is given by

$$
\begin{vmatrix}R_n(x) & \leq \dfrac{M}{(n+1)!}\end{vmatrix}x-\left.a\right|^{n+1}
$$

where $M$ is the maximum value of $\mid f^{(n+1)} \mid$ on the interval between $a$ and $x$." :tutorial/id #uuid "07b10e6a-1673-5d6e-8572-8b4505579f44" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1294 :tutorial/title "The General Result of the Lagrange Error Bound"} :step/id #uuid "13415159-b315-5389-bc81-61ef044820e2" :step/math-academy-id 4849 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097754}} {:db/id 17592186097754 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096821 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096563 :question/id #uuid "3f5e5945-cdaa-55b9-b360-9e68249480b7" :question/math-academy-id "e-746"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "79a10073-8798-597e-821c-691b0dad5ae7" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186096961} {:db/id 17592186096980}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Upper Bound for the Error Using the Third-Degree Taylor Polynomial"} :step/id #uuid "b70fcb39-7efc-50ad-a28c-73509579c61d" :step/math-academy-id 4850}] :activity/title "The Lagrange Error Bound" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186096869} {:db/id 17592186097751 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097803 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to *approximate*

17592186101729 :step/content {:db/id 17592186101916 :tutorial/content "Suppose that the base of a solid is the semicircle enclosed by the curve

$$
y=-\sqrt{4-x^2}
$$

and the $x$-axis, as shown in the picture below. Cross-sections perpendicular to the $x$-axis are rectangles. If the height of each rectangle is half of the length of its base, then what is the volume of the solid?

![](images/60/605b9bfd34ba7035ab9533679f35a76f72e2d10b78f75d02ff7b351f4e330957.png)

A sketch with a few cross-sections is shown in the picture below.

![](images/de/de3426f274dd0a779c9721b257c80b8482b2f13e42b2433569194520431facee.png)

If we are given the expression $A(x)$ for the area of each cross-section, then we find the volume as follows:

$$
V = \int_{a}^{b} A(x)\:\textrm{d}x
$$

Consider now a cross-section at some point $x$, where $x \in (-2,2)$:

![](images/b1/b14743ae0bbd16c7896762579397e766021c370f391d670d9bd6edbf8630c297.png)

If we project the rectangular cross-section onto the $xy$-plane, we get the following picture:

![](images/b7/b78d390bd7ce359377716c9ed757c52131cb9e0609f68b1c3b1d31d8368977c3.png)

Then the base of the cross-section is

$$
\begin{aligned}
b &= \mid y \mid \\
&= \mid - \sqrt{4 - x^{2}} \mid \\
&= \sqrt{4 - x^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the height ($h$) of each rectangle is

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

times the base ($b$), the area of the rectangle is

$$
A = bh = b \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{2} b \right) = \dfrac{1}{2}b^2
$$

So, the expression for the area of the cross-section is

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(x) &= \frac{1}{2}b^{2} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{4 - x^{2}})^{2} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}(4 - x^{2})
\end{aligned}
$$

We can now calculate the volume of the solid using the following integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V &= \int_{a}^{b}A(x)dx \\
&= \frac{1}{2}\int_{-2}^{2}(4 - x^{2})dx
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "98422b67-38f6-5ab8-855d-49dab00c658b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1035 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0d6b036f-4e13-5543-8030-db3a557fefa6" :step/math-academy-id 2033 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101730}} {:db/id 17592186101730 :step/content {:db/id 17592186100901 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100738 :question/id #uuid "a7e161d5-edb5-5adb-ab72-2edad67b0a9c" :question/math-academy-id "e-579"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e2e18711-6114-5c11-ad18-7b06bc0278d8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049608} {:db/id 17592186050272}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101266} {:db/id 17592186101460}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Volume When the Base Is Bounded by a Curve"} :step/id #uuid "012b20cf-a9ef-5688-858c-bc9067e86f98" :step/math-academy-id 2034 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101775}} {:db/id 17592186101731 :step/content {:db/id 17592186101917 :tutorial/content "Let's now suppose that the base of a solid is the right triangle enclosed by the line

$$
x=2y+2
$$

and the $y$-axis between $y=-1$ and $y=0$, as shown in the picture below.

![](images/8c/8cb3b29bfc46768c487e00416298829011302cb3d2641e80c7f9ca56466c44ac.png)

Suppose further that cross-sections perpendicular to the $\mathbf y$**-axis** are rectangles and that the height of each rectangle is

$$
\dfrac{3}{4}
$$

times the length of its base. How do we find the volume of that solid?

A sketch with a few cross-sections is shown in the picture below.

![](images/fc/fc2555c55658aa50b57da6f07a41bbc276eba7ac07ae42cd83fd078f20126cbf.png)

If we are given the expression $A(y)$ for the area of each cross-section, then we find the volume as follows:

$$
V = \int_{c}^{d} A(y)\:\textrm{d}y
$$

Consider now a cross-section at some point $y$, where $y \in (-1,0)$:

![](images/29/292852165b43623bd36923d13244f08f0d9c87a0b97b5b8437eb1ac3a9cee39a.png)

By projecting the rectangular cross-section onto the $xy$-plane, we get the following picture:

![](images/4e/4ef6cd638cac080303e1d62f6a5e82a63cd03793feafc59898e10da462abcc1b.png)

Then, the base of the cross-section is

$$
\begin{aligned}
b &= \begin{vmatrix}x|= & 2y + 2\end{vmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the height $h$ is

$$
\dfrac{3}{4}
$$

times the base $b$, the area of the rectangle is

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(x) &= bh \\
&= b \cdot (\frac{3}{4}b) \\
&= \frac{3}{4}b^{2} \\
&= \frac{3}{4}(2y + 2)^{2} \\
&= 3(y + 1)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

We can now calculate the volume of the solid using the following integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V &= \int_{c}^{d}A(y)dy \\
&= 3\int_{-1}^{0}(y + 1)^{2}dy
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6a961f5d-0ae1-54f8-bd71-bc7abf04c657" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1037 :tutorial/title "Cross-Sections Perpendicular to the y-Axis"} :step/id #uuid \end{aligned}
$$

Since the height ($h$) of each rectangle is

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

times the base ($b$), the area of the rectangle is

$$
A = bh = b \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{2} b \right) = \dfrac{1}{2}b^2
$$

So, the expression for the area of the cross-section is

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(x) &= \frac{1}{2}b^{2} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{4 - x^{2}})^{2} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}(4 - x^{2})
\end{aligned}
$$

We can now calculate the volume of the solid using the following integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V &= \int_{a}^{b}A(x)dx \\
&= \frac{1}{2}\int_{-2}^{2}(4 - x^{2})dx
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "98422b67-38f6-5ab8-855d-49dab00c658b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1035 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186101730 :step/content {:db/id 17592186100901 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100738 :question/id #uuid "a7e161d5-edb5-5adb-ab72-2edad67b0a9c" :question/math-academy-id "e-579"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e2e18711-6114-5c11-ad18-7b06bc0278d8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049608} {:db/id 17592186050272}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101266} {:db/id 17592186101460}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Volume When the Base Is Bounded by a Curve"} :step/id #uuid "012b20cf-a9ef-5688-858c-bc9067e86f98" :step/math-academy-id 2034 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101775}} {:db/id 17592186101775 :step/content {:db/id 17592186100932 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100764 :question/id #uuid "cd1bed05-184b-59ba-bfb8-ed49f0d5122c" :question/math-academy-id "e-6823"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8cae38a9-2bca-52d7-8948-d526a235eadf" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049042}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101463} {:db/id 17592186101524}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Volume When the Base Is Bounded by Two Curves"} :step/id #uuid "abeb624a-f236-52b4-b78b-940eb2a4cbc2" :step/math-academy-id 25319 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101731}} {:db/id 17592186101731 :step/content {:db/id 17592186101917 :tutorial/content "Let's now suppose that the base of a solid is the right triangle enclosed by the line

$$
x=2y+2
$$

and the $y$-axis between $y=-1$ and $y=0$, as shown in the picture below.

![](images/8c/8cb3b29bfc46768c487e00416298829011302cb3d2641e80c7f9ca56466c44ac.png)

Suppose further that cross-sections perpendicular to the $\mathbf y$**-axis** are rectangles and that the height of each rectangle is

$$
\dfrac{3}{4}
$$

times the length of its base. How do we find the volume of that solid?

A sketch with a few cross-sections is shown in the picture below.

![](images/fc/fc2555c55658aa50b57da6f07a41bbc276eba7ac07ae42cd83fd078f20126cbf.png)

If we are given the expression $A(y)$ for the area of each cross-section, then we find the volume as follows:

$$
V = \int_{c}^{d} A(y)\:\textrm{d}y
$$

Consider now a cross-section at some point $y$, where $y \in (-1,0)$:

![](images/29/292852165b43623bd36923d13244f08f0d9c87a0b97b5b8437eb1ac3a9cee39a.png)

By projecting the rectangular cross-section onto the $xy$-plane, we get the following picture:

![](images/4e/4ef6cd638cac080303e1d62f6a5e82a63cd03793feafc59898e10da462abcc1b.png)

Then, the base of the cross-section is

$$
\begin{aligned}
b &= \begin{vmatrix}x|= & 2y + 2\end{vmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the height $h$ is

$$
\dfrac{3}{4}
$$

times the base $b$, the area of the rectangle is

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(x) &= bh \\
&= b \cdot (\frac{3}{4}b) \\
&= \frac{3}{4}b^{2} \\
&= \frac{3}{4}(2y + 2)^{2} \\
&= 3(y + 1)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

We can now calculate the volume of the solid using the following integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V &= \int_{c}^{d}A(y)dy \\
&= 3\int_{-1}^{0}(y + 1)^{2}dy
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6a961f5d-0ae1-54f8-bd71-bc7abf04c657" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1037 :tutorial/title "Cross-Sections Perpendicular to the y-Axis"} :step/id #uuid "58505320-d804-56b2-b1d1-e26e0e56c0a9" :step/math-academy-id 2037 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101736}} {:db/id 17592186101917 :tutorial/content "Let's now suppose that the base of a solid is the right triangle enclosed by the line

17592186189107}} {:db/id 17592186189104 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189375 :tutorial/content "When constructing a differential equation to model a particular phenomenon, we sometimes combine several pieces of information to create the correct model.

Consider the following situation:

*The common cold virus spreads through a particular country. The rate at which the number of infected people increases is **proportional** to the **square of the time** $t$ (in days) since the outbreak started. 
Additionally, $100$ infected people **recover from the virus each day**.*

We want to find a differential equation that models $P(t),$ the number of infected people. We note the following:

- The statement describes the *rate* at which the *number of infected people* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d P}{\textrm d t}.
$$

- The rate at which the number of infected people increases is **proportional** to the **square of the time** $t.$ Therefore, if $I(t)$ represents the rate at which infections increase, then

$$
I(t) = kt^2,
$$

where $k$ is a positive constant.

- Additionally, $100$ infected people **recover from the virus each day**. Therefore, if $D(t)$ represents the rate at which infections decrease, then

$$
D(t) = 100.
$$

Therefore, the differential equation that describes this phenomenon is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}P}{\text{d}t} & ={{k{t}^{2}-100}_{⏟}}_{I(t)-D(t)}\end{aligned}
$$

Although we introduced the functions $I(t)$ and $D(t)$ here, we can usually write down the appropriate differential equation straight away. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "8a7ad3b5-e4de-56c0-8fc9-8a9b2c976094" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6270 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "37206e3d-9800-567e-82f6-eed74a977f1f" - The slope of the line that passes through $(x,y)$ and the origin equals $\dfrac{y}{x}.$

Suppose that this region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the horizontal line $y=-1$, generating a solid of revolution. How can we write an integral expression that gives the volume of the solid?

![](images/18/1880138e4a20cb5a47ba89cb3177d5dc6e74f998d7fdd428cdded7af38cadd02.png)

First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{4} &= x \\
x^{4} - x &= 0 \\
x(x^{3} - 1) &= 0 \\
x &= 0, 1
\end{aligned}

Hence, our limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=1$.

The vertical arrow

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=x^4$, and
- *leaves* though the outer curve $y=x$.

Now, we can express the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves, as follows:

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y=x$.![](images/35/352ff26bb5dce0a923c102c4528bd89555b49203c212fb73a42cf31cdf8b226e.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{outer} &= π\int_{0}^{1}[(upper) - (lower)]^{2}dx \\
&= π\int_{0}^{1}[(x) - (-1)]^{2}dx \\
&= π\int_{0}^{1}[x + 1]^{2}dx
\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{inner} &= π\int_{0}^{1}[(upper) - (lower)]^{2}dx \\
&= π\int_{0}^{1}[(x^{4}) - (-1)]^{2}dx \\
&= π\int_{0}^{1}[x^{4} + 1]^{2}dx
\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.
Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as
$V|= V_{outer} - V_{inner}; = π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}[x + 1]^{2}dx - π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}[x^{4} + 1]^{2}dx; = π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}([x + 1]^{2} - [x^{4} + 1]^{2})dx$." :tutorial/id #uuid "8e33de60-9df4-540e-b19b-f12088b349e2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1064 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "626bee34-cf24-50f9-b6b3-1fcbce8fe1a3" :step/math-academy-id 2092 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097659}} {:db/id 17592186097609 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096729 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096531 :question/id #uuid "b6dd2970-3cdc-58fc-8f28-0bfdcd738d6f" :question/math-academy-id "e-593"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e2e0268f-36a5-5f55-a0ae-9e0f34981dab" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097228} {:db/id 17592186097229}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Horizontal Line"} :step/id #uuid "52be5c09-e883-51da-a981-64e4b7986356" :step/math-academy-id 2093 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097610}} {:db/id 17592186097610 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097797 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose that the region enclosed by the curves

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
2y &= y^{2} \\

y &= 0, 2
\end{aligned}
$$

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x={y^2}$, and
- *leaves* though the outer curve $x=2y$.

$$
\begin{aligned}

&= π\int_{0}^{2}[(2y) - (-2)]^{2}dy \\
&= π\int_{0}^{2}[2y + 2]^{2}dy
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}

&= π\int_{0}^{2}[(y^{2}) - (-2)]^{2}dy \\
&= π\int_{0}^{2}[y^{2} + 2]^{2}dy
\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as
$V|= V_{outer} - V_{inner}; = π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}[2y + 2]^{2}dy - π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}[y^{2} + 2]^{2}dy; = π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}([2y + 2]^{2} - [y^{2} + 2]^{2})dy; = - **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=y^2$.![](images/cc/cca4c498956a16cb374a8d0b3341a09e52844026593557710525d07be79a233a.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{inner} &= π\int_{0}^{2}[(right) - (left)]^{2}dy \\
&= π\int_{0}^{2}[(y^{2}) - (-2)]^{2}dy \\
&= π\int_{0}^{2}[y^{2} + 2]^{2}dy
\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as
$V|= V_{outer} - V_{inner}; = π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}[2y + 2]^{2}dy - π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}[y^{2} + 2]^{2}dy; = π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}([2y + 2]^{2} - [y^{2} + 2]^{2})dy; = π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}(-y^{4} + 8y)dy; 17592186180353 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180792 :tutorial/content "Recall that a differential equation of the form

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt} = ky(a-y)
$$

is called a logistic growth equation. The positive constant $a > 0$ is the carrying capacity, and $k > 0$ is a constant of proportionality.

A typical solution curve $y = y(t)$ to this equation is shown below. 

![](images/0f/0f416479bbf72d3b9c1bf48861883e0e77bbc1c1d60d7fa48fb89e6f21c104eb.png)

It can be shown that the general solution to this equation is given by

$$
y(t) = \frac{a}{1+C e^{-ak t}}
$$

where $C$ is an integration constant. 

Note the following properties of this general solution:

- Since $a$ and $k$ are both positive, $e^{-akt}\to0$ as $t\to\infty.$ Therefore, $y(t)\to a$ as $t\to\infty.$ In other words, $y(t)$ approaches the carrying capacity as $t$ increases. This agrees with the behavior shown in our diagram.

- Since $e^{-akt}\to\infty$ as $t\to-\infty,$ we have that $y(t)\to 0$ as $t\to-\infty.$ This also agrees with our diagram.

We can use the general solution of the logistic growth equation to make predictions about a population governed by logistic growth. Let's see how." :tutorial/id #uuid "7ba42b62-b5a3-5c54-8a92-9ce67945fd36" :tutorial/math-academy-id 981 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3acea89b-a4db-5284-92df-1f9665ae536c" 17592186180398 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180682 :tutorial/content "The general solution to the logistic growth equation

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} t} = ky(a-y)
$$

is given by

$$
y(t) = \dfrac{a}{1+Ce^{-akt}}
$$

where $C>0$ is an integration constant. Let's now derive this formula.

Our differential equation is separable, so we start by separating variables and then integrating with respect to $t\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dt} & =ky(a-y) \\ \frac{1}{y(a-y)}\frac{dy}{dt} & =k \\ \int \frac{1}{y(a-y)}\frac{dy}{dt}\,\text{d}t & =\int k\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{y(a-y)}\,dy & =\int k\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{ 1}{y(a-y)} = \dfrac{1}{a}\left(\dfrac{1}{y} + \dfrac{1}{a-y}\right),
$$

we can rewrite the integrand on the left-hand side and complete the integration, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y(a-y)}\,dy & =\int k\,dt \\ \frac{1}{a}\int (\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{a-y})\,dy & =\int k\,dt \\ \int (\frac{1}{y}-\frac{1}{y-a})\,dy & =ak\int \,dt \\ -\int (\frac{1}{y-a}-\frac{1}{y})\,dy & =ak\int \,dt \\ \int (\frac{1}{y-a}-\frac{1}{y})\,dy & =-ak\int \,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}|y-a|-\operatorname{ln}|y| & =-akt+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{ln}|\frac{y-a}{y}| & =-akt+{C}_{1} \\ |\frac{y-a}{y}| & ={e}^{-akt+{C}_{1}} \\ |\frac{y-a}{y}| & ={e}^{{C}_{1}}{e}^{-akt} \\ \frac{y-a}{y} & =\pm {e}^{{C}_{1}}{e}^{-akt} \\ \frac{y-a}{y} & =\pm C{e}^{-akt}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=e^{C_1}$ is a positive constant. 

In our modeling, we have assumed that $0 < y  < a.$ Therefore, the left-hand side of the equation must be negative since the numerator is negative and the denominator is positive. Therefore, we discard the positive option, and we have

$$
\dfrac{y-a}{y}  =  -C e^{-akt}.
$$

Solving this equation for $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-a}{y} & =-C{e}^{-akt} \\ y-a & =-Cy{e}^{-akt} \\ y+y\cdot C{e}^{-akt} & =a \\ y(1+C{e}^{-akt}) & =a \\ y & =\frac{a}{1+C{e}^{-akt}}\,\,\,.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ba0b74de-5c49-5d2e-a9a6-207220dbb90e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4521 :tutorial/title "Deriving the General Solution"} :step/id #uuid "8237a905-9644-5c44-a21f-8bcd1b0638a5" :step/math-academy-id 27816}] :activity/title "Solving the Logistic Growth Equation" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179831} {:db/id 17592186180353 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180792 :tutorial/content "Recall that a differential equation of the form

- Since $a$ and $k$ are both positive, $e^{-akt}\to0$ as $t\to\infty.$ Therefore, $y(t)\to a$ as $t\to\infty.$ In other words, $y(t)$ approaches the carrying capacity as $t$ increases. This agrees with the behavior shown in our diagram.

- Since $e^{-akt}\to\infty$ as $t\to-\infty,$ we have that $y(t)\to 0$ as $t\to-\infty.$ This also agrees with our diagram.

We can use the general solution of the logistic growth equation to make predictions about a population governed by logistic growth. $$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} t} = ky(a-y)
$$

is given by

$$
y(t) = \dfrac{a}{1+Ce^{-akt}}
$$

where $C>0$ is an integration constant. Let's now derive this formula.

Our differential equation is separable, so we start by separating variables and then integrating with respect to $t\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dt} & =ky(a-y) \\ \frac{1}{y(a-y)}\frac{dy}{dt} & =k \\ \int \frac{1}{y(a-y)}\frac{dy}{dt}\,\text{d}t & =\int k\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{y(a-y)}\,dy & =\int k\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{ 1}{y(a-y)} = \dfrac{1}{a}\left(\dfrac{1}{y} + \dfrac{1}{a-y}\right),
$$

we can rewrite the integrand on the left-hand side and complete the integration, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y(a-y)}\,dy & =\int k\,dt \\ \frac{1}{a}\int (\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{a-y})\,dy & =\int k\,dt \\ \int (\frac{1}{y}-\frac{1}{y-a})\,dy & =ak\int \,dt \\ -\int (\frac{1}{y-a}-\frac{1}{y})\,dy & =ak\int \,dt \\ \int (\frac{1}{y-a}-\frac{1}{y})\,dy & =-ak\int \,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}|y-a|-\operatorname{ln}|y| & =-akt+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{ln}|\frac{y-a}{y}| & =-akt+{C}_{1} \\ |\frac{y-a}{y}| & ={e}^{-akt+{C}_{1}} \\ |\frac{y-a}{y}| & ={e}^{{C}_{1}}{e}^{-akt} \\ \frac{y-a}{y} & =\pm {e}^{{C}_{1}}{e}^{-akt} \\ \frac{y-a}{y} & =\pm C{e}^{-akt}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=e^{C_1}$ is a positive constant. 

In our modeling, we have assumed that $0 < y  < a.$ Therefore, the left-hand side of the equation must be negative since the numerator is negative and the denominator is positive. Therefore, we discard the positive option, and we have

$$
\dfrac{y-a}{y}  =  -C e^{-akt}.
$$

Solving this equation for $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-a}{y} & =-C{e}^{-akt} \\ y-a & =-Cy{e}^{-akt} \\ y+y\cdot C{e}^{-akt} & =a \\ y(1+C{e}^{-akt}) & =a \\ y & =\frac{a}{1+C{e}^{-akt}}\,\,\,.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ba0b74de-5c49-5d2e-a9a6-207220dbb90e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4521 :tutorial/title "Deriving the General Solution"} :step/id #uuid "8237a905-9644-5c44-a21f-8bcd1b0638a5" :step/math-academy-id 27816} {:db/id 17592186180682 :tutorial/content "The general solution to the logistic growth equation

$$
\dfrac 1 {10}
$$

For example, the number $0.\overline{8}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}
0.8^(―) &= 0.8 + 0.08 + 0.008 + … \\
&= \frac{8}{10} + \frac{8}{100} + \frac{8}{1000} + …
\end{aligned}
$$

We have

$$
a_1 = \dfrac{8}{10}
$$

and

$$
r = \dfrac {0.08}{0.8} = \dfrac 1 {10}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
0.8^(―) &= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)a_{1}r^{n - 1} \\
&= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)\frac{8}{10}(\frac{1}{10})^{n - 1} \\
&= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)8 \cdot \frac{1}{10} \cdot (\frac{1}{10})^{n} \cdot (\frac{1}{10})^{-1} \\
&= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)8 \cdot \frac{1}{10} \cdot (\frac{1}{10})^{n} \cdot (\frac{1}{10})^{-1} \\
&= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)8 \cdot \frac{1}{10} \cdot (\frac{1}{10})^{n} \cdot 10 \\
&= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)8(\frac{1}{10})^{n}
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3998b477-1c28-5edc-8605-2738ce474d94" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1212 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d0db37f3-c116-58a6-a33d-41ca478ae931" :step/math-academy-id 2380 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084210}} {:db/id 17592186084210 :step/content {:db/id 17592186083284 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186083086 :question/id #uuid "acebcd95-16ed-5087-8d04-0d6d503e31f3" :question/math-academy-id "e-694"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "367fe9fb-9d92-5105-9959-f3861994aa3c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050286}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186083792} {:db/id 17592186083793}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Repeating Decimal as an Infinite Geometric Series"} :step/id #uuid "af145878-806f-54bc-991b-28bc9b80cc8a" :step/math-academy-id 2381 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084211}} {:db/id 17592186084211 :step/content {:db/id 17592186083285 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186083087 :question/id #uuid "ed24fd0c-69c1-502a-a05f-6e859724214a" :question/math-academy-id "e-695"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8813b8a0-3b5e-5cd8-a37d-6b921f2882b8" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186083523} {:db/id 17592186083691} {:db/id 17592186234032}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Repeating Decimal as the Sum of a Number and a Geometric Series"} :step/id #uuid "4af12d7e-248c-5555-bd4c-98e9849f98a8" :step/math-academy-id 2385}] :activity/title "Repeating Decimals as Infinite Geometric Series" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186083401} {:db/id 17592186084209 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084397 :tutorial/content "A repeating decimal can be expressed as a geometric series whose common ratio is a power of

Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=t^3-1, \qquad y=2t-t^3, \qquad t \in (-\infty, \infty)
$$

The shaded area shown in the diagram is the finite region bounded between the curve, the $x$-axis, and the vertical lines formed by $x$-axis and the points on the curve corresponding to $t_1=0$ to $t_2=1$, as shown.

We know that the area of the curve is given by

$$
A = \int_{a}^{b} y \:\textrm{d}x
$$

Since our curve is defined parametrically, we need to change the variable of integration from $x$ to $t$ using the change of variables formula, given by

$$
A = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y(t) \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm d t}\:\textrm d t
$$

Now, in this case, we have

$$
\frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(t^{3} - 1) = 3t^{2}
$$

Applying the change of variables formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
A &= \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}y(t)\frac{dx}{dt}dt \\
&= \int_{0}^{1}(2t - t^{3}) \cdot 3t^{2}dt \\
&= \int_{0}^{1}6t^{3} - 3t^{5}dt \\
&= 6\int_{0}^{1}t^{3}dt - 3\int_{0}^{1}t^{5}dt \\
&= 6 \cdot \left.\frac{t^{4}}{4}\right|_{0}^{1} - 3 \cdot \left.\frac{t^{6}}{6}\right|_{0}^{1} \\
&= 6(\frac{1}{4} - 0) - 3(\frac{1}{6} - 0) \\
&= \frac{3}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shaded area shown in the picture has an area of $1$ square unit." :tutorial/id #uuid "1d0c890f-fbe0-5ded-948b-b94d13caac3b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1083 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "786032d8-d66a-579e-8336-348ca609cfb8" :step/math-academy-id 2136 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097747}} {:db/id 17592186097613 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096731 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096538 :question/id #uuid "85879186-0866-5159-905b-65d043681231" :question/math-academy-id "e-604"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f354f758-3745-5cee-9a4b-a0878c2c8578" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050929}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186096926} {:db/id 17592186097235}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve"} :step/id #uuid "296a64b2-a271-5186-bf37-e47d7b56624c" :step/math-academy-id 2138} {:db/id 17592186097653 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096758 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096561 :question/id #uuid "95cdc31d-c3f2-50b6-9447-b7317af775f9" :question/math-academy-id "e-7412"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f20da72e-5a93-5a4e-be39-d412bd8fee86" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048946} {:db/id 17592186050531}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097133} {:db/id 17592186097134}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Integral Expression for the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve"} :step/id #uuid "3a032caf-6330-5e24-bafb-d45c348ad375" :step/math-academy-id 27495 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097613}} {:db/id 17592186097747 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097915 :tutorial/content "In general, the area between the $x$-axis and the parametric curve

$$
x = x(t), \qquad y = y(t), \qquad t_1 \leq t \leq t_2
$$

is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
\int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t
$$

Note the following:

- When applying this formula, we assume that the chosen parametrization traverses the curve only once.
- It's possible that this integral gives a negative value for the area even when the corresponding region lies entirely above the $x$-axis! To see why, note that if the curve lies above the $x$-axis, we must have $y(t) > 0$. However, if the curve is parameterized so that it is traversed from right to left, then $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} < 0$, and we have
$y\cdot \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} < 0$
and thus, our integral turns out to be negative.
- To ensure that we get an unsigned area, we take the absolute value of the integral.
- In general, care must be taken when asked to compute the area bounded by a parametric curve when $y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}$ changes sign over the domain of integration. However, we won't consider that scenario here.

Let's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "89e96b74-e406-52f5-b64e-46267df927e4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7915 :tutorial/title "A General Formula for the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve"} :step/id #uuid "97757635-74ae-5269-ac75-2ea85021adb9" :step/math-academy-id 45599 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097653}}] :activity/title "Calculating Areas Bounded by Parametric Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186096851} {:db/id 17592186097612 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097798 :tutorial/content "![](images/d8/d8f08b1cc474cfee367ccf52e2299deaeec146ef7a7a860f64a75f7f7f25cb0b.png)

Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=t^3-1, \qquad y=2t-t^3, \qquad t \in (-\infty, \infty)
$$

The shaded area shown in the diagram is the finite region bounded between the curve, the $x$-axis, and the vertical lines formed by $x$-axis and the points on the curve corresponding to $t_1=0$ to $t_2=1$, as shown.

We know that the area of the curve is given by

$$
A = \int_{a}^{b} y \:\textrm{d}x
$$

Since our curve is defined parametrically, we need to change the variable of integration from $x$ to $t$ using the change of variables formula, given by

$$
A = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y(t) \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm d t}\:\textrm d t
$$

Now, in this case, we have

$$
\frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(t^{3} - 1) = 3t^{2}
$$

Applying the change of variables formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
A &= \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}y(t)\frac{dx}{dt}dt \\
&= \int_{0}^{1}(2t - t^{3}) \cdot 3t^{2}dt \\
&= \int_{0}^{1}6t^{3} - 3t^{5}dt \\
&= 6\int_{0}^{1}t^{3}dt - 3\int_{0}^{1}t^{5}dt \\
&= 6 \cdot \left.\frac{t^{4}}{4}\right|_{0}^{1} - 3 \cdot \left.\frac{t^{6}}{6}\right|_{0}^{1} \\
&= 6(\frac{1}{4} - 0) - 3(\frac{1}{6} - 0) \\
&= \frac{3}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shaded area shown in the picture has an area of $1$ square unit." :tutorial/id #uuid "1d0c890f-fbe0-5ded-948b-b94d13caac3b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1083 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186097747 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097915 :tutorial/content "In general, the area between the $x$-axis and the parametric curve

$$
x = x(t), \qquad y = y(t), \qquad t_1 \leq t \leq t_2
$$

is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
\int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t
$$

Note the following:

- When applying this formula, we assume that the chosen parametrization traverses the curve only once.
- It's possible that this integral gives a negative value for the area even when the corresponding region lies entirely above the $x$-axis! To see why, note that if the curve lies above the $x$-axis, we must have $y(t) > 0$. However, if the curve is parameterized so that it is traversed from right to left, then $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} < 0$, and we have
$y\cdot \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} < 0$
and thus, our integral turns out to be negative.
- To ensure that we get an unsigned area, we take the absolute value of the integral.
- In general, care must be taken when asked to compute the area bounded by a parametric curve when $y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}$ changes sign over the domain of integration. However, we won't consider that scenario here.

Let's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "89e96b74-e406-52f5-b64e-46267df927e4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7915 :tutorial/title "A General Formula for the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve"} :step/id #uuid "97757635-74ae-5269-ac75-2ea85021adb9" :step/math-academy-id 45599 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097653}} {:db/id 17592186097613 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096731 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096538 :question/id #uuid "85879186-0866-5159-905b-65d043681231" :question/math-academy-id "e-604"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f354f758-3745-5cee-9a4b-a0878c2c8578" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050929}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186096926} {:db/id 17592186097235}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve"} :step/id #uuid "296a64b2-a271-5186-bf37-e47d7b56624c" :step/math-academy-id 2138} {:db/id 17592186097653 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096758 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096561 :question/id #uuid "95cdc31d-c3f2-50b6-9447-b7317af775f9" :question/math-academy-id "e-7412"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f20da72e-5a93-5a4e-be39-d412bd8fee86" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048946} {:db/id 17592186050531}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097133} {:db/id 17592186097134}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Integral Expression for the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve"} :step/id #uuid "3a032caf-6330-5e24-bafb-d45c348ad375" :step/math-academy-id 27495 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097613}} {:db/id 17592186097915 :tutorial/content "In general, the area between the $x$-axis and the parametric curve

:step/id #uuid "35e1d4ff-896a-599d-bb79-ecb5cec36df6" :step/math-academy-id 31417} {:db/id 17592186167733 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168118 :tutorial/content "We can compute integrals containing hyperbolic functions using the hyperbolic counterparts of the Pythagorean identity. We use Osborn's rule to convert a trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity.

Osborn's rule states that to convert a trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity, we

- replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function, and
- for any product of two trigonometric sines, change the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

$$
\displaystyle \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
$$

For example, suppose we want to calculate the following integral:

$$
\int \cosh^2{x} - \sinh^2{x} \: \textrm{d}x
$$

First, we recall the Pythagorean identity

$$
\cos^2{x} + \sin^2{x} = 1
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the corresponding hyperbolic identity

$$
\cosh^2{x} - \sinh^2{x} = 1
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our integral as follows:

$$
\int\cosh^{2} x - \sinh^{2} x_(⏟)_(1)dx = \int1dx = x + C
$$

Let's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "250a3423-70a4-5d38-9b0f-6f801a0479d1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5553 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1283c2a5-d791-5099-bd72-546a74c8f4b8" :step/math-academy-id 34427 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167630}} {:db/id 17592186167734 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168119 :tutorial/content "$$
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
$$

We can use Osborn's rule to write down the hyperbolic equivalents of the sectant-tangent and cotangent-cosecant identities.

From the secant-tangent identity

$$
1 + \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x
$$

we have the equivalent hyperbolic identity

$$
1 - \tanh^2 x = \sech^2 x
$$

Similarly, from the cotangent-cosecant identity

$$
1+\cot^2 x = \csc^2 x
$$

we have the equivalent hyperbolic identity

$$
1-\coth^2 x = -\csch^2 x
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
\coth^2 x - 1 = \csch^2 x
$$

These identities can be used to solve certain integrals involving the expressions $\tanh^2{x}$, $\coth^2 x$, $\sech^2 x$, or $\csch^2{x}$." :tutorial/id #uuid "525b90c4-f6ea-5c55-8602-49547e261df1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5554 :tutorial/title "Calculating Integrals Using Related Hyperbolic Identities"} :step/id #uuid "ec6b416a-7645-5f7b-b41d-c553c9f1a62b" :step/math-academy-id 34428 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167631}}] :activity/title "Integration Using the Hyperbolic Pythagorean Identities" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186167027} {:db/id 17592186167733 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168118 :tutorial/content "We can compute integrals containing hyperbolic functions using the hyperbolic counterparts of the Pythagorean identity. Suppose we have a series

$$
\displaystyle \sum_{n =1} ^\infty a_n
$$

such that

$$
a_n \geq 0
$$

for all

$$
n \geq 1
$$

. We define $L$ as the following limit:

$$
L = \lim_{n \to \infty}\sqrt [n] {a_n} = \lim_{n \to \infty}\left({a_n}\right)^{1/n}
$$

Then, the root test states the following:

- if $L < 1$, the series converges.
- if $L >1$ or $L = \infty$, the series diverges.
- if $L = 1$, the root test is inconclusive.

Let's use the root test to show that the following geometric series converges:

$$
\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac {1} {2^n}
$$

In this case, our sequence $a_n$ is defined as

$$
a_n = \dfrac{1}{2^n}, \qquad n\geq 1
$$

To apply the root test, we calculate the limit of $\sqrt[n]{a_n}$ as $n\to\infty{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
L &= lim_(n → ∞)\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{2^{n}}} \\
&= lim_(n → ∞)\frac{\sqrt[n]{1}}{\sqrt[n]{2^{n}}} \\
&= lim_(n → ∞)\frac{1}{2} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
L=\dfrac12 < 1
$$

our series converges by the root test.

Finally, when applying the root test, it's worth bearing the following limit facts in mind:

- $\displaystyle \lim_{n \to \infty} \sqrt [n] {a} = 1$ for $a > 0$
- $\displaystyle \lim_{n \to \infty} \sqrt [n] {n} = 1$

Suppose we have a series

$$
\displaystyle \sum_{n =1} ^\infty a_n
$$

such that

$$
a_n \geq 0
$$

for all

$$
n \geq 1
$$

. We define $L$ as the following limit:

$$
L = \lim_{n \to \infty}\sqrt [n] {a_n} = \lim_{n \to \infty}\left({a_n}\right)^{1/n}
$$

Then, the root test states the following:

- if $L < 1$, the series converges.
- if $L >1$ or $L = \infty$, the series diverges.
- if $L = 1$, the root test is inconclusive.

Let's use the root test to show that the following geometric series converges:

$$
\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac {1} {2^n}
$$

In this case, our sequence $a_n$ is defined as

$$
a_n = \dfrac{1}{2^n}, \qquad n\geq 1
$$

To apply the root test, we calculate the limit of $\sqrt[n]{a_n}$ as $n\to\infty{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
L &= lim_(n → ∞)\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{2^{n}}} \\
&= lim_(n → ∞)\frac{\sqrt[n]{1}}{\sqrt[n]{2^{n}}} \\
&= lim_(n → ∞)\frac{1}{2} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
L=\dfrac12 < 1
$$

our series converges by the root test.

Finally, when applying the root test, it's worth bearing the following limit facts in mind:

- $\displaystyle \lim_{n \to \infty} \sqrt [n] {a} = 1$ for $a > 0$
- $\displaystyle \lim_{n \to \infty} \sqrt [n] {n} = 1$
- $\displaystyle \lim_{n \to \infty} \sqrt [n] {\dfrac 1 {n!}} = 0$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3a3259b2-b4b5-580c-a5f2-d1718c65a022" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6116 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6c859a87-7f6f-521b-9bcf-5d8691ae2dbc" :step/math-academy-id 37147 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084295}} {:db/id 17592186084492 :tutorial/content "When the $n$th term $a_n$ of an infinite series involves $n$th powers, we can determine whether the series converges or diverges using the **root test**.

Triple Integral Over a Type II Region"}] :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R 4x^3  \: \mathrm{d}V
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (y,z) \in D, \: 0 \leq x \leq \sqrt{y} \right\},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the $z$-axis, and the line $z = 4-y$ in the first quadrant." :question/worked-solution "Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} 4x^3 \, \textrm{d}V
= 
\iint\limits_{D} \left[ \int_{0}^{\sqrt{y}} 4x^3 \, \mathrm{d}x \right] \mathrm{d}A.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}4{x}^{3}\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}[{x}^{4}]_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{y}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{(\sqrt{y})}^{4}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate this double integral over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](images/3c/3c8712fa0a30ad94f503efe5e080ee89f83eb21f19fba45033bbedeab08ac816.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{y}^{2}z]_{z=0}^{z=4-y}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{y}^{2}(4-y)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}4{y}^{2}-{y}^{3}\,dy \\  & ={[\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=4} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}(64-0)-\frac{1}{4}(256-0) \\  & =\frac{64}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134267 :question/id #uuid "f3f05e28-f16f-584f-8405-9efa5bf16a61" :question/math-academy-id "q-40206"} {:db/id 17592186134268 :question/id #uuid "02ff2794-de30-53c1-a133-ec1abbd3f0b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-40208" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133914 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "90adf237-9627-55f1-8f90-8fbc4acf02fc" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Triple Integral Over a Type II Region"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3dfa63d1-2a3c-5f98-ac88-3e5a9c4a677a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186324472} {:answer/id #uuid "50f72eff-980c-5d6b-bc19-dfa625820604" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186324636} {:answer/id #uuid "6699b8d5-c375-5917-8a45-ab199058df5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186324827} {:answer/id #uuid "9313c2e6-4978-5466-83ec-9afb5f029598" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186325220} {:answer/id #uuid "dbdb866a-5a0b-5141-8de8-88e091ddbf5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186325887}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "9313c2e6-4978-5466-83ec-9afb5f029598" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186325220} :answer-field/id #uuid "51388a81-fbd8-54d3-b307-b0098d6fa5e9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186326357}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axes, the line $y=2$ and the line $z=y$ in the first quadrant." :question/worked-solution "Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2y\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z\sqrt{3}}2y\,dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z\sqrt{3}}2y\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}2y[x]_{x=0}^{x=z\sqrt{3}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}2yz\sqrt{3}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](images/63/63a8768b2769fad339ba7667357812d2dda0ea856e846ad666a100f8bc1336e9.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2yz\sqrt{3}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y}2yz\sqrt{3}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}y\sqrt{3}[{\int }_{0}^{y}2z\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}y\sqrt{3}[{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=y}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}y\sqrt{3}({y}^{2}-0)\,dy \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\,dy \\  & =\sqrt{3}{[\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =\sqrt{3}(\frac{16}{4}-0) \\  & =4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278562 :question/id #uuid "cf24dc38-62d4-5f8d-aead-cd979e84a570" :question/math-academy-id "q-161575"} {:db/id 17592186278563 :question/id #uuid $$
{∭}_{R}2x\,dV

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le yz},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the line $y=1$ and the parabola $z={y}^{2}$ in the first quadrant." :question/worked-solution "Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2x\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{yz}2x\,dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{yz}2x\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=yz}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}(yz)^{2}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](images/ac/acb173db9d28ed8b38e63c7bc365c20e5755aeb1af3f6340e7b9229a4b49101d.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{2}{z}^{3}]}_{z=0}^{z={y}^{2}}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{3}{y}^{2}({y}^{6}-0)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{3}{y}^{8}\,dy \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{[\frac{1}{9}{y}^{9}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{1}{9}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{27}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278566 :question/id #uuid "a816d812-5042-53f7-abc8-46b6718aff74" :question/math-academy-id "q-161585" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133914 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "90adf237-9627-55f1-8f90-8fbc4acf02fc" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Triple Integral Over a Type II Region"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4f8e4b7b-e3ec-5734-95c4-f3c524afc21a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{34}{81}" :db/id 17592186276189} {:answer/id #uuid "a467a30d-d76f-5115-be5a-fe13677662bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{72}{121}" :db/id 17592186276958} {:answer/id #uuid "c5a811da-034c-53e9-92a9-fa69054f8cf5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{61}{105}" :db/id 17592186277236} {:answer/id #uuid "cfccbb0d-2768-5c28-9ab0-be5dd2b5e9fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{67}{92}" :db/id 17592186277317} {:answer/id #uuid "d8cd8db2-d1c9-5016-968d-3ce6bf214109" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{79}{100}" :db/id 17592186277382}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "c5a811da-034c-53e9-92a9-fa69054f8cf5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{61}{105}" :db/id 17592186277236} :answer-field/id #uuid "fb0ee147-a553-542c-8e10-1d6e3f554db7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186278168}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le {y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the line $y=1$ and the parabola $z=-{y}^{2}$ in the fourth quadrant." :question/worked-solution "Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1}dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1}dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}[x]_{x=0}^{x={y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](images/38/38ea49a6fae41574107b2ba68a578586a306cf43d419d4de5699dcfa009137c2.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-{y}^{2}}^{0}{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{-{y}^{2}}^{0}{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[({y}^{2}+1)z+\frac{1}{3}{z}^{3}]}_{z=-{y}^{2}}^{z=0}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}+1)((0-(-{y}^{2}))+\frac{1}{3}(0-{(-{y}^{2})}^{3})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}+1){y}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{6}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{4}+{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{6}\,dy \\  & ={[\frac{1}{5}{y}^{5}+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{21}{y}^{7}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{21} \\  & =\frac{61}{105}\end{aligned}

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_D \left[ \int_{0}^{z} \dfrac{\cos (2y)}{1-y} \,\textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}A
$$

where the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane is given by

$$
D = \left\{ (y,z) \, : \, 0 \leq y \leq \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \: 0 \leq z \leq 2\sqrt{1-y} \right\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}[x]_{x=0}^{x=z}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}(z-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{\int }_{0}^{2\sqrt{1-y}}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}{[\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=2\sqrt{1-y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}(\frac{4(1-y)}{2}-0)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)]_{y=0}^{y=\pi /6} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134128 :question/id #uuid "1f663fe3-dd5b-577a-af75-1af60254b416" :question/math-academy-id "q-161574" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133915 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0bd48398-cb9d-579f-b7f7-0f6be19172ce" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Mixed Integral"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a14f67b0-77e7-5ad2-bed1-6f40742b91fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "32" :db/id 17592186130925} {:answer/id #uuid "aab2d86c-e157-5e56-8d6e-acbe88ccf262" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "28" :db/id 17592186130926} {:answer/id #uuid "ef563ce8-107d-527c-92e3-beb40d14a996" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "19" :db/id 17592186130927} {:answer/id #uuid "5c7d0390-01a3-59b0-a991-6ed1293f7ba7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "21" :db/id 17592186130928} {:answer/id #uuid "5cc9f6ca-4a76-5b98-9134-af437d186875" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186130929}] :answer-field/id #uuid "3e843666-e94f-5e5d-a692-2cd9aab8f479" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186130924}] :question/problem "Evaluate the mixed integral
