Evaluate the triple integral 
$\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R 12z^2 \: \mathrm{d}V$
over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*" :question/worked-solution "![](images/f2/f25c393f10c35ffd9b4fa91cdf672a516cf6cff974a8aa563d350619a64b79bd.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (y,z) \in D, \:\: 0 \leq x \leq 3-y-z \big\},
$$

where

$$
D = \big\{ (y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1 \big\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/14/145f0d494ffe24de84e3a289b3a7316d3f4933f193d734aed118609f7fb9f94f.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq x \leq 3-y-z \big\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
\iiint \limits_{R}  12z^2  \: \textrm{d}V 
= 
\int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{3-y-z}  12z^2  \: \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3-y-z}12{z}^{2}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{3-y-z}12{z}^{2}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}12{z}^{2}[x]_{x=0}^{x=3-y-z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}12{z}^{2}(3-y-z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(36{z}^{2}-12y{z}^{2}-12{z}^{3})\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(36{z}^{2}-12y{z}^{2}-12{z}^{3})\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}(36{z}^{2}-12y{z}^{2}-12{z}^{3})\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[12{z}^{3}-4y{z}^{3}-3{z}^{4}]_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(12-4y-3)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9-4y)\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(9-4y)\,dy & =[9y-2{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(9-2)-0 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134265 :question/id #uuid "1bca43d8-d1e1-57af-b381-d0bcf72d6b11" :question/math-academy-id "q-40203"} {:db/id 17592186134271 :question/id #uuid Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le x\le 2+2y-z}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2+2y-z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(2+2y-z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2{y}^{2}z+2{y}^{3}z-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}\,dy & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2})-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278569 :question/id #uuid "bbdba5ca-83e0-5a85-b98f-07e26739da4e" :question/math-academy-id "q-161594"} {:db/id 17592186281322 :question/id #uuid Evaluate the triple integral 
${∭}_{R}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,dV$
over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*" :question/worked-solution "![](images/2a/2a20f2651c24e48871028b44fe61da4600d632481877ef32ccdfd3241262a53b.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 5-y-\frac{z}{2}},
$$

where

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 4}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/1b/1ba7c02f254313a73a813e4e43c44c25523ce77dd47e594a1db3b412a6bd5c3d.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 4,\,\,0\le x\le 5-y-\frac{z}{2}}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{5-y-z/2}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{5-y-z/2}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{5-y-z/2}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}[x]_{x=0}^{x=5-y-z/2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}(5-y-\frac{z}{2})\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{2}\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{2}\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{2}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{z}{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=4}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}2\,dy & =[2y]_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =6-0 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281324 :question/id #uuid "78eec2a4-7ee5-59eb-8402-37f965ae8bd1" :question/math-academy-id "q-161784" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133922 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e612d4ba-b772-5f56-a031-fdfc05d63221" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Triple Integral Over a Type II Region Given a Diagram"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "56db55ba-db05-567a-9988-071184b844d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186279386} {:answer/id #uuid "688f55f5-366d-5010-ab2b-a189e5f23bc1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186279543} {:answer/id #uuid "8cf90354-3814-59d5-a7cf-c0bc9a3254d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186279848} {:answer/id #uuid "f3a47d8f-8a5c-5150-8c7d-8102990223cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186280724} {:answer/id #uuid "fd1c3683-c4dd-5443-82b2-d8994d7dbb7f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{9}" :db/id 17592186280807}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "688f55f5-366d-5010-ab2b-a189e5f23bc1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186279543} :answer-field/id #uuid "7566d184-eeca-5394-8d91-0aadcdbc31b4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186281048}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/ca/ca49b92d602d04a73dc7ab9936d601654bd293ce3fb7950372ac86155875aca3.png)

Evaluate the triple integral

over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*" :question/worked-solution "![](images/00/0008ba406cfe8a5b61d683a6854260897cb441752a5333add281ab1279e31b0b.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 2-\frac{y}{3}+z},
$$

where

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 3}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/bb/bbe6b6b897e5d53421080ae8e8b9dc49f2ea1b7e135f8426ee3f11af01cc2401.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,0\le 2-\frac{y}{3}+z}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2-y/3+z}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2-y/3+z}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{2-y/3+z}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2-y/3+z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}(2-\frac{y}{3}+z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}{[z]}_{z=0}^{z=3}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}(3)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\,dy & =[y]_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186133924 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133484 :question/id #uuid "b51667a8-f48a-59a2-b09e-59c6fcad5507" :question/math-academy-id "e-12398"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a22ed84a-4b6f-53b3-8336-bf592aed8686" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048175} {:db/id 17592186050197}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134266 :question/id #uuid "b7e48828-2b5f-5a93-ace2-8e07e11d9709" :question/math-academy-id "q-40204"} {:db/id 17592186134274 :question/id #uuid "53226692-6bc3-5825-815b-b63652cdaabe" :question/math-academy-id "q-40230"} {:db/id 17592186278549 :question/id #uuid "ef487dd1-5505-5bf5-9562-86954dcf2c40" :question/math-academy-id "q-161545"} {:db/id 17592186278550 :question/id #uuid "587a8773-2afe-542a-990e-6aafa5beb6ef" :question/math-academy-id "q-161548"} {:db/id 17592186278555 :question/id #uuid "6000b721-5977-5631-b5d7-c481cdaa3368" :question/math-academy-id "q-161563"} {:db/id 17592186278556 :question/id #uuid "4ac74bdd-4f55-52a9-8415-18543bfb88ec" :question/math-academy-id "q-161564"} {:db/id 17592186278557 :question/id #uuid "29632302-5883-5021-9de6-855ebf0325c6" :question/math-academy-id "q-161566"}] :knowledge-point/title "Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral"} {:db/id 17592186133484 :question/id #uuid "b51667a8-f48a-59a2-b09e-59c6fcad5507" :question/math-academy-id "e-12398" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186133924 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a22ed84a-4b6f-53b3-8336-bf592aed8686" :knowledge-point/title "Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral"}] :question/problem "Find the missing limits in the repeated integral below

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \: \textrm{d}V
= 
\int_{\ast}^{\ast} 
\int_{\ast}^{\ast} 
\int_{\ast}^{\ast} 
f(x,y,z) \: \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y
$$

where $R$ is the type II region defined as

$$
R=\left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 1 \leq y \leq 4, \: -y^2 \leq z \leq \sqrt{y}, \: -2 \leq x \leq ye^{z+2} \right\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z)  \: : \: (y,z) \in D, \: u_1(y,z) \leq x \leq u_2(y,z) \big\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](images/1b/1b49704bf6d5837a18d8b5dbb8b420d430d5e3881507540fb62a45cf1f6ce52f.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z)\,\textrm d V = \iint\limits_{D} \left[\int_{u_1(y,z)}^{u_2(y,z)} f(x,y,z)\,\textrm{d}x \right]\,\textrm d A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
u_1(y,z) = -2, \qquad u_2(y,z)  = ye^{z+2}.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \: \textrm{d}V 
= 
\iint\limits_{D} \left[ \int_{-2}^{ye^{z+2}} f(x,y,z) \: \mathrm{d}x \right] \mathrm{d}A.
$$

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D =\left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 1 \leq y \leq 4, \: -y^2 \leq z \leq \sqrt{y} \right\}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2}^{y{e}^{z+2}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{-{y}^{2}}^{\sqrt{y}}[{\int }_{-2}^{y{e}^{z+2}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dz\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{-{y}^{2}}^{\sqrt{y}}{\int }_{-2}^{y{e}^{z+2}}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dz\,dy.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050197} {:db/id 17592186134266 :question/id #uuid "b7e48828-2b5f-5a93-ace2-8e07e11d9709" :question/math-academy-id "q-40204"} {:db/id 17592186134274 :question/id #uuid [{:db/id 17592186134909 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135156 :tutorial/content "Let's evaluate the triple integral

where the region ![](images/08/085f4d77675f3cb7323d94feaa9eaa38f2fecb26c0f8483895f9ddf36b8d319d.svg) is shown below.

![](images/3e/3ee0df491365ac117eef84055f9d14aff9e7e5073b69e8e48b0a8bb93bb2f7ee.png)

The region ![](images/08/085f4d77675f3cb7323d94feaa9eaa38f2fecb26c0f8483895f9ddf36b8d319d.svg) is a type II region. So, our first task is to fully describe this region.

We start by drawing an arrow parallel to the ![](images/fc/fcc5df999e3b49fae1685ee0ab5bd03709804e1dd49f2ee722c4269eb0f5506d.svg)-axis that 

- enters the region through the *back* surface ![](images/89/89c97ad93c125fc2b6f61d44fe9a90845fd289329d79d506c857f970d7586540.svg) and

- leaves the region through the *front* surface ![](images/7b/7b823cb4664e2fe98090b6a778eba3030abf589930d2526ef5a50fb0aa792b5f.svg)

as shown below.

![](images/e6/e63827168c78ff5d13898bc436e02f99d834fbd2a10ce43aa98f47001e35044d.png)

So, our solid can be written as the type II region

![](images/c4/c4a007ae116844babbe81721267c0526be0ee44b8b8007a799031eae12485a59.svg)

where

![](images/12/12d667e2c74a83bd8f7fe58be763862fc793d22774695995b56ccda713308381.svg)

is the projection of ![](images/08/085f4d77675f3cb7323d94feaa9eaa38f2fecb26c0f8483895f9ddf36b8d319d.svg) onto the ![](images/3f/3f84f2f8778b7916a5ee013c8a92440e5cbd510ba2768435c3139b45806d2f90.svg)-plane, shown below.

![](images/ea/ea267107ec908087a99eaea952caabb0d1a08488657b2c0f70a2502bbf4b869b.png)

![](images/13/13957704101661a7e52fa89ed897918c142fd1725742cf7b082d72eb54672e66.svg)

Now, since the region ![](images/59/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) is a type I plane region, we can express the region ![](images/08/085f4d77675f3cb7323d94feaa9eaa38f2fecb26c0f8483895f9ddf36b8d319d.svg) as

![](images/53/535700690396dd4444e6f79015a447900af741cf14001fc2c552224e597a948b.svg)

and therefore, our mixed integral can be written as the following repeated integral:

For example, suppose we wish to evaluate

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R f(x,y,z)  \: \mathrm{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the type II region given by 

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: {\color{red}a} \leq y \leq {\color{red}b}, \: {\color{blue}v_1(y)} \leq z \leq {\color{blue}v_2(y)}, \: {\color{purple}u_1(y,z)} \leq x \leq {\color{purple}u_2(y,z)} \right\}.
$$

Notice that the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane is a type I plane region. Therefore, we can immediately express our triple integral as a repeated integral as follows:

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} f(x,y,z)\: \textrm{d}V 
= 
\int_{\color{red}a}^{\color{red}b} \int_{\color{blue}v_1(y)}^{\color{blue}v_2(y)} \int_{\color{purple}u_1(y,z)}^{\color{purple}u_2(y,z)} f(x,y,z)\: \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y.

For example, suppose we wish to evaluate

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R f(x,y,z)  \: \mathrm{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the type II region given by 

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: {\color{red}a} \leq y \leq {\color{red}b}, \: {\color{blue}v_1(y)} \leq z \leq {\color{blue}v_2(y)}, \: {\color{purple}u_1(y,z)} \leq x \leq {\color{purple}u_2(y,z)} \right\}.
$$

Notice that the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane is a type I plane region. Therefore, we can immediately express our triple integral as a repeated integral as follows:

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} f(x,y,z)\: \textrm{d}V 
= 
\int_{\color{red}a}^{\color{red}b} \int_{\color{blue}v_1(y)}^{\color{blue}v_2(y)} \int_{\color{purple}u_1(y,z)}^{\color{purple}u_2(y,z)} f(x,y,z)\: \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bcc6b25b-ebf4-5b46-9d69-4e4e068d107d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7133 :tutorial/title "Skipping the Intermediate Step"} :step/id #uuid "edc485dc-08a7-548e-b81e-e51516f53537" :step/math-academy-id 42712 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134923}} {:db/id 17592186135157 :tutorial/content "When writing down a triple integral as a repeated integral, we can often skip the intermediate step of expressing our triple integral as a mixed integral.

$$

Find the average rate of change of $y$ over the interval $[0,5]$." :question/worked-solution "Let

$$
f(x)=2x^2
$$

Applying the formula for the average rate of change, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{Δy}{Δx} &= (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a) \\
&= (f(5) - f(0))/(5 - (0)) \\
&= ((2(5)^{2}) - (2(0)^{2}))/(5) \\
&= \frac{50}{5} \\
&= 10
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048652} {:db/id 17592186064565 :question/id #uuid "e460d45e-d406-504b-ba46-cb34526931e8" :question/math-academy-id "q-20832" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186064267 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "68635d27-a9ef-541b-a57b-d9f5f422ae85" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Average Rate of Change of a Function"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9bb2e6d9-a77d-57a2-9067-88938b25fdf4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186061586} {:answer/id #uuid "c9c43b9e-95bc-527c-aaa8-97ef8fe71eb9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186061587} {:answer/id #uuid "eab80576-cf3c-565b-8b70-625ee7c85497" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186061588} {:answer/id #uuid "ecdbf5c9-b46e-558c-a271-c8dd2bf11f35" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186061589} {:answer/id #uuid "1bdd418b-40e8-5c8b-9aee-f67c99347494" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186061590}] :answer-field/id #uuid "258c7721-283b-58d1-a5c6-b9d2648fb034" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186061585}] :question/problem "A curve is defined as $y = x^{4} - 3x^{3} + 3x$. Problem"}] :question/problem "Dave plants a tree in his garden. After $x$ months the tree is $2\sqrt x + 1$ feet high. What is the average rate of growth of the tree over the first six months?" :question/worked-solution "Let

$$
f(x)=2\sqrt{x}+1
$$

be the height of the tree after $x$ months. The average rate of growth of the tree over the first six months is the average value of $f(x)$ on the interval $[0,6]$.

Applying the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{Δf}{Δx} &= (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a) \\
&= (f(6) - f(0))/(6) \\
&= (2\sqrt{6} + 1 - (2\sqrt{0} + 1))/(6) \\
&= \frac{2\sqrt{6}}{6} \\
&= \frac{\sqrt{6}}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average rate of growth is

$$
\dfrac {\sqrt 6} 3 \approx 0.82
$$

feet per month."} {:db/id 17592186064573 :question/id #uuid "7b937295-21d3-5d88-8e0d-4526eb861e99" :question/math-academy-id "q-21121"} {:db/id 17592186064636 :question/id #uuid Rate of Change is Zero"}] :question/problem "Find the interval where the average rate of change of $f(x)$ equals $0$ given the following table of values for $f(x)$:

| $x$ | $\,-2\,$ | $\,-1\,$ | $\,0\,$ | $\,1\,$ | $\,2\,$ | $\,5\,$ | $\,7\,$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $f(x)$ | $\,2\,$ | $\,1\,$ | $\,4\,$ | $\,-5\,$ | $\,-7\,$ | $\,2\,$ | $\,-2\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "We have

$$
\dfrac{\Delta f}{\Delta x}=0
$$

if and only if

$$
\Delta f = 0
$$

So

$$
Δf = 0; f(b) - f(a) = 0; f(b) = f(a)
$$

This means we have to find an interval $[a,b]$ such that

$$
f(a)=f(b)
$$

Since

$$
f(-2)=f(5)=2
$$

we conclude that

$$
\dfrac{\Delta f}{\Delta x}=0
$$

on the interval $[-2,5]$."} {:db/id 17592186064523 :question/id #uuid "4b33e69f-81bd-53be-9853-29b2f662d419" :question/math-academy-id "q-15941"} {:db/id 17592186064524 :question/id #uuid The **average rate of change** of $y=f(x)$ on the interval $x\in[a,b]$ is computed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{\text{change in}y}{\text{change in}x} = \dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}
$$

Geometrically, the average rate of change represents the slope of the **secant line** which passes through $(a,f(a))$ and $(b,f(b))$.

**Note:** In general, a secant is a line that intersects a curve at two or more distinct points." :tutorial/id #uuid "4e32384d-35c4-578e-b254-9cf90914529e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 312 Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\textrm{Var}\big\begin{bmatrix}Y \, & \, X=3\big\end{bmatrix}$ given that the conditional probability mass function $f_{Y\mid X}(y \, \mid \, 3)$ is shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is $\mu_{Y \mid 3} = \dfrac{8}{3}$." :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}
Var\begin{bmatrix}Y & X = x\end{bmatrix} &= E\begin{bmatrix}(Y - μ_{Y \mid x})^{2} & X = x\end{bmatrix} \\
&= E\begin{bmatrix}Y^{2} & X = x\end{bmatrix} - μ_{Y\begin{vmatrix}x}^{2} \\ = [∑_(y)y^{2}f_{Y\mid X}(y \mid x)] - μ_{Y\end{vmatrix}x}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
Var\begin{bmatrix}Y & X = 3\end{bmatrix} &= [∑_(y)y^{2}f_{Y\mid X}(y \mid 3)] - μ_{Y \mid 3}^{2} \\
&= [(1)^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3} + (2)^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{6} + (4)^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2}] - (\frac{8}{3})^{2} \\
&= \frac{1}{3} + \frac{2}{3} + 8 - \frac{64}{9} \\
&= \frac{17}{9}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048872} {:db/id 17592186188634 :question/id #uuid "48465d77-709a-5798-8d0f-b9b350792570" :question/math-academy-id "q-145550"} {:db/id 17592186188635 :question/id #uuid "88a6f652-2dd2-5b0b-9432-59ef465ca5aa" :question/math-academy-id "q-145561" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186188327 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4c80ef8f-1073-5e41-bec3-860209a731bd" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Conditional Variance Given a Conditional Mass Function"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8efe7779-a68e-5320-9296-47bd49330142" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.69" :db/id 17592186186091} {:answer/id #uuid "b9f78844-51fc-53d4-8e04-b0c325e2012f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.17" :db/id 17592186186092} {:answer/id #uuid "0a1760c4-2536-5c77-a1ab-0e41464ef0b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.21" :db/id 17592186186093} {:answer/id #uuid "0b97bdb2-55bb-51a0-a1e5-c0f1c24cfb35" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1.24" :db/id 17592186186094} {:answer/id #uuid "53d94e20-9ee4-5882-97b4-bfc5c3196345" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.44" :db/id 17592186186095}] :answer-field/id #uuid "a8b5e94e-afe5-5762-95d7-8bafbffc617d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186186090}] :question/problem "| $y$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\textrm{Var}\big\begin{bmatrix}X \, & \, Y=2\big\end{bmatrix}$ given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is $\mu_{X \mid 2}=\dfrac{10}{9}$." :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}
Var\begin{bmatrix}X & Y = y\end{bmatrix} &= E\begin{bmatrix}(X - μ_{X \mid y})^{2} & Y = y\end{bmatrix} \\
&= E\begin{bmatrix}X^{2} & Y = y\end{bmatrix} - μ_{X\begin{vmatrix}y}^{2} \\ = [∑_(x)x^{2}f_{X\mid Y}(x \mid y)] - μ_{X\end{vmatrix}y}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find $f_{X \mid Y}(x \, \mid \, y)$, let's first find the marginal distribution of $Y$, corresponding to the column totals:

| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| $X=1$ | $\dfrac{1}{2}$ | $\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
| $X=2$ | $\dfrac{1}{16}$ | $\dfrac{3}{16}$ |
| $f_Y(y)$ | $\dfrac{9}{16}$ | $\dfrac{7}{16}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$ is

$$
f_{X \mid Y}(x \, \mid \, y) = \dfrac{f(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding column total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y{:}$

| $f_{X\mid Y}(x\, \mid \,y)$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| $X=1$ | $\dfrac{8}{9}$ | $\dfrac{4}{7}$ |
| $X=2$ | $\dfrac{1}{9}$ | $\dfrac{3}{7}$ |
|  | $1$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
Var\begin{bmatrix}X & Y = 2\end{bmatrix} &= [∑_(x)x^{2}f_{X\mid Y}(x \mid 2)] - μ_{X \mid 2}^{2} \\
&= [1^{2} \cdot \frac{8}{9} + 2^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{9}] - (\frac{10}{9})^{2} \\
&= \frac{8}{9} + \frac{4}{9} - \frac{100}{81} \\
&= \frac{8}{81}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186188637 :question/id #uuid "87429b89-e333-5492-85d9-bf5d6ddc4038" :question/math-academy-id "q-145581" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186188328 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "92a52324-627c-5796-bc4f-ddeb5380f129" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Conditional Variance Using Column Totals"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2452ce83-dc52-55f6-8ada-4270840e5f0d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{5}{9}" :db/id 17592186186103} {:answer/id #uuid "3112bbd0-2efd-5af4-9183-d529b43787f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186186104} {:answer/id #uuid "32a79aa0-324a-576c-b24a-9dda030a3055" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{5}{6}" :db/id 17592186186105} {:answer/id #uuid "496b21b0-10f4-5ed9-a567-35580e353507" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2}{9}" :db/id 17592186186106} {:answer/id #uuid "7c5cc2f6-63db-5ee3-a19a-a655c587bd7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186186107}] :answer-field/id #uuid "7b0e8466-e71c-51fa-a1f3-58418768c396" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186186102}] :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y = 0$ | $Y = 1$ |

Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=2]$ given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is ${\mu }_{X|2}=5.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ let's first find the marginal distribution of $Y,$ corresponding to the column totals: 

| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=3$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ |
| $X=9$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{3}{16}$ | $\frac{1}{16}$ |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $\frac{3}{8}$ | $\frac{5}{16}$ | $\frac{5}{16}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$ is

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding column total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y:$

| ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=3$ | $\frac{2}{3}$ | $\frac{2}{5}$ | $\frac{4}{5}$ |
| $X=9$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{3}{5}$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ |
|  | $1$ | $1$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=2] & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,2)]-{\mu }_{X|2}^{2} \\  & =[{3}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}+{9}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}]-{5}^{2} \\  & =6+27-25 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186511582 :question/id #uuid "fa585366-16bd-5221-b5b1-a80000ac4783" :question/math-academy-id "q-146282" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186188328 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "92a52324-627c-5796-bc4f-ddeb5380f129" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Conditional Variance Using Column Totals"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "14738cb2-b471-5d99-b3eb-4afbb5fa348a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186510824} {:answer/id #uuid "20ae5337-49f2-5726-8ce9-b5fca604cf7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186510853} {:answer/id #uuid "518547db-16ad-50af-8a24-b4267aa35a9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186510957} {:answer/id #uuid "a50bc467-b427-559a-829c-9f60582a46c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186511128} {:answer/id #uuid "ee546c20-c60e-59e8-af15-1c8202fb7fba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186511274}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "14738cb2-b471-5d99-b3eb-4afbb5fa348a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186510824} :answer-field/id #uuid "0f312ee4-2cb7-5564-9f11-50b74da2484d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186511318}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ |

Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\textrm{Var}\big\begin{bmatrix}Y \, & \, X=1\big\end{bmatrix}$ given that $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is $\mu_{Y \mid 1} = \dfrac{9}{4}$." :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}
Var\begin{bmatrix}Y & X = x\end{bmatrix} &= E\begin{bmatrix}(Y - μ_{Y \mid x})^{2} & X = x\end{bmatrix} \\
&= E\begin{bmatrix}Y^{2} & X = x\end{bmatrix} - μ_{Y\begin{vmatrix}x}^{2} \\ = [∑_(y)y^{2}f_{Y\mid X}(y \mid x)] - μ_{Y\end{vmatrix}x}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find $f_{Y \mid X}(y \, \mid \, x)$, let's first find the marginal distribution for $X$, corresponding to the row totals:

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ | $f_X(x)$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $X=1$ | $\dfrac{1}{10}$ | $\dfrac{1}{10}$ | $\dfrac{1}{5}$ | $\dfrac{2}{5}$ |
| $X=2$ | $\dfrac{3}{10}$ | $\dfrac{1}{5}$ | $\dfrac{1}{10}$ | $\dfrac{3}{5}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x$ is

$$
f_{Y \mid X}(y \, \mid \, x) = \dfrac{f(x,y)}{f_X(x)}
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding row total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x{:}$

| $f_{Y \mid X}(y \, \mid \, x)$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ |  |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $X=1$ | $\dfrac{1}{4}$ | $\dfrac{1}{4}$ | $\dfrac{1}{2}$ | $1$ |
| $X=2$ | $\dfrac{1}{2}$ | $\dfrac{1}{3}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
Var\begin{bmatrix}Y & X = 1\end{bmatrix} &= [∑_(y)y^{2}f_{Y\mid X}(y \mid 1)] - μ_{Y \mid 1}^{2} \\
&= [1^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{4} + 2^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{4} + 3^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2}] - (\frac{9}{4})^{2} \\
&= \frac{1}{4} + 1 + \frac{9}{2} - \frac{81}{16} \\
&= \frac{11}{16}
\end{aligned}

that $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables, where the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is given by $\mu_{X \mid y}$. In other words,

$$
\textrm{E}\begin{bmatrix}X\, & \,Y=y\end{bmatrix} = \mu_{X \mid y}
$$

The **conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$** is defined as

$$
\textrm{Var}\begin{bmatrix}X\, & \,Y=y\end{bmatrix} = \textrm{E}\big\begin{bmatrix}(X - \mu_{X \mid y} \big)^2 \, & \, Y=y\end{bmatrix}
$$

This is similar to the definition of $\textrm{Var}[X]$ in that it represents the average (squared) distance of the random variable $X$ from the mean. The difference here is that the expected values are now dependent on the outcome of $Y$.

Similarly to the case of $\textrm{Var}[X]$, this often isn't the easiest formula to use in practice. However, it can be shown that the definition of conditional variance is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}
Var\begin{bmatrix}X & Y = y\end{bmatrix} &= E\begin{bmatrix}X^{2} & Y = y\end{bmatrix} - μ_{X\begin{vmatrix}y}^{2} \\ = [∑_(x)x^{2}f_{X\mid Y}(x \mid y)] - μ_{X\end{vmatrix}y}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $f_{X\mid Y}(x \, \mid \, y)$ is the conditional PMF of $X$ given $Y$. Note that these formulas are analogous to those for $\textrm{Var}[X]$.

Finally, we have an analogous definition for the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Var\begin{bmatrix}Y & X = x\end{bmatrix} &= E\begin{bmatrix}(Y - μ_{Y \mid x})^{2} & X = x\end{bmatrix} \\
&= E\begin{bmatrix}Y^{2} & X = x\end{bmatrix} - μ_{Y\begin{vmatrix}x}^{2} \\ = [∑_(y)y^{2}f_{Y\mid X}(y \mid x)] - μ_{Y\end{vmatrix}x}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ce4fb1c3-94ee-51c3-b10d-ce6ea0c7ff38" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6431 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "12bb1f79-4af3-56c1-b495-e654c2cf5d1c" :step/math-academy-id 38850 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189167}} {:db/id 17592186189183 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188339 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186188046 :question/id #uuid "3764cb54-7fd2-584a-9dc7-eda88368b032" :question/math-academy-id "e-10352"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "abfaf356-6b74-5dfd-8070-e3a60dc372c5" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188680} {:db/id 17592186188687} {:db/id 17592186511456} {:db/id 17592186511574}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Conditional Variance Using Row Totals"} :step/id #uuid "7f447a96-6d58-5356-934d-4d4a94738359" :step/math-academy-id 38984 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189168}}] :activity/title "Conditional Variance for Discrete Random Variables" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186188511} {:db/id 17592186189169 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189401 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables, where the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is given by $\mu_{X \mid y}$. Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z) = z-y$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle u^2, \: -v, \: v \big\rangle
$$

for $(u,v) \in D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ where $u \geq 0.$ What is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that $\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \| = 2\sqrt{2}u.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \| = 2\sqrt{2}u.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(z-y)\,{|}_{x={u}^{2}\,y=-v\,z=v} \\  & =v-(-v) \\  & =2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,4\sqrt{2}uv\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048384} {:db/id 17592186172375 :question/id #uuid "25e44fde-444d-5880-ba2e-43dd4bc039db" :question/math-academy-id "q-160711" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186172130 $$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=xyz$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,uv⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,v⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & v \\ 0 & 1 & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & v \\ 1 & u\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & v \\ 0 & u\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-v,\,-u,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨-v,\,-u,\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-v)^{2}+(-u)^{2}+(1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(xyz)\,{|}_{x=u\,y=v\,z=uv} \\  & =u\cdot v\cdot uv \\  & ={u}^{2}{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}{v}^{2}\sqrt{{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}+1}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186172376 :question/id #uuid "a99cdea7-3ae5-5a3e-abca-eaac3de706cf" :question/math-academy-id "q-160712"} {:db/id 17592186278393 :question/id #uuid \begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}-{u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2u,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}-{u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2v,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -2u & 1 \\ 0 & 2v & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}-2u & 1 \\ 2v & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & -2u \\ 0 & 2v\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-2u,\,0,\,2v⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨-2v,\,0,\,2v⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-2v)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(2v)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+4{v}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(-x-y-z)\,{|}_{x=u\,y={v}^{2}-{u}^{2}\,z=u} \\  & =-u-({v}^{2}-{u}^{2})-u \\  & ={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}-2u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}-{v}^{2}-2u)\sqrt{8}v\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278464 :question/id #uuid "616b2956-33ca-5451-b2d1-058d45da4207" :question/math-academy-id "q-161290"} {:db/id 17592186414460 :question/id #uuid :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=-x-{z}^{2}$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨{u}^{3},\,v,\,{v}^{2}⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{3}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{3}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3{u}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2v\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}3{u}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}3{u}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-6v{u}^{2},\,3{u}^{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨0,\,-6v{u}^{2},\,3{u}^{2}⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+(-6v{u}^{2})^{2}+(3{u}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{v}^{2}{u}^{4}+9{u}^{4}} \\  & =3{u}^{2}\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(-x-{z}^{2})\,{|}_{x={u}^{3}\,y=v\,z={v}^{2}} \\  & =-{u}^{3}-({v}^{2}\cdot {v}^{2}) \\  & =-{u}^{3}-{v}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,3{u}^{2}(-{u}^{3}-{v}^{4})\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+1}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186418479 :question/id #uuid "e6c3f387-d028-56cc-8550-337dfde31023" :question/math-academy-id "q-161135" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186172130 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e5256297-c928-54e3-bf4d-35f5734f5632" :knowledge-point/title "Constructing Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "059c12fe-eab5-50d3-812e-daede28e5fce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(-uv-v)\sqrt{1+4{v}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186418466} {:answer/id #uuid "a69adeb6-2c36-5a75-b29d-f701876ba59a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(-u{v}^{2}+v)\sqrt{1+4{v}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186418471} {:answer/id #uuid "cbbd9a36-5d62-5a45-a0b6-211a1e349cc3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(u{v}^{2}-{v}^{2})\sqrt{1+4{v}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186418473} {:answer/id #uuid "ded9ba33-54e3-5794-92a9-b6db153210e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(-u{v}^{2}-v)\sqrt{1+4{v}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186418474} {:answer/id #uuid "e264331f-dc93-54c6-bb93-c8cd29731c14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(-u{v}^{2}+{v}^{2})\sqrt{1+4{v}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186418475}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "ded9ba33-54e3-5794-92a9-b6db153210e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(-u{v}^{2}-v)\sqrt{1+4{v}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186418474} :answer-field/id #uuid "de80caed-f292-5fbc-ae6d-5bf6abf46eda" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186418477}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$

:question/math-academy-id "e-12346" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186172131 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4b529430-3406-506c-b67d-c067dfee44d5" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces"}] :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
\iint\limits_{S} (x-y)\: \textrm{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x = u+v, \qquad 
y = u-v, \qquad 
z = v
$$

for $0 \leq u \leq 3$ and $0 \leq v \leq 3.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \left\langle u+v, \: u-v, \: v\right\rangle.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,-2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨1,\,-1,\,-2⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+4} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =x-y\,{|}_{x=u+v\,y=u-v\,z=v} \\  & =(u+v)-(u-v) \\  & =2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D = \{ (u,v) \: : \: 0 \leq u \leq 3, \: 0 \leq v \leq 3\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}(x-y)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2v\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{D}\,2v\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}2v\,\text{d}v\cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}1\,\text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{3}\cdot [u]_{0}^{3} \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot 9\cdot 3 \\  & =27\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-2yz\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x=u+v,\,y=u,\,z=v
$$

for $-1\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le 1.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u+v,\,u,\,v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+-{1}^{2}+-{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & ={x}^{2}-2yz\,{|}_{x=u+v\,y=u\,z=v} \\  & =(u+v)^{2}-2uv \\  & ={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D={(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-2yz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}+{v}^{2})\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}({\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+u{v}^{2}]}_{u=-1}^{u=1}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{3}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{[\frac{2}{3}v+\frac{2}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278411 :question/id #uuid "f3da3d1c-88b2-5b2c-b1c5-adc3acc48bde" :question/math-academy-id "q-161180"} {:db/id 17592186278412 :question/id #uuid "c6424aa2-1e21-5507-975b-b73e043b3939" :question/math-academy-id "q-161182" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186172131 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4b529430-3406-506c-b67d-c067dfee44d5" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ebe36cd-b1cf-5ce2-8a67-8db3468807b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}" :db/id 17592186275603} {:answer/id #uuid "18ad7ac0-5137-5083-9463-529f4f7e3804" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186275706} {:answer/id #uuid "4891c5fb-95c8-5c1c-a256-07260e4f9797" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}" :db/id 17592186276121} {:answer/id #uuid "9e1ef9b7-1bf5-5710-8957-97f3d292a525" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186276898} {:answer/id #uuid "c983dee7-7745-56ff-a7b7-c03e844d53b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186277265}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "18ad7ac0-5137-5083-9463-529f4f7e3804" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186275706} :answer-field/id #uuid "92141582-6640-51e0-ab76-f6c1c7dbae93" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186277984}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral

{∬}_{S}6xyz\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by 

$$

$$

 
over the domain $D={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1}.$

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{3}.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{3}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =6xyz\,{|}_{x=u\,y=u+v\,z=v} \\  & =6(u)(u+v)(v) \\  & =6({u}^{2}v+u{v}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,6({u}^{2}v+u{v}^{2})\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}v+u{v}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}({\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{2}v+u{v}^{2})\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{u}^{3}v}{3}+\frac{{u}^{2}{v}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}v \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{v}{3}+\frac{{v}^{2}}{2})\,\text{d}v \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{[\frac{{v}^{2}}{6}+\frac{{v}^{3}}{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6\sqrt{3}(\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278425 :question/id #uuid "80e5707a-3b53-57aa-aa8c-7db876d69b93" :question/math-academy-id "q-161209"} {:db/id 17592186278427 :question/id #uuid "aaa6b101-413b-5c8f-a474-bfd4f4726f2b" :question/math-academy-id "q-161212" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186172131 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4b529430-3406-506c-b67d-c067dfee44d5" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4f7d03c6-d0d9-529a-bce7-fcfcb60d6f23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "42" :db/id 17592186276187} {:answer/id #uuid "6ca921c6-81e9-5022-989e-b96d7ae33f08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "36" :db/id 17592186276453} {:answer/id #uuid "8b30494f-8e6d-5099-9018-d53a7f2a115d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "45" :db/id 17592186276740} {:answer/id #uuid "b4db6155-6904-59b9-b3a7-494630d4b44a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "48" :db/id 17592186277090} {:answer/id #uuid "c41eebb1-ad78-5933-9beb-c7c83212c490" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "50" :db/id 17592186277221}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "b4db6155-6904-59b9-b3a7-494630d4b44a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "48" :db/id 17592186277090} :answer-field/id #uuid "17135030-c131-5443-8329-4345c0e7edd5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186277766}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral

$$

for $0\le u\le 2$ and $0\le v\le 2.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,u+v,\,2v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =2xz\,{|}_{x=u\,y=u+v\,z=2v} \\  & =2u(2v) \\  & =4uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}2xz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,4uv\cdot 3\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{∬}_{D}\,4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =3\cdot [{u}^{2}]_{0}^{2}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =3\cdot 4\cdot 4 \\  & =48.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278442 :question/id #uuid "81e32a26-4f8e-507c-9b65-da0df62a940b" :question/math-academy-id "q-161242" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186172131 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4b529430-3406-506c-b67d-c067dfee44d5" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0bfe6a46-a159-59d8-bee6-18072e5661ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "95" :db/id 17592186275577} {:answer/id #uuid "5d212cf2-6ea0-53a0-9bcc-5ecd7212b036" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "75" :db/id 17592186276306} {:answer/id #uuid "76f545bd-11b2-5ae1-929d-c2f25977a30f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "80" :db/id 17592186276549} {:answer/id #uuid "b08aefb8-1f20-592d-9092-298b802a0a77" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "85" :db/id 17592186277056} {:answer/id #uuid "b1167d7b-282c-533d-bad4-77099f24e2f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "90" :db/id 17592186277062}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "76f545bd-11b2-5ae1-929d-c2f25977a30f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "80" :db/id 17592186276549} :answer-field/id #uuid "e6564796-0979-5996-bb99-982fadfe08ba" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186278126}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral

$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$

for $0\le u\le 2$ and $0\le v\le 2.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2u,\,-3v,\,4v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-3v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(4v)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-3v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(4v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-3,\,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-8,\,-6⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨0,\,-8,\,-6⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+(-8)^{2}+(-6)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+64+36} \\  & =\sqrt{100} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =x(y+z)\,{|}_{x=2u\,y=-3v\,z=4v} \\  & =2u(-3v+4v) \\  & =2uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by 

$$

$$

 
over the domain $D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,-1\le v\le 0\}.$

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=2\sqrt{2}.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=2\sqrt{2}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(3x-2y+3z)\,{|}_{x=2u+v\,y=2u+v\,z=-v} \\  & =3(2u+v)-2(2u+v)+3(-v) \\  & =2(u-v)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2(u-v)\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,(u-v)\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}({\int }_{-1}^{1}u-v\,\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}-vu]}_{-1}^{1}\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(0-2v)\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{[-{v}^{2}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

"4f46c12e-9985-5c0f-879f-f155a81c2351" :topic/math-academy-id 3386} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186173080 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173252 :tutorial/content "Consider the surface integral of the function

$$
f(x,y,z) = x^2+y^2+z^2
$$

 
over the parametric surface $S,$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle u, \: 2v, \: -u \big\rangle, \quad (u,v)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is the unit square in the $uv$-plane given by

$$
D = \{(u,v) \: | \: 0\leq u\leq 1,\: 0\leq v\leq 1\}.
$$

Let's compute the surface integral of $f$ over $S.$

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the surface integral of $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the fundamental vector product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨2,\,0,\,2⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,{|}_{x=u\,y=2v\,z=-u} \\  & ={u}^{2}+(2v)^{2}+(-u)^{2} \\  & ={u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}+{u}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2})\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate this integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+8\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5620ba9b-3795-5fdb-bc39-1699fb66c6b7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7623 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "44c6f181-59d4-55f2-b782-d9635d1f8d52" {:db/id 17592186173256 :tutorial/content "Consider a continuous scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ and a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ defined for $(u,v) \in D,$ where $D\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ 

If our surface is "sufficiently smooth," we can define the **surface integral** of $f$ over $S.$ Let's discuss how we might construct such an integral.

For the sake of simplicity, let's assume that our region $D$ is rectangular. We start by creating a partition $P$ of $D$ in the usual way:

$$
P = \left\{u_0, u_1, \ldots, u_m\right\} \times \left\{v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_n\right\}
$$

Our partition is shown schematically below.

![](images/6a/6a15c7b587503c82a57d0734c5bc5fda990824ad162724236868461cd92e4fbe.png)

 

The area $\delta A = \delta u\delta v$ of the small rectangle highlighted in the diagram corresponds to a particular patch $S_{ij}$ of area $\delta S_{ij}$ on our surface. 

![](images/1a/1a8774b7aa366d3328b6f81cfe7315b7784a1f5783f14c1f19f83a459cef5434.png)

 

Let $P_{ij}^*$ be a point on the surface within the patch $S_{ij}.$ We consider the product 

$$
f(P_{ij}^*) \cdot \delta S_{ij}.
$$

If we compute this product for all patches and add them together, we get the Riemann sum

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n f(P_{ij}^*)\cdot\delta S_{ij}.
$$

Taking the limit as $\delta u, \delta v\to 0$ gives our definition of the surface integral of $f$ over $S,$ which we denote as

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S.
$$

From previous discussions, we know that the area of the small patch can be approximated as follows:

$$
\delta S_{ij} \approx \| \mathbf r'_u \times \mathbf r'_v\|\,\delta u\delta v = \| \mathbf r'_u \times \mathbf r'_v\|\,\delta A
$$

It follows that we can calculate our surface integral using the following formula:

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A
$$

This formula is also valid when $D$ is non-rectangular.

$$
f(x,y,z) = x^2+y^2+z^2
$$

 
over the parametric surface $S,$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle u, \: 2v, \: -u \big\rangle, \quad (u,v)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is the unit square in the $uv$-plane given by

$$
D = \{(u,v) \: | \: 0\leq u\leq 1,\: 0\leq v\leq 1\}.
$$

Let's compute the surface integral of $f$ over $S.$

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the surface integral of $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the fundamental vector product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨2,\,0,\,2⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,{|}_{x=u\,y=2v\,z=-u} \\  & ={u}^{2}+(2v)^{2}+(-u)^{2} \\  & ={u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}+{u}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2})\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate this integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+8\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5620ba9b-3795-5fdb-bc39-1699fb66c6b7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7623 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "44c6f181-59d4-55f2-b782-d9635d1f8d52" :step/math-academy-id 44238 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173081}} {:db/id 17592186173252 :tutorial/content "Consider the surface integral of the function

$$
x=2t+3, \quad y=t^3-4t, \qquad -\infty < t <\infty.
$$

What is the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $t=-1?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=-1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2(-1)+3=1, \\ y & =(-1)^{3}-4(-1)=-1+4=3.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(1,3).$ The plot below shows the curve and the tangent line at this point.

![](images/0f/0fa3fc12e83e2a581499680145df9229917c7426e6a3d12c51d88e115a42033e.png)

To find the slope of the tangent line, we need to find $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
x'(t) = 2, \qquad y'(t) = 3t^2-4 .
$$

So, we have

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)} = \dfrac{3t^2-4}{2}.
$$

At the point where $t=-1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=-1} & =\frac{3(-1)^{2}-4}{2}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $(x_1,y_1) = (1,3)$ and the slope $m=-\dfrac{1}{2}.$ We get

$$
y - 3 = -\frac{1}{2}\left(x-1\right).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050644} {:db/id 17592186083912 :question/id #uuid "b94e72be-f23a-535e-b719-cf664553611b" :question/math-academy-id "q-6857"} {:db/id 17592186083913 :question/id #uuid "![](images/9d/9dcc4c97bd296ef4627b02b6cfafcdb643f475cd8dacd36a820db760bd6fb045.png)

The following parametric equations define the curve shown above:

$$
x=2\cos{t} +\sin{2t},\quad y=\cos{t} - 2\sin{2t},\qquad 0\leq t<2\pi
$$

Calculate the equation of the normal to the curve at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (shown as a dashed line in the plot above)." :question/worked-solution "First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}+1, \\  \\ y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2(1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the normal at the point $\left(\sqrt{2}+1,\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} -2\right).$ For this, we need to find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
x'(t) = -2\sin t + 2\cos 2t, \qquad y'(t) = -\sin t - 4 \cos 2t .
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t+4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},$ the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi /4} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}))} \\  & =-\frac{\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}+4(0)}{2(0-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope $m_n$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
m_n = -\dfrac{1}{m} = -\dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)} = -2
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the normal line, we use the point-slope form 

$$
y - y_1 = m_n(x-x_1),
$$

with

$$
(x_1,y_1) = \left(\sqrt{2}+1,\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} -2\right), \qquad m_n=-2,
$$

and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2) & =-2(x-(\sqrt{2}+1)) \\ y-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+2 & =-2x+2\sqrt{2}+2 \\ y+2x & =\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049119} {:db/id 17592186083545 :question/id #uuid "8def6986-b021-50a6-91db-c2da4068ed38" :question/math-academy-id "q-15558"} {:db/id 17592186083547 :question/id #uuid "cbab7bcf-6a8b-5a33-ae85-61d0acf13fd7" :question/math-academy-id "q-15570" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186083245 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "898e04b8-1b7e-59e7-b03f-3ece54aa093b" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Normal Line to a Parametric Curve"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1129c14f-0c46-52c4-9b9a-b4200ce4b285" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "y=x+1" :db/id 17592186272542} {:answer/id #uuid "5e5faf98-bf15-5a2b-9fdc-09a9a727c6b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "y=x+2" :db/id 17592186273199} {:answer/id #uuid "5f37ca8d-3ea5-5dc1-85e2-3a3270cb4ca0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "y=x" :db/id 17592186273206} {:answer/id #uuid "7e745226-ecb3-5bd0-91a4-532e194cf6a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "y=2x+1" :db/id 17592186273471} {:answer/id #uuid "818af87a-0a7b-5074-95df-e9381f58f773" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "y=2x+3" :db/id 17592186273496}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "1129c14f-0c46-52c4-9b9a-b4200ce4b285" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "y=x+1" :db/id 17592186272542} :answer-field/id #uuid "bb3ec910-ef36-5928-896c-acb859df3e11" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186274961}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,y=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,,\,t\in (0,\pi ).
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ on the curve. Find the equation of the normal to the curve at $C.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})]=\operatorname{ln}⁡1=0, \\ y & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the normal at the point $(0,1).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$  the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi /2} & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,(-1)\,}=1
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(0,1)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =1\cdot (x-0) \\ y & =x+1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186256744 :question/id #uuid "45f7632b-4b69-541a-a152-af5eeab4cd2b" :question/math-academy-id "q-122898"} {:db/id 17592186319376 :question/id #uuid $$
m = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

The tangent line is vertical if $x'(t)=0$ while $y'(t) \neq 0 .$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
x'(t) = 2t, \qquad y'(t) = -1 .
$$

Solving $x'(t) = 0$ gives

$$
2t=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t=0.
$$

the parametric equations 

$$
x=2t^3-1,\quad y=t^2-t+1,\qquad-\infty < t <\infty.
$$

Determine the values of $t$ at which the **normal** to the curve is horizontal." :question/worked-solution "The normal is horizontal if the tangent is vertical. Therefore, we require $x'(t)=0$ while $y'(t) \neq 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=6{t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving $x'(t) = 0$ gives

$$
6t^2 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t = 0.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =2\cdot 0-1=-1\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed horizontal when $t = 0.$"} {:db/id 17592186523091} {:db/id 17592186083612 :question/id #uuid "57cb918d-01c6-5793-92dd-c253fd54156c" So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=7,\,{y}^{′}(t)=6{t}^{2}-18.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
6({t}^{2}-3)=0\,⟹\,t=\pm \sqrt{3}.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(-\sqrt{3}) & =7\ne 0, \\ {x}^{′}(\sqrt{3}) & =7\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed vertical when $t=\pm \sqrt{3}.$"} {:db/id 17592186256752 :question/id #uuid "259b7265-587e-5b30-9b76-d6e0205b048e" :question/math-academy-id $y=f(x),$ we compute the derivative:

$$
m = \dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx} = f'(x)
$$

Likewise, to find the slope $m_n$ of a normal line to a function $y=f(x),$ we take the negative reciprocal of the tangent slope:

$$
m_n = -\dfrac{1}{m} = -\dfrac{1}{f'(x)}
$$

With parametric equations $x=x(t), \, y=y(t),$ it works the same way. The slope of the tangent line is still the derivative of $y$ with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
m = \dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}
$$

Likewise, the slope of the normal line is still given by the negative reciprocal:

$$
m_n = -\dfrac{1}{m} = -\dfrac{x'(t)}{y'(t)}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "48431a98-af5d-5fb6-a9c9-0c0a82d65d84" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1071 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c94cfe31-d0e9-529d-b6dd-34491bfb6e2d" :step/math-academy-id
